Q_EC.text: I told my manager directly that I needed time off after my mother passed — grief was affecting my ability to focus and I wasn't functioning well. They were supportive and helped arrange a leave of absence without much friction. When I came back we checked in regularly for a few weeks, which honestly helped with the transition.

Q_CC.text: I was fairly open with my team about why I was stepping away — I didn't want them to wonder or worry. Most were kind, a few sent notes, and when I returned nobody made it awkward. it felt like they took their cue from how I handled it.

Q_CW.text: One of my direct reports came to me about six months before my own leave — they were dealing with anxiety and weren't sure if they could ask for accommodations. I told them they could, and we worked something out with HR. I think my being open later probably made sense to them in hindsight.

Q_PC.text: At a previous job the culture was different — I didn't really talk about mental health with coworkers there. it wasn't that anyone was hostile, just that nobody did. So there isn't much to describe honestly.

Q_CA.text: Taking leave was visible and I was open about the reason, so yes, I've been "identified" in that sense. I haven't seen it close any doors, though I'm aware other workplaces might read it differently. At my current job it's been pretty much neutral -- if anything, being open seems to have made it easier for others on my team to do the same.

Q_BH.text: At the previous job, there wasn't one incident -- it was more that mental health just wasn't acknowledged as a legitimate thing to bring up. When I was going through a hard stretch I kept it to myself because the unspoken norm was that you pushed through. nobody said anything unkind, but the silence was its own kind of message.

Q_SH.text: My current employer handled it well from the start. When I told my manager I needed leave, they didn't ask me to justify it or push back on the timing — they just asked what I needed and made it happen. HR was straightforward to work with and I was kept in the loop on how my team was being covered. Coming back was the part I was most uncertain about, but my manager set up regular check-ins for the first few weeks and that made the transition feel manageable rather than abrupt.

Q_ID.text: Normalize it the way physical health is normalized -- managers trained to actually have these conversations, not just route everything to HR, and leave policies that don't require employees to justify themselves. honestly, a lot of it comes down to whether leadership models the behavior or just posts a policy on an intranet page nobody reads.

Q_AE.text: I'll note that my experience was shaped a lot by the specific reason for my leave — grief isn't always framed as a mental health issue, but it is one. I think surveys like this would benefit from asking about bereavement explicitly, because people navigating it may not identify with the "mental health" framing even when they're struggling in ways that are very relevant here.

It was a pretty genuine exchange rather than one person just venting at the other.

Q_PE.text: The experience with my previous employer was pretty different -- I was a lot less open back then and mostly tried to manage things on my own. When I did eventually mention the anxiety to my manager at the time, the reaction was polite but fairly surface-level, a quick "let me know if you need anything" that didn't really go anywhere.

Q_PC.text: At my previous job I didn't really talk about it openly -- the culture wasn't quite there, and I wasn't as comfortable being upfront about the anxiety as I am now. A couple of colleagues noticed I seemed stressed at times, but those conversations stayed pretty surface-level, nothing like the mutual exchanges I've had more recently.

Q_CA.text: Honestly, less than I feared it would. Being open about the anxiety has actually built some trust with my team, and I haven't noticed it affecting how I'm evaluated or given opportunities -- at least not in a negative way.

Q_BH.text: The previous employer situation I mentioned -- when I brought up the anxiety and got a polite but hollow "let me know if you need anything." There was no follow-up, no resources offered, it just kind of got left there and we both moved on.

Q_SH.text: The experience with my current manager after the panic attack stands out most. They took time to actually follow up over the next few weeks rather than treating it as a one-time conversation -- checked in, made sure the workload adjustments were helping, and reminded me the EAP was available without making it feel awkward. it felt like genuine care rather than liability management.

Q_ID.text: More consistent follow-through would help a lot -- not just EAP links in an onboarding doc, but actual check-ins built into how teams operate. Normalizing mental health conversations at the manager level seems like the biggest lever, honestly, because it shapes whether people feel safe bringing things up at all.

Q_AE.text: I just want to say that peer connection has been the thing that's helped most -- more than any formal program. When colleagues feel comfortable being mutual about this stuff, it changes the whole dynamic of a team.

Q_SH.text: My manager set aside time for a one-on-one after I mentioned I was struggling. I used the word depression directly and they responded in kind — no deflection, just practical support. that kind of response shows what one's workplace culture is really made of.

Q_ID.text: Normalizing the language is the first step — managers should be trained to hear the word depression without flinching. when one's workplace treats mental health like any other health concern, it removes the barrier to seeking help. that shift in culture is honestly the most important thing.

Q_AE.text: I hope this survey data helps make the case that workplaces can do better. one's experience with depression doesn't have to be isolating — when the culture supports naming it directly, people heal faster and contribute more. that's worth investing in.

Q_EC.text: I brought it up with my manager fairly openly -- burnout, as it pertained to my workload at the time. Their response was genuinely supportive, which honestly surprised me a little. We adjusted some responsibilities and I was pointed toward the EAP resources available.

Q_CW.text: It was the same commute conversation, really -- they opened up about feeling isolated in their role, like the work had started to feel disconnected from any real purpose. Hearing that actually made it easier for me to share what I'd been carrying too.

Q_PC.text: That kind of openness was actually somewhat rare in previous roles -- I'd had a couple of brief exchanges, nothing as substantive as what I've experienced more recently. Q_CA.text: Honestly, less negatively than I feared it might. Being open about burnout with my manager led to adjustments that actually helped me stay and perform better. I think the context mattered -- the right environment makes a real difference in how that kind of disclosure lands.

Q_SH.text: I requested a one-on-one specifically because I'd reached a point where I needed to say something. I was pretty direct about the burnout and how it was affecting my focus, and my manager listened without jumping straight to solutions -- that space made it a lot easier to be honest about the full scope of it.

Q_ID.text: More normalization at the structural level, I think -- not just EAP resources sitting in a benefits doc nobody reads, but managers who are actually trained to have these conversations without it feeling like an HR event. The culture piece matters as much as the policy piece, honestly.

Q_AE.text: I'd just add that the framing of these questions around individual conversations is useful, but the relational and contextual factors -- who you're with, what the culture signals -- probably shape disclosure more than any formal policy does. Q_EC.text: I've had a couple of these conversations at different jobs. At my current place, I told my manager I was in therapy and sometimes needed flexibility around appointments — she was genuinely supportive, helped me adjust my schedule without making it a big deal. A previous job was harder, more of a "just push through it" culture, so honestly the contrast made me appreciate where I am now.

Q_CC.text: A few coworkers and I have actually gotten pretty open with each other about this stuff over time. One colleague mentioned she was seeing a therapist, and I said "yeah, me too" — and that was kind of the start of it. It's become this informal thing where we check in on each other. Not everyone is at that level, but the ones who are have been really grounding, honestly. It helps to know you're not the only one navigating it.

Q_CW.text: It was pretty casual, honestly — she brought it up almost offhandedly during lunch, mentioned she'd been struggling with anxiety and had finally started seeing someone. I think she wasn't sure how I'd react, but once I shared that I was doing the same thing it kind of opened up. She talked about how hard it had been to admit she needed help, especially in a field where everyone's supposed to just be on top of everything.

Q_PE.text: I did try to bring it up once at my old job — kind of vaguely, just mentioned I was dealing with some stress and might need a bit of flexibility. My manager at the time nodded along but then basically said everyone has stress and I should try to manage my time better. Nothing changed. It wasn't hostile exactly, just... dismissive. I left that place not long after, tbh.

Q_PC.text: At my old job I didn't really open up much — the culture wasn't there for it. I mentioned once to a coworker I trusted that I was having a rough time, and she was kind about it, but it kind of stopped there. Nobody else really talked about that stuff, and honestly given how my manager responded when I tried to bring it up, I wasn't gonna push it. I kept a lot more to myself at that place.

Q_CA.text: Honestly, it's been mixed. At my current job I don't think it's hurt me — if anything, being open about it has probably made me a better communicator with my team. But I do carry some wariness from my last place, where I always had the sense that being seen as "struggling" could count against you quietly, even if no one said it outright. I watch for that now.

Q_BH.text: It was the conversation with my previous manager I mentioned — I'd worked up the nerve to say I was struggling and might need some flexibility, and his response was basically to tell me that stress is part of the job and I should look at how I was managing my workload. no acknowledgment, no follow-up. it felt like I'd just handed him something real and he handed it right back.

Q_SH.text: My current manager, honestly. When I told her I was in therapy and sometimes needed to shift my schedule for appointments, she just said "of course, let's figure out how to make that work" and we sorted out a flexible arrangement on the spot. No big deal made of it, no prying questions. She checked in a couple weeks later just to see how things were going — not in a weird way, just genuinely. It made such a difference after my last job.

Q_ID.text: Normalize it the same way we've normalized physical health stuff — like, you wouldn't tell someone to "manage their workload better" if they broke their arm. I think concrete things matter: actual flexibility around appointments, benefits that cover therapy without a ton of hoops, and managers who get trained to not just deflect. And honestly, it starts at the top — if leadership talks about this stuff openly, it gives everyone else permission to do the same.

Q_AE.text: I just want to say that surveys like this feel meaningful to me — it's easy to think mental health at work is a solved problem because the conversation has gotten more visible, but visibility isn't the same as support. I've been lucky to land somewhere good, but I know that's not the norm. I hope the data from this actually gets used to push for something real.

Q_EC.text: Told my manager I was dealing with depression and needed some flexibility on deadlines during a rough patch. She was pretty great about it — we adjusted my sprint load for a few weeks and honestly it made a real difference.

Q_ID.text: More normalization at the team level, honestly — not just top-down wellness programs that nobody uses. Managers actually being trained to have these conversations without making it weird. And maybe treating burnout like a real workload problem instead of a personal resilience issue.

I told my manager I was dealing with some health issues and might need occasional flexibility — I wasn't about to use the words "mental health" and just see what happened. Q_PE.text: I didn't really get into it with any previous employer — it's not something I've ever felt safe enough to bring up. The few times mental health came up at all it was in the context of "stress management" or performance, which just reinforced why I keep it to myself.

Q_PC.text: Honestly, I haven't — not at previous jobs. I didn't have the kind of relationships there where that felt like a reasonable risk. the colleague I mentioned is someone I've stayed in touch with across jobs, so she's kind of the exception. Otherwise I've always kept that side of things pretty separate from work.

Q_CA.text: I haven't been fully identified, which is kind of the point — I've been careful enough that it hasn't become a defining thing at work. But the fear of it affecting my career is pretty real and honestly shapes how I behave. I downplay things, I don't ask for accommodations, I just manage around it quietly.

Q_BH.text: At a previous job I was having a rough stretch and my manager tied it directly to a performance review — basically implied I needed to "manage my stress better," like it was a productivity problem I just wasn't trying hard enough to fix. That framing made it pretty clear that going any deeper would've been a mistake.

Q_SH.text: The one supportive response I can actually point to was that conversation with my colleague -- the one with her own anxiety history. I told her I was having a hard time and she just listened, didn't try to fix it or minimize it. Simple, but honestly that was enough.

Q_ID.text: Decoupling mental health from performance conversations would be a start -- they're too easy to conflate, and that framing just keeps people quiet. More discreet access to support would help too, so you're not flagging yourself to HR just to get resources. Normalizing it without making it a whole thing would honestly go a long way.

Q_AE.text: I guess the thing that doesn't get said enough is that formal policy and actual culture are pretty different things. A company can have all the right resources on paper and still have a floor-level environment where using them feels career-limiting. That gap is where most people like me actually live, and surveys don't always capture it well.

Q_EC.text: When I spoke with my manager about the anxiety I was experiencing, they were genuinely understanding -- more so than I'd expected, honestly. They suggested temporarily adjusting my workload and pointed me toward the employee assistance programme, which I probably wouldn't have found on my own. it helped, though it took a few weeks to notice any real difference.

Q_CC.text: A couple of colleagues knew what was going on -- I'd mentioned it in passing rather than making any kind of formal announcement. Their reactions were kind, if a bit awkward at first; I think people genuinely aren't sure what to say. one coworker checked in on me periodically after that, which I appreciated more than I probably let on at the time.

Q_CW.text: One colleague came to me a while back -- I think in part because they knew I'd been through something similar. They were dealing with burnout, though they didn't use that word exactly. I tried to listen without offering too much advice, which I can't say I always get right. it felt like the right call in that moment.

Q_PE.text: At a previous job the experience was more mixed. I did disclose, mostly because my performance was visibly affected and it felt dishonest not to. My manager at the time was sympathetic in the moment but I'm not sure much actually changed -- there was no follow-up, no adjustment to expectations, and the EAP was mentioned once and never again. it wasn't hostile, just kind of passive, which in a way may have been harder to navigate than outright skepticism would have been.

Q_PC.text: The dynamic at that job was a bit different. I told one person I was close to, more or less out of necessity -- we worked closely enough that they'd noticed something was off. Their response was warm and I don't think they treated me differently afterward, which mattered. the broader team never knew, and I didn't feel a particular pull to change that given how the overall environment felt at the time.

Q_CA.text: Honestly, I can't say it's been straightforwardly harmful -- at my current job, if anything, being open about it may have increased the trust I have with my manager. The previous situation is harder to assess; nothing overtly bad happened, but I did wonder for a while whether I'd been quietly categorised in a way that limited what I was considered for. That's difficult to prove, and I'm genuinely not sure.

Q_BH.text: The previous employer situation is what comes to mind most readily. My manager expressed sympathy in that initial conversation, but when I followed up a few weeks later hoping to discuss adjusting my workload -- even temporarily -- the response was pretty brief. The sense I got was that it had already been "handled." I left feeling more isolated than before I'd spoken up, which I hadn't anticipated. I cant say whether it was deliberate or just a kind of institutional inertia, but it made me considerably more cautious about disclosing in professional contexts afterward.

Q_SH.text: The conversation with my current manager is the clearer example. When I raised it -- I'd been careful about how I framed it, having learned something from before -- the response was immediate and practical rather than just sympathetic. They asked what would actually help, which sounds small but isn't; a lot of people stop at "that sounds hard." We agreed on a temporary reduction in meeting load and a check-in every couple of weeks, which they actually followed through on. I didn't have to remind them or re-raise it. the EAP referral came up again at one of those check-ins, unprompted, which told me they'd been thinking about it. it felt like being treated as a whole person rather than a problem to be noted and filed away.

Q_ID.text: The gap I keep coming back to is follow-through. It's relatively easy for an organisation to list an EAP in an onboarding document; it's considerably harder -- and more meaningful -- to have managers who actually return to those conversations after the initial one. Training focused on active follow-up rather than just acknowledgement would probably do more good than most policy documents I've seen. And honestly, the more mental health is treated as something discussable in ordinary work conversations rather than a formal disclosure event, the more likely people are to raise things early, before they're visibly struggling. The formal structures matter, but so does the everyday language.

Q_AE.text: I suppose the one thing I haven't touched on is how much informal peer networks matter alongside any formal structure. The colleague who checked in on me periodically didn't do so because of any policy -- they just did it, and it made a real difference. i think surveys and organisational frameworks tend to focus upward (managers, HR, EAPs) in a way that undersells how much lateral support shapes day-to-day experience. That's not a criticism of this survey, just something I notice when I think about what actually helped.

Q_EC.text: At my previous employer I disclosed my depression to HR after the bullying situation had gotten bad enough that I couldn't keep ignoring it. The reaction was a referral to an EAP pamphlet and a gentle suggestion to "try to focus on the positives." No follow-up, no structural change, nothing. The more memorable part came later -- I found out my manager had mentioned my therapy to the rest of the team, apparently as context for why I'd been "difficult lately." So the main action taken was, involuntarily, outing me to my colleagues.

Q_CC.text: After the disclosure got back to my team (the involuntary way, not how I would have chosen), a few colleagues reached out privately and were actually kind about it -- said they'd had their own struggles. The people outside my immediate team were genuinely easier to talk to, tbh. Within the team itself there was this awkward awareness that I hadn't chosen to share, which made any subsequent conversations feel a bit loaded.

Q_CW.text: One of the colleagues who reached out after my situation became "known" ended up sharing that they'd been dealing with anxiety for years and had never told anyone at work. it was actually a pretty honest conversation -- they said seeing how badly my disclosure had gone through no choice of my own made them more determined to keep theirs private, which honestly I understood completely.

Q_PE.text: Same situation I described -- at my previous employer, I went to HR after the bullying had gotten bad enough that it was affecting my ability to function. Their response was an EAP pamphlet and advice to "try to focus on the positives." That was it. No investigation into the bullying, no structural anything. The follow-up I did get, I didn't ask for: my manager apparently shared with the team that I'd been in therapy, framed as an explanation for why I'd been "difficult." So the main action taken on my mental health was an accidental privacy breach.

Q_PC.text: After the involuntary disclosure, the reactions within my immediate team were pretty uncomfortable -- there was this sense that everyone knew something I hadn't chosen to tell them, which made normal interactions feel weirdly charged. Outside that team though, a few people were genuinely warm about it. one colleague in particular told me they'd been dealing with something similar for years. The people who responded with any actual empathy were almost exclusively ones who had their own experience with it.

Q_CA.text: Being labelled "difficult" before I'd even had a chance to frame my own situation meant that any subsequent advocacy I did for myself got filtered through that lens. I'm fairly sure it affected how my contributions were evaluated in those last months -- there's no paper trail, but the shift in how I was treated after the disclosure was noticeable. I ended up leaving that job sooner than I'd planned, which is its own kind of career impact. At my current employer it's been more manageable, but I'm a lot more careful now about what I disclose and to whom, which is exhausting in its own right.

Q_BH.text: The HR meeting was prompted by a formal complaint I'd made about bullying -- so the stakes were already high before I even mentioned my depression. When I disclosed it as context for why things had deteriorated, the response was an EAP leaflet and a note in the meeting summary. No action on the bullying itself. Then separately, my manager apparently used my therapy as explanation to the team for my behaviour, which I only found out about secondhand. Neither person involved ever acknowledged it as a problem.

Q_SH.text: The colleagues who reached out privately after the involuntary disclosure were the only genuinely supportive part of the whole thing. A couple of them just... showed up, which sounds small but wasn't. One person in particular said something to the effect of "that should never have happened the way it did" -- no advice, no silver lining, just an acknowledgment that it was wrong. That was honestly more useful than anything the formal process produced. It didn't fix anything structurally, but it made the workplace survivable for the time I stayed.

Q_ID.text: Actual confidentiality enforcement would be a start -- not "we take privacy seriously" in a policy document, but real consequences when a manager casually outs someone to their team. Most of what I've seen is performative: EAP referrals that no one follows up on, mental health awareness months that coexist fine with a bullying culture. The gap between what companies say and what they do when something actually goes wrong is where the damage happens. Training managers to not make things worse would be more useful than another wellness webinar.

Q_AE.text: The thing that probably doesn't come through clearly in individual questions is how much the privacy breach changed my baseline. Before it happened, I was someone who talked about my depression fairly openly -- I'd made a considered choice to not treat it as shameful. After it, I still talk about it, but there's always this background calculation now about what happens if the wrong person hears. That's not a cost I chose; it was imposed. And I don't think most employers understand that bad handling doesn't just affect the immediate situation -- it recalibrates how someone navigates disclosure for years afterward.

Q_EC.text: I disclosed my ADHD diagnosis to my manager about three years into the job. Their initial reaction was cautious -- they weren't sure what to make of it, tbh. I ended up doing a fair bit of explaining: what ADHD looks like in a work context, what kinds of accommodations actually help. eventually we landed on some flexibility around scheduling and carving out blocks of uninterrupted time. It took patience but it felt like a real conversation, not just a checkbox exercise.

Q_CC.text: A couple of coworkers already knew -- one of them has anxiety and we'd talked pretty openly about the overlap between that and ADHD, the focus issues especially. When I told a few others, the reactions were mostly fine, kind of a "oh that makes sense" moment for some of them. I think having already been open about it with my manager made it easier to mention casually, like it wasnt this big reveal. No one made it weird.

Q_CW.text: They came to me after a team meeting where they'd seemed pretty off, and kind of just opened up about the anxiety they'd been dealing with. I think they knew I'd been open about my own stuff so it felt safer. Mostly I just listened -- they weren't looking for advice so much as someone to not make it weird. it meant a lot that they trusted me with it.

Q_PE.text: I didn't really have that kind of conversation with any previous employer -- I wasn't diagnosed until a few years into my current job, so there was nothing to disclose before that. Looking back I can see the signs were there, but I didn't have the language for it yet.

Q_PC.text: With previous jobs, mental health just wasn't something that came up. I didn't have the diagnosis yet, so there was nothing to disclose -- and even if something had felt off, I don't think I would've named it at the time.

Q_CA.text: Honestly, I think it's been more neutral than I expected. There was a period where I worried it might affect how I was perceived -- whether people would second-guess my reliability -- but that didn't really materialise. If anything, being open about it probably helped because I got the accommodations I needed to actually do my job well. I dont think it's held me back.

Q_BH.text: The managers initial reaction wasn't hostile -- more like they just didn't know what to do with the information. There was a stretch where nothing really changed and I kind of felt like the conversation had stalled. I had to be the one to bring it back up and push for something concrete. It wasnt malicious, but it definitely put the burden on me to move things forward.

Q_SH.text: Once things actually moved, my manager was pretty good about following through. They worked with HR to formalize the scheduling flexibility, which I hadn't expected -- I'd braced for more pushback. And they checked in a few times after to see if the adjustments were actually helping rather than just assuming. I think what made it feel supportive was that they treated it like a practical problem to solve together, not a liability to manage. That shift made a real difference.

Q_ID.text: I think the biggest gap is normalization -- not waiting until someone is in crisis to have the conversation. Employers don't need to have all the answers, they just need to be willing to engage without putting the burden entirely on the employee to educate them. having clearer, documented pathways to accommodation would also help a lot, so people aren't just hoping their manager happens to be receptive.

Q_AE.text: I appreciate that this survey exists -- mental health in tech doesn't get talked about as systematically as it should. One thing I didn't have space to say elsewhere: the peer piece has probably mattered as much as anything my employer did. Knowing someone else on the team was dealing with something similar made the whole thing feel less isolating. I think that kind of informal solidarity is real and worth accounting for, even if it's harder to measure than policy.

There's still an expectation that my performance is on par as my coworkers and that I won't use my ADHD as a crutch, but I'm allowed to use coping mechanisms to help me succeed.

Q_EC.text: I told my manager I was burning out, struggling to focus. He listened, or seemed to. Then said I was probably just stressed and should take some time off. Two weeks leave was approved. When I came back, nothing had changed -- same workload, and a new project already assigned to me. Felt like a box-ticking exercise more than any real support.

Q_CC.text: I didn't really open up to coworkers about it. Mentioned I was taking some time off, kept it vague. A couple of people said the usual -- "hope you feel better soon", that kind of thing. Nobody asked questions and I wasnt gonna explain. I think people sensed something was off but didn't push. Probably better that way.

Q_PE.text: Same story, different employer. I told my manager things were getting to me -- the workload, the pressure. Got told it was probably just stress and that everyone goes through it. No real action taken. Eventually I pushed hard enough that they let me take a week off. Came back to the same situation, nothing addressed. It felt like they just wanted me to stop raising it.

Q_PC.text: Kept it pretty vague with coworkers there too. Said I needed some time off, left it at that. A few people were sympathetic -- "take care of yourself", the usual stuff. One person made a comment about everyone being stressed, which wasn't helpful. I wasnt looking for that kind of solidarity. Nobody really followed up when I got back. Just moved on, same as always.

Q_CA.text: Hard to say for certain, but I think it has. After I came back from leave, I was left off a couple of project proposals -- no explanation given. My manager was cordial but distant. I cant prove it was connected, but the timing felt pretty clear. I stopped raising anything after that. You learn pretty quickly that being seen as struggling comes with a cost.

Q_BH.text: Went to my manager, told him I was struggling to function. He didn't ask follow-up questions, didn't suggest resources. Just said it sounded like burnout and recommended time off. Two weeks approved. When I came back the workload was identical -- actually worse, because a new project had been handed to me while I was out. Nothing was addressed. it was a way to close the conversation, not resolve anything.

Q_SH.text: There was one conversation with HR -- not my direct manager. She actually listened without jumping straight to "take some time off." Asked a few questions, pointed me to the EAP. Nothing changed structurally after that, but at least I didn't feel like I was being managed out of the conversation. Low bar, honestly. But compared to everything else it stood out.

Q_ID.text: Stop treating it like a PR exercise. Most companies have an EAP listed somewhere on an intranet page and call it done. Managers need actual training -- not a one-hour workshop, something that changes how they respond when someone says they're struggling. And there has to be some accountability when they handle it badly. Right now there isnt any. You just absorb it and move on.

Q_AE.text: I think the thing that sticks with me is how normal it all felt -- for the company, not for me. My manager wasn't unusually bad. That's kind of the point. This is just how it gets handled most places. The system isn't broken, its working exactly as designed. Just not in anyone's interest except the company's.

Q_CW.text: One of my closer colleagues came to me during a period where I could tell something was off -- they seemed more withdrawn than usual. Q_PE.text: The experience with my previous employer was honestly pretty different from where I am now. I did bring up some stress I was dealing with at the time -- my manager listened, or seemed to, but the follow-up was basically nothing. No mention of any EAP, no workload adjustment. I got a "let us know if things get worse," and that was about it. it wasn't hostile, just kind of hollow.

Q_PC.text: It was a bit more hit or miss compared to where I am now. A couple of colleagues were warm and genuinely checked in on me, but it felt more like individual personality than any kind of shared culture -- there was no equivalent of our current Slack channel or anything like that. Q_CA.text: Honestly, I don't think it has -- at least not negatively. If anything, being open about it at my current company has made me more connected to my team. I've never felt passed over for anything or treated differently in a way that felt punitive. I recognize I'm probably in a better situation than a lot of people in this industry, and I don't take that for granted.

Q_BH.text: That was at my previous job. I'd flagged that I was struggling with stress during a particularly heavy project cycle -- brought it up directly with my manager, which honestly took some nerve. The response in the moment seemed fine, but nothing changed afterward. No EAP referral, no check-in a week later, nothing. It just kind of got absorbed and forgotten, like I'd mentioned something minor about my commute.

Q_SH.text: That was at my current job, during the stretch I mentioned where my performance had taken a dip. My manager took the conversation seriously from the start -- she didn't immediately pivot to performance management or treat it as a problem to be solved quickly. We had a real back-and-forth about what I was dealing with, and she followed up the next day to check in. HR reached out within the week with EAP information, and my workload got adjusted in a way that actually gave me room to recover. Honestly it felt like the system worked the way it's supposed to, which I know isn't everyone's experience.

Q_ID.text: The biggest gap I see is companies treating mental health support as a checkbox -- an EAP link buried in the benefits portal that nobody finds until they're already in crisis. What actually makes a difference is normalization: making it a topic that surfaces in regular team conversations, not just during open enrollment. Managers need real training on how to respond when someone brings something up, not just a hotline number to hand over.

Q_AE.text: I think the survey covered the main bases pretty well. One thing I'd add is that the difference between my previous employer and my current one has been pretty striking -- not just in terms of formal policy but in how mental health shows up in everyday interactions. It's made me realize how much culture matters beyond what's written in the handbook. I feel lucky to be where I am, and I hope more companies move in that direction.

Q_EC.text: I actually went to my manager proactively after a rough patch that had become visible enough I knew I couldn't just wait it out. Told her I had depression and anxiety, which I think genuinely surprised her -- she'd always seen me as upbeat and on top of things, so I think the high-functioning thing had kind of masked it. She was really kind about it, honestly. we talked about flexibility on deadlines during harder weeks, and she started checking in more regularly after that. The thing that surprised me most was that she didn't treat me differently in a bad way after knowing, just... actually listened.

Q_CC.text: There was one coworker I told around the same time -- someone I'd worked closely with on a project and trusted enough to be honest with. Her reaction was kind, but I could tell she was a bit thrown, same as my manager. she said something like "you always seem so together," which I get, but honestly it's a little frustrating to hear, because it sort of implies you have to be visibly falling apart for it to count. I also felt like I needed to apologize for times I'd been quieter or less responsive than usual, which I did -- and that actually felt really important to me, owning the impact even when it wasn't intentional.

Q_CW.text: There was a colleague who came to me maybe six months before my own disclosure -- I think she'd sensed I was a safe person to talk to, or maybe just needed to tell someone. She was dealing with anxiety that had gotten worse during a particularly intense sprint, and she was worried about how it would land if anyone on the team found out. I mostly just listened, tried not to make it weird or clinical. I didn't have the language then that I have now, so I probably wasn't as helpful as I could've been, but I hope it meant something that she felt she could say it out loud to someone at work.

Q_PE.text: At a previous job I did briefly mention that I was going through something, though I was much more vague about it than I've been since -- didn't name depression or anxiety, just said I was having some personal stuff affecting my focus. The response was pretty surface-level, like "let us know if you need anything" and then... nothing. No follow-up, no real conversation. I think they assumed it would just resolve on its own. honestly that experience probably delayed me being more open later, because it kind of confirmed the fear that naming it wouldn't actually change anything.

Q_PC.text: At that job I didn't really tell coworkers directly -- given how surface-level the employer response had been, I wasn't exactly feeling like the environment was safe enough to be specific. There was one person I was friendly with who kind of noticed I was off for a stretch and asked if I was okay, and I said something vague like "yeah just dealing with some stuff outside work." She was warm about it, didn't push, which I appreciated. But I think I was also a little relieved she didn't push, because I wasn't ready. looking back, I wonder if being that guarded cost me some connection I could've had there.

Q_CA.text: Honestly, less than I feared it would. At my current job, my manager knowing has actually made things easier in practical ways -- more flexibility when I need it, less pressure to perform "fine" when I'm not. But there's a background anxiety about it that doesn't fully go away, especially when I think about future jobs or new teams where I'd be starting from zero again. the disclosure question becomes live all over again each time. I think the longer-term career effect has been more internal than external -- I'm more attuned to whether an environment feels psychologically safe early on, and I'll weigh that pretty heavily now when making decisions about where to work.

Q_BH.text: It was at the previous job -- the one where I'd been pretty vague about what I was going through. I think part of what made it badly handled was how ordinary it felt in the moment, like nothing had happened. I said I was struggling, my manager nodded, said the right words, and then we just moved on. No check-in the next week, no acknowledgment in our next one-on-one, nothing. it was handled the way you'd handle someone mentioning a dentist appointment. And because I'd already soft-pedaled it -- didn't say depression, didn't say anxiety -- I felt like I couldn't exactly go back and demand more. The non-response sort of locked me into the vagueness I'd started with. That's the part that stuck with me: the silence wasn't hostile, it was just indifferent, and somehow that was harder to push back against.

Q_SH.text: That was the conversation with my current manager. I'd gone in half-expecting to have to make a case that it was real -- I think I'd internalized this idea that if you seem functional you have to work harder to be believed, especially after the previous job. But she didn't make me do that. she just took it seriously, pretty quickly. We talked through what would actually help -- some flexibility around deadlines during harder weeks, and she started doing brief check-ins that weren't clinical or heavy, just a genuine "how are you really doing this week." the part that's stayed with me is that afterward the dynamic between us didn't shift in some uncomfortable way. She kept treating me like a capable colleague who happened to have told her something real. That was honestly what I'd been most afraid of, and it turned out not to be an issue at all.

Q_ID.text:
The biggest thing, honestly, is training managers to actually follow up. "Let me know if you need anything" is a sentence that means nothing if there's no check-in the next week. My previous employer said the right words and then acted like the conversation had never happened -- and the silence was worse than a bad response would've been, because at least a bad response acknowledges something real occurred.

I also think the industry needs to stop equating "high-functioning" with "fine." the fact that two different people at work expressed surprise that I was struggling because I seemed together -- that's a cultural thing, not just an individual failure. If support only kicks in when someone is visibly falling apart, it's arriving too late for most people.

Q_AE.text:
I guess I mostly just want to say that putting all of this into words -- even in a survey -- has been kind of unexpectedly useful. there's something clarifying about having to articulate it, and I found myself reflecting on things I usually just carry around without examining too closely.

One thing I didn't mention anywhere: having a formal diagnosis actually helped me in ways I didn't anticipate, not because it changed my experience, but because it gave me language to use when I needed to explain something real to someone else. The framing of "this is a thing with a name" made the disclosure conversations easier than they might've been otherwise. I went in less worried about being disbelieved, which I think made a difference in how those conversations landed.

Q_EC.text: The most direct conversation was with my manager in 2019, after I disclosed I was enrolled in a partial hospitalization program for depression. His response was essentially "we all have bad days" and then -- almost immediately -- a pivot to project timelines. No formal accommodation was offered, and honestly, three months later I was placed on a performance improvement plan.

Q_CC.text: I've been open with a few close colleagues over the years -- particularly after returning from the PHP, when the absence was hard to obscure. Reactions were mixed: two people were genuinely kind and checked in periodically. others became visibly uncomfortable and honestly just... reduced contact. That informal drift lasted longer than any formal consequence.

Q_CW.text: A senior engineer came to me around 2017, shortly after I had returned from the PHP. He clearly knew something had happened with me and used it as an opening -- said he'd been struggling with anxiety for months and hadn't told anyone. I mostly listened. I gave him a few referrals, including the EAP, though I warned him honestly that my own experience with it had been underwhelming. He appreciated the candor, I think.

Q_PE.text: The layoff in 2008 was the first time I disclosed to an employer formally. My manager responded with what I can only describe as practiced sympathy -- "we appreciate your honesty, this takes courage" -- and then nothing changed. Six weeks later I was in the first wave of the RIF. I never established a causal link, but honestly, the timing wasn't subtle.

Q_PC.text: At the company where the layoff happened, I was less open — the culture was visibly competitive and I had learned early that any sign of difficulty was risk. One colleague found out indirectly, through the accommodation request I'd filed, and was supportive in a private way. The rest I simply didn't tell. Silence felt safer than the alternative, and honestly, 2008 proved me right.

Q_CA.text: The two clearest data points are the performance improvement plan in 2019 -- initiated within months of my PHP disclosure -- and the 2008 layoff, where disclosing preceded the RIF by six weeks. I can't prove causation in either case. But the pattern across two separate employers is honestly hard to write off as coincidence.

Q_BH.text: The 2019 case is the clearest. I disclosed my PHP enrollment to my direct manager -- his response was essentially "we all have bad days," and the conversation ended there. No accommodation was offered or discussed. Three months later I was placed on a performance improvement plan, with no documented performance concerns predating the disclosure. HR would characterize it differently, I'm sure, but I was there.

Q_SH.text: The clearest example was informal rather than institutional. After I returned from the PHP in 2019, a director on an adjacent team -- someone I'd worked with across two companies -- reached out privately, said she'd noticed the absence, and asked directly if I needed anything. She adjusted a cross-team dependency without requiring explanation. No documentation, no HR loop. Just a practical accommodation made quietly by someone with enough standing to make it.

Q_ID.text: The gap I keep encountering is between stated policy and actual manager behavior. Companies can publish mental health commitments all they want -- if the person your employee discloses to responds with "we all have bad days" and then initiates a PIP three months later, the policy is decoration. Training that has real accountability attached to it, not a checkbox module, would be a start.

Q_AE.text: I've been managing this since approximately 2002 -- over twenty years, across eight or nine employers. I've been through partial hospitalization twice, investigated ECT, and more recently completed a ketamine therapy evaluation. The treatment landscape has genuinely improved. The workplace response to mental illness has not kept pace with it, and that gap is honestly where people get hurt.

Q_EC.text: I brought it up with my manager pretty early on -- let them know I was seeing a therapist and might need occasional flexibility for appointments. they were genuinely supportive, no awkwardness, no probing questions. We agreed on a standing arrangement that's worked well ever since.

Q_CC.text: I've had several of these conversations over the years, and honestly they've all gone pretty well. a few colleagues have opened up to me in return after I mentioned being in therapy, which felt like a real trust moment. the general reaction has been curiosity and relief, not judgment.

Q_CW.text: One colleague came to me after I'd mentioned therapy in a team meeting -- they were clearly nervous at first, but once I just listened without offering unsolicited advice, they really opened up. they said they'd been struggling for months and hadn't told anyone. I helped connect them with our EAP and checked in regularly after that.

Q_PE.text: At my previous employer the culture was a bit more traditional, but I still raised it when I needed an accommodation for therapy appointments. My manager was professional about it -- not warm exactly, but they made it work. Honestly it wasn't as open as where I am now, but I didn't experience any real pushback either.

Q_PC.text: It was a mixed group -- some colleagues were openly curious and supportive, others were a bit more reserved, which I get. a couple of people actually came to me afterward to share their own experiences, which I wasn't expecting. the overall vibe was respectful, even if it wasn't quite as warm as what I've experienced in my current workplace.

Q_CA.text: Honestly, it's been mostly positive -- I think being open about it has made me more approachable as a colleague and advocate. there was a brief moment early on where I wondered if it might affect how I was perceived, but those concerns didn't materialize. If anything, it's added a dimension to my professional reputation that I'm genuinely proud of.

Q_SH.text: The clearest example was with my current manager -- I brought it up in a one-on-one, pretty matter-of-factly, and they responded by asking what I actually needed rather than making assumptions. we landed on a flexible schedule for appointments, and they never made it a thing after that.

Q_ID.text: Training managers to respond to mental health disclosures with practical questions rather than discomfort would make a huge difference -- honestly that single shift changes everything downstream. Normalizing EAP use so it doesnt feel like a crisis-only resource, and building mental health into team culture from onboarding rather than treating it as an HR edge case.

Q_AE.text: I just want to say that the framing of these questions -- treating mental health as a workplace issue, not just a personal one -- is exactly the kind of shift that matters. Surveys like this help make the case that this is a systemic concern, and I hope the data actually reaches decision-makers who can act on it.

Q_PE.text: At my previous job the situation was actually worse — I mentioned once to a team lead that I was going through a difficult period, and the response was mostly silence and then changing the subject. Q_CA.text: Honestly I'm not sure it had big career impact in direct way — nobody has passed me over for promotion openly because of it. Q_EC.text: I requested accommodations through the formal HR process and mostly got silence for months. The real "conversation" happened without my consent -- my VP mentioned my "special needs" to the whole team during a meeting, framing it as context for why I'd been given some schedule flexibility. I hadn't authorized any of that, and I had to sit there and stare at the floor while my colleagues absorbed something I'd shared in confidence. He clearly thought he was helping (which honestly made it worse). A previous employer handled the same situation quietly and without incident, so I know it's possible to do this right.

Q_CC.text: The conversations that followed were ones I didn't choose to have -- they were a consequence of what the VP disclosed. A few colleagues approached me afterward to say something supportive, and I appreciated the intention, but honestly it was mortifying to have to receive their sympathy about something I hadn't decided to share. I mostly deflected and said things were fine. There's a peer support group at work that I've found genuinely helpful, where conversations feel safe and bounded, but that's a different thing entirely from having your private information handed to your team without warning.

Q_CW.text: The peer support group I mentioned has been the main context for that kind of sharing, and I'm careful to think of those conversations as belonging to that space. A colleague there has talked to me about burnout and some anxiety that had gotten pretty severe, and I tried to listen without projecting or giving advice they didn't ask for -- partly because I know what it's like to have someone handle your information badly. I took it seriously and kept it entirely within that context. It's honestly one of the few parts of the current workplace I'd call genuinely functional.

Q_PE.text: The previous employer conversation went through proper channels and stayed there. I disclosed my diagnosis and accommodation needs to HR directly, had one follow-up conversation with my manager about logistics, and that was essentially it -- the adjustments were made without fanfare or announcements. I never had to wonder who knew what. it was handled like any other workplace accommodation, which is honestly all I'd ever wanted.

Q_PC.text: At the previous job, there wasn't really much to describe -- because the information stayed where it was supposed to, I didn't have to navigate those conversations at all. A couple of close colleagues knew in a general way that I'd had some health-related adjustments, and they treated it as unremarkable, which is exactly what I needed. I didn't have to manage anyone's reactions or field questions I wasn't ready for. That absence of drama was, honestly, the whole point.

Q_CA.text: Honestly, it's hard to separate the impact of having mental health conditions from the impact of having them disclosed without my consent. The accommodations themselves were never a career problem -- what created friction was the visibility. After the VP's announcement, I noticed a shift in how some colleagues interacted with me, a kind of careful distance that hadn't been there before. I can't prove anything changed in terms of advancement, but I also can't entirely dismiss the feeling that I'm now seen through a particular lens I didn't choose.

Q_BH.text: The accommodation request that preceded the VP's announcement had been sitting with HR for about three months with no meaningful response -- I'd followed up twice and gotten vague reassurances. So the silence was its own kind of badly handled response, honestly. Then at a department-wide meeting, the VP brought up my schedule adjustments in front of roughly fifteen colleagues, presenting it as a positive accommodation success story without having asked whether I wanted it framed that way or mentioned at all. No warning. I hadn't been given the chance to decline. He seemed genuinely pleased with himself, which left no room for me to express how violated I felt -- doing so would have meant making a scene in front of the same people I now had to work alongside, all of them suddenly knowing something I'd shared in a private HR conversation.

Q_SH.text: The previous employer is the clearest example I have. When I disclosed my diagnosis and accommodation needs, HR handled it with what I can only call appropriate gravity -- they asked what I needed, confirmed what adjustments were being made, and then there was essentially no further mention of it. My manager knew the minimum required to implement the changes and left it there. it didn't feel like a significant event, which was the whole point. The contrast with where I am now is something I find myself thinking about more than I'd like.

Q_ID.text: The most basic thing would be treating accommodation requests as confidential personnel matters rather than team announcements or success stories to share. Beyond that, actually responding to them -- the months of silence I experienced are not unusual, and that gap between request and response is where a lot of damage happens. I think employers tend to focus on having a policy and underestimate how much the execution of that policy is the thing that either builds or destroys trust.

Q_AE.text: I'm not sure there's much the survey didn't touch on, but if anything feels underweighted in my answers, it's probably how much the consent piece matters to me -- not just as a complaint about what happened, but as a design principle. Confidentiality isn't a nicety; it's what makes disclosure possible in the first place. If people can't trust that sharing information with HR stays with HR, they won't share it, and then you end up with a workforce that's struggling invisibly and not asking for what they need. The peer support group at my current workplace exists partly because formal channels have such a poor track record -- people are routing around the system because the system hasn't earned trust. That seems like something worth naming directly.

She didn't minimize it or pivot to productivity concerns — she asked what I actually needed, helped me figure out a schedule adjustment that worked, and followed up a week later to check in. that follow-up is what made it feel real rather than just a polite response in the moment.

Q_ID.text: Normalize the conversation first — and I mean actually normalize it, not just post a wellness policy on the intranet that nobody reads. Leadership modeling vulnerability goes a long way; when a VP talks openly about burnout, it gives everyone else permission. I'd also love to see real investment in peer support structures, because EAPs are underused partly because people are scared of the paper trail. And honestly, manager training is probably the highest-leverage thing — a bad reaction at that level can set someone back years.

Q_AE.text: I just want to say that surveys like this actually matter — it's easy to feel like advocacy happens in big moments, but data collection is part of it too. The fact that someone is trying to measure this stuff gives me hope. And for anyone reading these responses who's on the fence about speaking up at work: it's worth finding even one person you trust. That's usually where it starts.

Q_EC.text: I brought it up during a one-on-one -- told my manager I'd been having anxiety attacks at work. She was pretty understanding about it, and we agreed I could step away when things got bad. HR followed up with some EAP information after that.

Q_CW.text: One coworker came to me after they heard about my situation -- said they'd been dealing with something similar and hadn't told anyone. We talked for maybe twenty minutes. I mostly just listened and pointed them toward the EAP resources HR had sent me.

Q_PE.text: It was a different experience. I mentioned I'd been dealing with anxiety and the manager kind of nodded and moved on -- no follow-up, no resources. nothing was really done about it, which is part of why I made sure to be more direct the next time around.

Q_PC.text: Word got around a bit at that job too -- I was less deliberate about it but people figured it out. the reactions were more mixed than at my current place, a couple people were fine about it but one made a comment about needing to "toughen up." I didn't push back at the time.

Q_CA.text: Honestly, it's been mixed. At my current job I don't think it's held me back -- if anything people seem to trust me more for being upfront about it. the previous job is harder to assess, but I do wonder sometimes if being known for it contributed to me feeling like I had to leave.

Q_BH.text: The situation at my previous job -- the manager who just nodded and moved on. I'd flagged that I was struggling with anxiety, enough that it was affecting my work, and the response was basically nothing. No check-in afterward, no mention of any support options. A coworker made the "toughen up" comment around the same time, which didn't help. It felt like the expectation was just to deal with it quietly.

Q_SH.text: The situation at my current job. When I told my manager about the anxiety attacks, she actually followed up the next day to check in -- didn't just leave it at the initial conversation. The agreement to step away when things got bad was treated as a real accommodation, not something I had to re-justify every time. HR reaching out with EAP info the same week made it feel like there was a system behind it, not just one sympathetic manager.

Q_ID.text: Managers need actual training on how to respond -- not just a policy doc, but knowing what to say and what not to say. And making EAP resources visible before there's a crisis, not just after someone discloses. The "just deal with it" culture is still pretty common and that's the thing that needs to change.

Q_AE.text: Just that the disclosure process felt less scary than I expected it to -- both times, actually, even when the response was bad. Knowing I'd said something was better than not. I think that's underrated in conversations about why people don't come forward.

Q_PC.text: I didn't really talk to coworkers about it at that job -- the whole HR experience made me pretty cautious, so I kept it to myself after that. Q_CA.text: Honestly it's been mixed -- at my current job I don't think it's hurt me at all, if anything being open about it has made me a better collaborator. But at my previous job I do think the HR conversation changed how people saw me, even if nothing was said directly.

Q_BH.text: It was at my previous job -- I'd gone to my direct manager to ask about adjusting my start time a couple days a week for therapy, and instead of just saying yes or no they looped in HR almost immediately. The HR meeting felt like a risk assessment more than a conversation, they ran through resources I already knew about and that was basically it. Nobody checked in afterward, and I got the sense my manager started being a bit more careful around me after that, like I'd disclosed something that made me a liability rather than just a person dealing with something normal.

Q_SH.text: At my current job, honestly it was pretty simple -- I mentioned to my manager that I was in therapy and asked if I could shift my schedule slightly on appointment days, and they just said "of course, let me know what works." No escalation, no HR, no weird energy afterward. They checked in a couple weeks later to see if the arrangement was okay, which I actually wasn't expecting. Q_ID.text: Honestly the biggest thing is normalizing it at the manager level -- a manager who can just say "of course, what do you need" does more than any EAP program. Training managers to respond like humans rather than risk assessors would go a long way.

Q_SH.text: It was during my regular 1-on-1 -- I brought it up myself, mentioned that a breakup was affecting my concentration at work. I think he quietly gave a couple teammates a heads up because a few of them checked in on me over the next week or so. it happened really organically, which honestly made it a lot easier to just accept the support.

Q_ID.text: I think the biggest thing is just normalizing the conversation -- not waiting for someone to hit a wall before offering support. Managers don't need special training to just check in and ask how someone's doing. If my experience showed me anything, it's that small gestures make a real difference. honestly the industry just needs more of that, teams where people actually look out for each other rather than treating work as purely transactional.

Q_AE.text: I guess the main thing I'd add is that my experience was genuinely a positive one, and I'm aware that's not the norm. I've talked to people at other companies who've had really different outcomes when they opened up about personal stuff at work, and it made me realize how much of it comes down to luck -- who your manager is, what the team culture happens to be. I'd love to see that kind of psychological safety be something companies actually build intentionally rather than it just being a happy accident like it was for me.

Q_EC.text: The first time I actually tried to name it directly — during my second burnout, not the first — I told my manager something like "I think I'm in burnout, I need things to slow down." His response was to say the project timeline couldn't change, and did I try meditating. That was honestly the entirety of it. No referral, no workload adjustment, not even real acknowledgment that what I described was serious. I ended up taking sick leave on my own initiative, supported by my doctor, but the organisation itself offered nothing. It confirmed something I'd been circling around for years: workplace burnout gets treated as private failure rather than systemic dysfunction, and that framing protects the institution, not the person in distress.

Q_CC.text:
With coworkers it was completely different, honestly. The first person I told — a developer I'd worked alongside for two years — just said "yes, I can see it, I've been worried about you." That was more than I got from any manager. We ended up talking for a long time, over coffee, about how the environment itself was the problem, not some deficiency in either of us. it was relief and grief at the same time, if that makes sense.

Over time I became, I think, something of a reference point for colleagues going through similar things. People would come to me quietly, often not naming what they were experiencing — just "I'm exhausted, I don't know what's wrong with me" — and I'd gently say, well, here's what happened to me. The reactions were almost always recognition, sometimes tears. What strikes me now is how many of us were carrying the same thing in parallel without knowing it, each thinking we were somehow uniquely fragile. Coworkers gave me what the organisation wouldn't, a kind of lateral solidarity that kept me functional when the structure above was indifferent or actively hostile.

Q_CW.text:
One in particular stays with me. A colleague — a senior developer, someone I'd considered solid and unshakeable — came to my desk one afternoon and said, very quietly, "I think something is wrong with me." Not with the project, not with the team. With him. He'd been waking up at 3am for weeks, he said, unable to stop replaying certain client interactions, convinced he was about to be exposed as incompetent despite fifteen years of demonstrable skill. what he was describing was textbook imposter syndrome compounded by, I suspected, early burnout, but I didn't say that immediately. I just listened.

His reaction when I shared my own experience — the two burnouts, the sick leave — was almost disbelief. Like he'd assumed he was uniquely weak for struggling in an environment that would have ground anyone down. That moment of recognition, when he realised the problem was partly structural and not some private pathology, you could see something physically relax in him. We talked for maybe an hour and a half. I pointed him toward occupational health resources, recommended he speak to his doctor before things escalated further, and we agreed to check in weekly for a while. He did eventually take leave. I think it helped that he had someone who'd already walked through it say: this is real, it is serious, and you are not inventing it.

Q_PE.text:
The first burnout was with a previous client — a large financial services firm, the kind of place where "agile" meant moving fast and never stopping to ask whether what you were building was worth building. When I finally said something to my direct supervisor there, I was more tentative than I later learned to be, I didn't even use the word burnout. I said I was struggling to concentrate, that the pace felt unsustainable, that I was making small errors I normally wouldn't.

His response was essentially administrative. He pointed me to the HR wellness portal — a website, basically — and suggested I use my remaining vacation days. That was it. No conversation, no curiosity about what was actually happening. I remember thinking afterward that he'd handled it the way you'd handle a software incident: log the ticket, assign the standard resolution, close it out.

What made it harder was that I didn't yet have the framework to understand what was happening to me as a systemic thing. I still had enough internalised the idea that struggling meant I wasn't resilient enough, not that the environment was extractive. that first employer, in saying nothing useful, also inadvertently delayed my understanding by probably two years.

Q_PC.text:
At that financial services firm it was harder, for several reasons. The culture there was more guarded — people kept a careful professional distance that I think most of them would have called "staying focused" and I would now call fear. Nobody spoke openly about being exhausted or overwhelmed, even though in retrospect it's obvious many of us were.

There was one colleague, another consultant, who noticed something was off before I said anything. She didn't ask directly — that wasn't the register of that environment — but she started sending me messages saying things like "take your time on this one" or "I've got the client call if you need." It was care expressed entirely through logistics. I found it moving, actually, that she worked within the constraints of the culture to offer what she could without either of us having to name what was happening.

When I did eventually say something more explicit to a second colleague — I said I was "running low," which was as much as I felt safe being — the response was sympathetic but also a little frightened, I think. he said "yeah, I know the feeling," and then changed the subject. Not because he didn't care. I think naming it felt dangerous, like acknowledging it would make it real for both of us. That culture punished visible fragility, and we had both absorbed that lesson without quite realising it.

What strikes me comparing that to later experiences is how much the organisation shapes what coworkers are even able to offer. The solidarity I eventually found came later, in environments where people had more psychological safety — or perhaps just less to lose.

Q_CA.text:
It's complicated, and it's changed over time. In the short term — particularly after the second burnout — I became aware of a certain wariness from some clients, a subtle recalibration of how much they'd rely on me for high-stakes, high-visibility work. Nothing ever said explicitly, that's rarely how it works. But you notice when you stop being invited into certain conversations, when the project scoping starts to include quiet provisions around "availability." That kind of ambient demotion is hard to name and impossible to contest.

What I didn't expect is that it also opened doors, in a different direction. Being someone who'd gone through it and come back — and been willing to talk about it — made me more trustworthy to certain colleagues and, eventually, certain clients who valued that kind of honesty. I've been brought into organisations specifically because someone wanted a consultant who understood psychological sustainability, not just delivery velocity.

So the career effect has been a kind of sorting. I lost some clients and opportunities that, in retrospect, were not places where I would have thrived anyway. And I found a clearer sense of which environments were actually compatible with doing good work without destroying yourself in the process. I dont think I'd undo that, even though the early cost was real.

Q_BH.text:
The one that stays with me most clearly is the second burnout — my current employer at the time, not the financial services firm. I had done everything right, or what I believed was right: I waited until I was certain, I framed it carefully, I didn't catastrophize. I said "I think I am in burnout, I need the pace to change." And my manager — someone I had worked with for over a year, someone who I thought understood the complexity of what we were doing — looked at me and said the project timeline couldn't move, and then asked, genuinely, whether I had tried meditation.

What made it badly handled wasn't the inadequacy of the suggestion, though that was stark enough. It was the speed of it. There was no pause, no "tell me more," no visible recognition that I had just said something that cost me something to say. He moved through the conversation like it was a minor scheduling conflict. I remember watching him and thinking: he is not uncomfortable because he doesn't care, he is uncomfortable because he has no idea what to do and has decided the fastest route through discomfort is to produce an answer, any answer, and close the loop.

The absence of any follow-up in the days after was its own message. He never asked how I was doing. I took sick leave two weeks later, arranged entirely through my doctor, and the organisation's formal response was to email me the HR absence policy. That was the sum of institutional care on offer. it confirmed that burnout, in that environment, was classified as a private medical problem — something happening to me, not something the workplace had participated in creating.

Q_SH.text:
The clearest example, honestly, is the coworker I mentioned — the one who said "I can see it, I've been worried about you." What made it well handled, I think, was that he didn't try to solve it. He didn't reach for a suggestion or a reframe or a wellness resource. He just confirmed that what I was experiencing was visible, was real, and had been concerning someone who knew me. That's an underrated thing to do. In a context where every institutional response had been some version of "here is a portal, now let's move on," simple acknowledgment felt almost radical.

But if I'm looking for something closer to a formal or structural response that worked — there was a period, about a year after the second burnout, when a client organisation I was brought into had actually trained their team leads in psychological first aid. Not deeply, not perfectly, but enough that when I mentioned I was monitoring my load carefully because of a history with burnout, my contact there said "okay, tell me what that means in practice, what should I watch for." she asked what signals to look for. That was a question no manager had ever asked me before.

It changed the texture of the whole engagement. I didn't have to perform invulnerability, which meant I could actually flag early when things were tipping rather than waiting until I was already past the threshold. That's the practical argument for taking this seriously — not just that it's more humane, which it is, but that it produces better work and fewer crises downstream. that client got more from me, not less, because they handled it well.

Q_ID.text:
The first thing is to stop treating wellness as a product — the portal, the meditation app, the ping-pong table. those things exist to discharge the appearance of responsibility without requiring any structural change. What actually helps is simpler and harder: managers trained not to diagnose or advise but to listen and refer; workloads that are honest about what a human being can sustain; and a genuine separation between performance evaluation and mental health disclosure, so people aren't weighing career risk every time they consider saying something true.

At the industry level, I think we need to be honest that burnout is a design outcome, not a personal fragility. if you build organisations that require unsustainable intensity to be considered adequate, you will produce burnout — predictably, repeatedly. The fix is different decisions at the system level, not resilience training for individuals.

Q_AE.text:
One thing that hasn't come up is the temporal dimension — the way these experiences dont end when you leave the situation. I still carry what I'd call residue from the second burnout: certain kinds of client pressure will trigger a physical response, a kind of bracing, that has nothing to do with my current capacity and everything to do with pattern-matching to period that was genuinely damaging. Nobody warned me to expect that. I found out about it by living it, and I think it qualifies as something close to a trauma response, even if nobody in a professional context would call it that.

I also want to name the gender layer, because it shapes everything and surveys like this often don't capture it well. As a crafts·woman in a field that still, in 2024, routinely treats women as less technically credible, the threshold for being taken seriously is already higher. Disclosing vulnerability on top of that is not a neutral act — the calculus is different, and I think any intervention that doesn't account for that will miss a significant portion of the people most at risk. The two things compound each other in ways that are hard to disentangle.

And honestly, I filled this out because I believe the data matters. I've watched too many colleagues leave the industry entirely -- not because they weren't skilled enough, but because the environment made staying too costly. If this research contributes to something that changes that, even marginally, it's worth the time.

Q_EC.label: Describe the conversation you had with your employer about your mental health, including their reactions and what actions were taken to address your mental health issue/questions.
Q_EC.text: Oh my... An open question... First of all, sorry, English is not my main language, so please bare with me. I work in an IT consulting firm and I faced 2 burnouts, clients were to blame every-time because they were looking for code monkeys instead of software crafts·men·women that care a  about quality (the vast majority of my coworkers). My company was supportive, I had the time to put myself back together but no real solution was found (yet) to prevent consultants to be appointed to unhealthy environments. But they are working on it. In France, it's called occupational stress prevention (prévention des risques psychosociaux), many people here fell very uneasy about the term mental health, to be honest, I really don't know what to do to raise awareness about this issue.

Q_CC.label: Describe the conversation with coworkers you had about your mental health including their reactions.
Q_CC.text: It was a mixed bag. We all react differently to oppression (that lead to depression) in the workplace. Some said to me to "man up" some others were compassionate. I described my experiences and detailed the many defence mechanisms I developed over the years to fight against unhealthy behaviours. Oppression, alienation at work, sexism, lack of quality in our craft, lack of empathy, rejected ideas for unfair and political reasons and so on. Politics is everywhere nowadays, I believe that everyone is politically engaged and it's hard to find a common ground that allow us to move forward.

Q_CW.label: Describe the conversation your coworker had with you about their mental health (please do not use names).
Q_CW.text: One of my coworker faced the same issue as me back then, I was alerted by my human resource manager to help him out. I was grateful to be part of that process and I believe I helped him to recover a bit. We discussed about the gap that exist between the corporate culture of the client he was working with and his desire as a software craftsman. I told him that it wasn't his fault, that he was doing what felt right to him, but his arguments was falling on deaf ears, they weren't interested about his expertise, they just wanted a mindless robot that can work tirelessly without asking too much questions. I told him that he was more than competent, that he was not an impostor.

Q_AE.text: Post-traumatic Stress Disorder

They are deeply reflective about workplace dynamics — oppression, alienation, sexism, and political friction — and have developed coping mechanisms while also becoming a peer support figure for colleagues in similar distress.
