persona_portrait.writing_style: Writes in medium-length sentences with an earnest, conversational register that occasionally shifts into philosophical abstraction; distinctive patterns include self-interrupting asides, French cultural references, and gender-inclusive language markers (crafts·men·women) that signal deliberate values-signaling.

Q_EC.text: I talked with my direct manager about some of what I was dealing with -- I didn't lay out the full picture, more like I flagged that I was struggling with anxiety and that certain situations (back-to-back meetings, unexpected last-minute pivots) were harder for me to absorb than they might look from outside. their reaction was genuinely better than I expected, honestly -- no visible discomfort, no awkward pivot to "have you tried just taking a walk?" They asked what would actually help, and we worked out some small adjustments to how my schedule was structured. I think what made it feel safe was that I'd already seen them handle a similar conversation with a colleague with real care, so the trust felt established before I even opened my mouth.

Q_CC.text: It's gone both ways, which I didn't entirely expect. A few colleagues have come to me -- I think partly because I'd been open enough that I became a safe person to approach, which is its own kind of responsibility. when I've shared my own stuff, the reactions have mostly been warm, maybe a little surprised, like they weren't sure what to do with the information but wanted to get it right. One person said something like "I had no idea, you always seem so together," which I took as a compliment even though it also made me think about how much we all mask without meaning to. Honestly those conversations have felt like the most real ones I've had at work -- a little uncomfortable to start, but worth it.

Q_CW.text: One that stays with me -- a colleague pulled me aside after a team retrospective, quietly, and said they'd been having a really hard time and didn't know who else to bring it to. they talked about feeling like they were disappearing inside the job, like the work was consuming everything and they didn't have language for what was happening to them yet. I mostly just listened, which felt like the right call even though part of me wanted to jump in with resources or reassurances. What struck me was how much courage it took for them to start that sentence -- you could hear it. I tried to reflect back what I was hearing without projecting, and I mentioned (carefully, not as a prescription) that I'd found talking to someone outside work helpful for me too. I think they just needed to say it out loud to another person who wasn't going to treat it like a problem to be solved.

Q_PE.text: The experience was pretty different from what I described with my current employer -- which is partly why the contrast feels so stark when I think back on it. I did raise something, fairly tentatively, around burnout and what I now recognize was the early edge of an anxiety spiral. the reaction wasn't hostile, exactly, more like... polite management of an inconvenient conversation. My manager nodded, said something about workload review, and then nothing really changed. What stung more than the inaction was the sense that I'd handed over information about myself and gotten nothing back -- not even acknowledgment that it landed. I think that experience shaped how carefully I approach disclosure now, which is maybe why I pay so much attention to whether the trust actually feels established before I say anything real.

Q_PC.text: Honestly, I was more guarded at that job in general, so the conversations were fewer and shallower by design. I remember mentioning something offhand to a colleague I was friendly with -- framing it lightly, more "I've been a bit overwhelmed lately" than anything specific. they were kind in the moment, sympathetic even, but I noticed the conversation moved on pretty quickly, which I didn't push back on. there was one person I came close to being more honest with, but something in the office culture -- the way people performed competence, I guess -- made me pull back at the last second. It's hard to open up in an environment where vulnerability feels like a liability, even if no one's ever actually said that out loud.

Q_CA.text: Honestly, it's hard to fully separate cause and effect here -- I've been deliberate enough about *how* and *when* I disclosed that I don't think I've ever been fully "identified" in the way the question implies, like someone found out without me choosing to tell them. at my current job, being known as someone who's navigated this stuff has actually built a kind of quiet credibility, especially with colleagues who come to me with their own things. That feels like a net positive, though I'm aware that's not everyone's experience. At my previous job, I sometimes wonder whether raising it at all left a mark on how I was perceived -- I'll never really know, and I've mostly made peace with that uncertainty. I think the calculus has always been: disclose intentionally, in the right relationship, and you keep more control over the narrative than you might expect.

Q_BH.text: It was the one I mentioned with my previous employer -- I'd flagged burnout and some early anxiety symptoms, fairly carefully, because I wasn't sure how it would land. The conversation itself wasn't aggressive or dismissive in any obvious way, which is almost what made it worse. my manager listened, said the right approximate things, mentioned something about checking in on workload -- and then just... didn't. No follow-up, no acknowledgment in the next one-on-one that it had even happened. The thing that felt badly handled wasn't the moment itself, it was the silence after it, the way the conversation seemed to get quietly filed away as something mildly awkward rather than something real. I left that interaction with less trust than I'd gone in with, which I don't think was the intended outcome -- but it was definitely the actual one

Q_SH.text: The conversation with my current manager is the one that comes to mind -- the one I described earlier, where I flagged the anxiety and the specific situations that made things harder. what made it land differently wasn't just that they were kind, it was that they were actually curious. they asked follow-up questions, not in a clinical way but in a "help me understand what that actually looks like for you" way, and I could feel them sitting with what I was telling them rather than already planning their response. The adjustments we made were small -- some buffer time between meetings, a bit more lead time on pivots -- but the gesture behind them mattered as much as the logistics. And honestly what's stayed with me is that they checked in a few weeks later, unprompted, just to ask how things were going. That's such a simple thing but it's also not nothing -- it said that the conversation hadn't been quietly filed away somewhere, that it was still alive for them too. I think that's what a well-handled response actually looks like: not a perfect speech or a formal accommodation plan, just genuine follow-through that treats you like a whole person rather than a situation that got managed.

Q_ID.text: The thing I keep coming back to is that most of what actually helped me wasn't a program or a policy -- it was a manager who knew how to respond when I said something real. So I think a lot of the infrastructure stuff (EAPs, mental health days, workshops) is genuinely worth having, but it only lands if the people in positions of power have actually been taught how to receive a disclosure without flinching or immediately problem-solving their way out of the discomfort. that's a skill, and it's teachable, and I don't think we invest in it nearly enough. Beyond that, I think normalizing mental health as a topic in ordinary work conversations -- not in a forced "wellness check-in" kind of way, but in the way psychological safety actually gets built, through leaders being willing to be a little vulnerable first -- would do more than most formal initiatives. the culture has to come before the policy, or the policy just becomes a checkbox.

Q_AE.text: The one thing I don't think the questions quite captured is what it's like to occupy that informal-support role -- being the colleague others come to. it's meaningful, and I don't resent it. But it also carries weight I've had to learn to manage: figuring out where my capacity ends and where I need to redirect someone toward actual professional support rather than just absorbing what they're carrying. I'm not a therapist, and there's a version of being "the safe person" that can blur that line without anyone meaning it to. I've gotten better at holding that boundary, but it took me longer than I'd expected to even recognize it as something I needed to hold

Q_EC.label: Describe the conversation you had with your employer about your mental health, including their reactions and what actions were taken to address your mental health issue/questions.
Q_EC.text: I have openly discussed my struggles with anxiety and complex PTSD with my team, including my supervisor. I didn't do this until I knew that I was in a welcoming, supportive environment and my boss, who is the owner of the company, sets the tone himself by being a supportive, open person when it comes to those things like taking time to go to therapy or do other things that help them with mental health like meditate, exercise, or engage in other therapeutic activities (i.e. reiki, drawing, photography classes). People at my company talk openly about going to therapy ("I'm leaving at 5:00 today to go to therapy" or "I talked with my therapist about being more open to public speaking and that's something we're working on") and there isn't any consequence to leaving for those kind of appointments

Q_CC.label: Describe the conversation with coworkers you had about your mental health including their reactions.
Q_CC.text: I've talked with my coworkers about my mental health on more than one occasion. I try to be intentional and considerate when I have those conversations because it puts some emotional burden on them to hear it and because it is always a risk, even in a supportive environment. Has to be the right person at the right time and sometimes I worry I overshare. But my anxiety symptoms are evident in my work and I think it helps others to know I am self-aware and am working on those issues. I think my coworkers have always been supportive and understanding.

Q_CW.label: Describe the conversation your coworker had with you about their mental health (please do not use names).
Q_CW.text: I had a coworker share with my their struggles with anxiety via Slack. This was after hours and we were the only ones in the office.  I felt very honored that this person would share this info with me. I do not know if this person shared this info with me because I had been open with them first or if they have shared this info with others. Oh, also since I speak openly about therapy, other employees have privately asked me - often via slack, how to find a therapist or how our mental health benefits work.  (My therapist doesn't take insurance, so...)

Q_PC.label: Describe the conversation you had with your previous coworkers about your mental health including their reactions.
Q_PC.text: It was a long time ago, but I had a coworker that I became close with after some time working together and we had casual conversations about mental health -- esp about therapy, therapists, things that work, things that didn't work.

Q_AE.text: Probably the biggest thing the survey doesn't capture is how much the manager lottery matters. You can work somewhere with good policies on paper but if your direct manager isn't on board, none of it reaches you.

Q_EC.text: When my partner died, I told my manager I needed some flexibility — reduced hours for a few weeks and the option to work from home. The reaction was sympathetic but pretty vague. No formal accommodation came through; HR sent a generic EAP email and that was about it. I ended up handling most of it on my own.

Q_CC.text: A few coworkers already knew I was in treatment for depression before my partner died, so when I told them what had happened there was less explaining to do. The reactions were more genuine than what I got from management — people checked in, covered for me during meetings without being asked, and one colleague mentioned he'd gone through something similar a couple years back. That kind of normalization makes a real difference. It's honestly easier to talk about this stuff peer-to-peer than through any official channel.

Q_CW.text: The colleague I mentioned -- the one who'd been through a loss a couple years before mine -- brought it up pretty matter-of-factly. He said he'd dealt with depression for a while and had taken some time off, and that the hardest part wasn't the grief itself but feeling like he had to perform normality at work before he was ready. He wasn't asking for anything specific, I think he just wanted me to know I wasn't the only one who'd managed this kind of thing while staying in the job. That conversation stuck with me more than most.

Q_PE.text: At a previous job, maybe five or six years ago, I disclosed that I was being treated for depression after a performance review flagged some inconsistencies in my output. My manager at the time was uncomfortable — not hostile, just clearly unsure what to do with the information. He said he appreciated me telling him and then mostly didn't bring it up again. There was no accommodation conversation, no HR involvement that I could see. things just went back to normal on the surface, which I suppose was the best I expected at the time.

Q_PC.text: At that same job, I was more cautious about what I said to coworkers — the manager's reaction had made it clear the culture wasn't exactly open. I mentioned it to one person I trusted, someone I'd worked closely with for a couple of years, and she was decent about it, sympathetic without making it a whole thing. But I kept it contained after that. It wasn't a place where you'd want that kind of information circulating too widely.

Q_CA.text: Honestly, the effects have been subtle rather than dramatic. At that previous job I noticed my visibility shifted after the disclosure -- fewer project assignments for a while, though I can't say definitively that was causal rather than just coincidence. Here it's been more neutral, maybe slightly positive in terms of the trust I've built with close colleagues. no dramatic career consequences either way, which I suppose is about the best outcome you can realistically hope for.

Q_BH.text: The one that stands out is the response after my partner died. I made a pretty direct ask -- reduced hours for a few weeks, work-from-home flexibility -- and what came back was an EAP referral email from HR. No follow-up conversation, no one asking what accommodation would actually look like in practice. I had to piece it together on my own, which I managed, but the whole thing felt like the request had been quietly filed away rather than taken seriously. it wasn't hostile, just absent.

Q_SH.text: The clearest example is actually the peer stuff I described — the colleague who told me about his own time off, the coworkers who covered meetings without being asked. None of that was formal or structured, but it was responsive in a way the institutional response wasn't. if I had to point to one moment, it's probably that conversation with my colleague. He didn't offer solutions or escalate anything, he just made it clear that staying in the job while managing this was something people had done and survived. that was genuinely useful to hear.

Q_ID.text: The gap I keep coming back to is the difference between having a policy and having a culture. Most companies have EAP programs; almost nobody uses them because they feel clinical and disconnected from actual work relationships. What would help more is managers being trained to have real accommodation conversations — not "here's the hotline number," but "what does your workload need to look like for the next month." Peer-level normalization does a lot of the heavy lifting informally, but that shouldn't be the only safety net people have.

Q_AE.text: One thing that doesn't fit neatly into survey questions: managing depression isn't a resolved state, it's an ongoing one. I think surveys like this tend to capture discrete events -- a disclosure, a conversation, a response -- but the day-to-day reality is more about maintenance and calibration than incidents. The accommodations I've needed over the years have shifted as the job changed and as I've gotten better at knowing what I actually require versus what I think I should be able to handle. I don't know how you'd measure that, but it feels relevant to any honest picture of mental health at work.

Q_EC.label: Describe the conversation you had with your employer about your mental health, including their reactions and what actions were taken to address your mental health issue/questions.
Q_EC.text: I told my direct supervisor (the CTO) that I would be out for therapy appointments every two weeks for approximately three months. I told him so that he wouldn't think I was interviewing. He was supportive and told me to do what I needed.

Q_PE.label: Describe the conversation you had with your previous employer about your mental health, including their reactions and actions taken to address your mental health issue/questions.
Q_PE.text: After my boyfriend died, I had to discuss accommodations I would need to return to work while dealing with difficulty concentrating, flashbacks of time in the hospital, and stress level. They seemed uncomfortable but were accommodating and said I could do whatever was needed. They were very good about allowing me time off after his death, up to a point. Then hints were made that I should be returning to work (about 2 weeks after he entered the hospital, 1 week after his death). I returned to work 1 1/2 weeks after his death. I was definitely not ready, but didn't know how to broach the topic.

After my boyfriend died, I asked my co-workers to meet me to work at a coffee shop for a half day, so I could ease back into working. They all agreed and were very generous and accommodating.

Q_SH.text: At my current company it was pretty straightforward -- I flagged burnout to my manager, they took it seriously, and we worked out a temporary workload reduction. HR followed up with the EAP referral. no drama, just a practical response.

Q_ID.text: More proactive awareness rather than reactive responses. Having EAP resources actually promoted throughout the year, not just during onboarding, would help. managers being trained to recognize burnout signs early -- that probably makes the biggest difference.

Q_AE.text: Normalizing mental health conversations at the team level matters as much as having formal programs in place -- I've found that mentoring relationships are often where people actually open up, not HR channels.

Q_EC.text: I raised concerns about secondary trauma and emotional exhaustion with my supervisor, framing it in the clinical terms we both understood. Her response was pretty receptive -- she treated it as a structural occupational hazard rather than a personal failing, and we agreed on a temporarily modified caseload alongside additional supervision

Q_CC.text: Several colleagues and I talked fairly regularly about secondary trauma, projection, and the cumulative weight of emotionally demanding caseloads. Those conversations were unusually candid by most workplace standards -- I think partly because we had a shared professional vocabulary that made it easier to name what we were experiencing without it feeling like a purely personal disclosure.

Q_CW.text: One colleague came to me after a particularly difficult period with a client family and disclosed that they'd been experiencing intrusive thoughts and disrupted sleep -- what they described sounded like a subclinical stress response, honestly. I tried to listen without immediately pathologizing it, and gently suggested they bring it up in supervision rather than managing it alone.

Q_PE.text: At a previous role in a more corporate-adjacent healthcare organization, I raised concerns about unsustainable workload and early burnout symptoms with my line manager. The response was polite but fairly surface-level -- he acknowledged it briefly and suggested I use the EAP, which felt like the conversation was being redirected rather than actually engaged with. No structural changes followed.

Q_PC.text: The culture there was noticeably different — colleagues were generally sympathetic but less equipped with the kind of shared vocabulary I was used to. A few conversations touched on stress and workload, but they tended to stay at the surface level, more commiseration than genuine reflection. Honestly, it reinforced how much professional context shapes what people feel safe naming.

Q_CA.text: Within my primary clinical setting, the effect was minimal — openness about occupational stress was professionally normalized and didn't carry the stigma I'd expect elsewhere. in the earlier corporate-adjacent role, I sensed a subtle shift in how I was perceived after disclosing burnout symptoms, nothing overt, but I noticed being passed over for a high-visibility project shortly after.

Q_BH.text: The conversation I described with my line manager at the corporate-adjacent organization -- the one where I raised burnout concerns and was pointed toward the EAP. what made it feel badly handled wasn't hostility, it was the speed of the redirect. He nodded, said the right words, and moved on within about two minutes. The EAP referral functioned as a closure mechanism rather than an opening, and nothing about my workload or working conditions changed afterwards.

Q_SH.text: The experience with my supervisor in the clinical setting stands out clearly. what made it feel genuinely well handled was that she didn't treat my disclosure as a problem to be routed to HR or a checklist to complete -- she engaged with the substance of what I was describing. we talked for close to forty minutes, she asked follow-up questions that showed she understood the occupational dynamics involved, and the outcome was a concrete, if temporary, adjustment to my caseload.

Q_ID.text: The most meaningful shift would be moving away from referral-based responses — EAP links, hotline numbers — toward structural changes: normalized supervision practices, reasonable caseloads, and managers who are trained to engage rather than redirect. Honestly, the EAP model often functions as a liability buffer more than actual support, and the industry could do better than that.

Q_AE.text: I'd note that the survey's framing assumes a fairly standard tech industry context, which didn't map cleanly onto my experience in a clinical mental health setting. The occupational hazards there -- secondary trauma, projection, compassion fatigue -- are real but distinct from what most tech workers face, and I'm not sure the questions fully captured that dimension.

Q_EC.text: When I disclosed -- after an attendance issue made it basically unavoidable -- the response was pretty dismissive. No referral to HR, no follow-up, just a vague suggestion to "try to manage it better," which honestly felt less like a conversation and more like someone closing a tab they didn't want open

Q_CC.text: It was a pretty different experience from the employer side of things -- a couple of close colleagues knew about the ADHD and depression, and those conversations felt genuinely mutual, like they were sharing back rather than just receiving information and moving on. one of them had their own stuff going on, so there was this real reciprocity to it that made it feel safe rather than risky.

Q_CW.text: It came up pretty naturally, actually -- we'd already been talking about my situation, and at some point it shifted into them sharing that they were dealing with anxiety and had been for a while (maybe longer than they'd admitted to themselves, was how they put it). There wasn't a formal moment of disclosure so much as a gradual opening up, which I think made it easier for both of us.

Q_PE.text: The previous employer was actually where things got worse in some ways -- the injury made attendance unpredictable for a stretch, and when I tried to explain what was going on (the physical stuff compounding the ADHD and depression, which I'd had longer), the response was mostly impatience. I got the sense they were more concerned about coverage than about what I was actually dealing with. Nothing was offered, no adjustments, no signposting to any kind of support -- it just kind of sat there unaddressed until I left.

Q_PC.text: I didn't talk to many people there, tbh -- the environment didn't really feel like one where that kind of conversation was welcome. There was one person I was closer to, and I did mention some of what was going on when the absences started becoming obvious, but their reaction was mostly sympathetic in a surface way, like they felt bad without quite knowing what to do with it. it wasn't cold exactly, just kind of... limited, I guess, in a way that matched the overall culture of the place.

Q_CA.text: It's hard to fully separate out what's attributable to being identified versus what was already in motion -- the injury affected things regardless, and the ADHD and depression had their own trajectory. That said, I do think there's a version of my career path that looks different if I hadn't had to disclose under pressure at that previous job. The impatience I encountered there left me more cautious about transparency going forward, which has its own costs -- you spend energy managing perception rather than just doing the work. At my current place it's been less of an active issue, but I'm still more guarded than I probably would be in an ideal world.

Q_BH.text: The circumstances at the previous job were probably the clearest case -- it came up because the injury had made my absences visible and I couldn't really avoid explaining, so disclosure happened under practical pressure rather than by choice. When I tried to give some context (the physical recovery layered on top of conditions I'd been managing for years), the conversation was short and fairly transactional. There was no follow-up, no mention of any occupational health process or adjustments, and the overall message I took away was that the disruption to scheduling was the actual concern -- not what was causing it. The absence of any support structure became obvious in that moment, and I think what made it feel badly handled wasn't any single thing that was said so much as what wasn't offered at all.

Q_SH.text: The most genuinely well-handled responses came from peers rather than any formal structure -- the colleagues I mentioned earlier, where disclosure felt mutual rather than one-directional. What made it work, I think, was that there was no performance of concern; they responded like the information was normal and continued treating me like a full person rather than someone to be managed carefully from a distance. One of them in particular checked in without making it a whole thing, which is harder than it sounds. At my current employer it's been handled more by omission than active support -- nobody has made it worse, which I'm aware is a low bar, but after the previous experience it registered as meaningful.

Q_ID.text: Honestly the biggest gap, in my experience, is the absence of any proactive structure -- not just an EAP buried in onboarding docs, but managers with actual training so that disclosure doesn't have to become a scheduling problem before anyone takes it seriously.

Q_AE.text: I'd just add that the physical health and mental health intersection felt pretty underprepared for in every workplace context I've been in -- there's a reasonable amount of awareness (at least nominally) around mental health as a category, but when the two compound each other, the systems don't really know what to do with that. My situation wasn't unusual in that sense, I don't think, and it might be worth asking about more directly in future versions of this survey.

Q_EC.text: I told my manager I had been experiencing suicidal ideation. The response was compassionate, honestly, but I perceived a subtle wariness afterward — a carefulness in how they spoke to me that hadn't been there before the conversation.

Q_CC.text: A few colleagues found out, I think through my manager. They were kind initially, but as I recall there was that same subtle shift — a carefulness, a slight pulling back that hadn't been there before.

Q_CW.text: A colleague came to me, as I recall, somewhat hesitantly, and disclosed they were struggling with anxiety. I tried to respond with the warmth I'd wished for myself -- though honestly I'm not sure I fully succeeded.

Q_PE.text: At a previous role I disclosed I was struggling — not the full extent, as I recall, just that I was dealing with something serious. The response was polite but fairly perfunctory; I don't think they quite knew what to do with that information.

Q_PC.text: At that previous role, the colleagues who knew were largely supportive on the surface, but I perceived the same pattern -- a warmth that coexisted with a kind of social distance that hadn't been there before. it was subtle, but noticeable.

Q_CA.text: I don't think it affected my formal career trajectory in any measurable way — no lost opportunities I can point to directly. But I perceived a shift in how I was regarded, a kind of quiet recalibration in people's expectations of me, that I suspect has shaped things in ways that are harder to quantify.

Q_BH.text: The previous employer, I think, was the clearer case. When I disclosed I was struggling, the response was a kind of managed politeness — HR was notified, a pamphlet was produced, and the conversation was effectively closed. it felt like containment rather than support.

Q_SH.text: My current manager's response was the better one, I think. There was a genuine pause — they asked questions rather than reaching for a procedure. They checked in with me over the following weeks, which, as I recall, made a real difference at the time.

Q_ID.text: More genuine engagement and less procedural response, I think. Employers could start by training managers to actually sit with discomfort rather than reach for a pamphlet -- the difference between being heard and being managed is something employees notice. And honestly, normalising disclosure without the subtle social recalibration that tends to follow it is probably the harder, more important work.

Q_AE.text: The social shift that followed disclosure -- that quiet wariness -- was, honestly, harder to navigate than the original crisis in some ways. It has no formal name and no HR process to address it, and I think that's worth naming.

Q_EC.text: My manager was genuinely great about it. I came to her during a particularly rough stretch with anxiety and she didn't immediately jump into problem-solving mode -- she actually listened first, which I appreciated more than I expected. We talked about adjusting my workload temporarily and she made clear that I had full control over how I wanted to handle it, whether that meant leaning out of some responsibilities for a bit or just having more flexibility in my schedule. She checked in periodically without making it feel like surveillance, and honestly the whole conversation made me feel like I wasn't gonna be penalized for being human.

Q_CC.text: There was one coworker in particular who I'd gotten closer with over the past year, and at some point it came out that we were both dealing with similar things -- anxiety, the pressure of always appearing "on," that kind of thing. It felt less like a formal conversation and more like we just kind of stumbled into honesty with each other, which was actually really nice. She mentioned she'd started therapy and I told her I had too, and from there it became something we'd check in about occasionally without it being a big deal. I think having that one person at work who gets it makes a real difference -- you dont have to translate the experience for them.

Q_CW.text: It kind of unfolded gradually rather than being one single conversation. We'd been working closely together and I think we'd both picked up on little signals -- the occasional "ugh, today is a lot" comment, the moments where you could tell someone was stretched thin. At some point she opened up about some of the anxiety she'd been managing, and I think what made it feel safe was that I'd already hinted at my own stuff. it wasn't a dramatic disclosure, more like the honesty just crept in naturally over a few weeks. She was really thoughtful about it -- she wasn't looking for me to fix anything, just to be heard, and I tried to show up that way for her the same way she did for me.

Q_PE.text: Honestly it was a pretty different experience with my previous employer, and I think that contrast is part of why I appreciated my current manager so much. I did try to raise it once -- I was going through a stressful period and mentioned to my then-manager that I was struggling with anxiety and it was affecting my focus. The reaction wasn't hostile exactly, more like... politely acknowledged and then sort of shelved. He said something like "yeah that's tough, let me know if you need anything" and that was basically it. No follow-up, no real adjustment, just a kind of performative openness that didn't lead anywhere. I didn't bring it up again after that -- it felt clear the door was technically open but not actually welcoming. looking back, I think I learned from that experience what *not* to do when someone comes to you, which is maybe the silver lining.

Q_PC.text: At my previous job I was a lot more guarded generally, so I didn't really have the kind of open conversations there that I've had more recently. I remember venting to a couple of colleagues about stress in a pretty surface-level way -- the "ugh, this sprint is killing me" kind of thing -- but nothing that got into actual mental health territory. Part of that was just the culture; it didn't feel like a place where that kind of honesty was particularly safe or encouraged, and I think people could sense that. there was one person I was friendly with who I think was struggling too, but we never quite got there with each other. I don't regret it exactly, more like I understand now what was missing -- we were all just kind of quietly managing on our own.

Q_CA.text: Honestly, I've been pretty fortunate in that it hasn't derailed anything in any obvious way -- at least not at my current job, where the conversation went well and I don't think it changed how I'm perceived professionally. If anything, I think being open about it helped me perform better because I wasn't burning energy trying to mask it. The previous job is harder to assess; I never disclosed fully there, so I can't really say. I do think about whether being known as someone who "has anxiety" could limit opportunities in more subtle ways -- the kinds of assumptions people make without realizing -- but I haven't experienced that directly, or at least not in ways I could point to definitively.

Q_BH.text: The previous employer situation I mentioned -- that's the clearest example I have. I'd waited until I felt like things were genuinely affecting my work before saying anything, so it took real effort to bring up. When I finally told my manager I was dealing with anxiety, the response was just so... surface-level. Sympathetic enough in tone, but you could tell there was no follow-up plan, no thought about what support might actually look like. the "let me know if you need anything" framing puts all the labor back on the person who just made themselves vulnerable, which is kind of the opposite of supportive. I never did bring it up again, and honestly I think that silence communicated a lot about where the real limits were.

Q_SH.text: My current manager, honestly. I've described the broad strokes already but what made it feel genuinely well-handled was the specificity of her response -- it wasn't just warmth in the abstract, it was actual concrete adjustments. She helped me temporarily step back from a project I was leading so I could stabilize without feeling like I was failing at something visible, and she framed it as a normal thing managers do, not a special accommodation I should feel grateful for. That reframing mattered more than I expected. she also followed up a few weeks later not to check whether I was "fixed" but just to see how things were going in a low-stakes way, like she was checking in on a colleague, not monitoring a liability. I think what made it land was that she never made it weird -- and honestly that's a higher bar than it sounds.

Q_ID.text: The biggest thing I'd want to see is a shift away from "we have an EAP" as the end of the conversation. Access to resources matters, but what actually moved the needle for me was a manager who knew how to respond in the moment -- and that's a skill that has to be taught, not assumed. I think companies should invest in training managers specifically on how to receive a disclosure without either over-reacting or doing the polite-but-useless thing my previous employer did. Beyond that, normalizing therapy and mental health care the same way we normalize going to the doctor would help -- it sounds small but the framing companies use in benefits communications, all-hands talks, that stuff shapes whether people feel safe bringing it up at all. the culture is the policy, really, and you cant just write your way out of a bad one with a wellness stipend.

My current manager probably didn't realize how much that conversation meant, or how much it changed my baseline assumption about whether work could be a place where you're allowed to be a full person. I've thought about that a lot since, especially when I'm in positions where someone else might be looking to me for that same thing. therapy helped me enormously with the anxiety itself, but the workplace piece felt like a separate problem that therapy alone couldn't solve -- you kind of need both, the internal work and the external environment actually meeting you halfway. I guess what I'd want whoever reads this to know is that the good outcomes are possible, they're just not evenly distributed, and that inequality is the part worth fixing.

It wasn't a dramatic confrontation, which in some ways made it harder -- there was nothing to push back against. it just got absorbed and forgotten.

Q_SH.text: My current manager. I came to him in a pretty bad state -- I'd just been hospitalized and told him what had happened. He didn't panic or get weird about it. He said something like "okay, let's figure out what you need" and then actually followed through -- moved deadlines, told me to take the time I needed, checked in every week or so without making it feel like surveillance. He treated it like a work problem we could solve together rather than a personal failing I needed to hide. That made a real difference.

Q_ID.text: More open acknowledgment that mental health is a real workplace issue, not just a personal problem people need to sort out on their own. Concrete flexibility -- adjusted hours, low-drama leave options -- without employees having to justify themselves extensively. And managers trained to actually respond when someone brings something up, not just say "everyone has hard days" and move on. Q_EC.text: I brought it up with my manager during a one-on-one when I was going through a rough patch with depression. she was really supportive -- no awkwardness, just practical. We adjusted my workload for a few weeks and I was encouraged to use our EAP.

Q_CC.text: It's come up naturally a few times, honestly. A couple of colleagues have dealt with similar stuff and we kind of just... look out for each other. No one made it weird. I think the culture here makes it easier for everyone to be open about that kind of thing.

Q_CW.text: One of my colleagues came to me after a team meeting -- they'd been struggling with anxiety and weren't sure if they should say anything to our manager. I just listened mostly, shared a bit of my own experience so they knew they weren't alone. They seemed relieved to have someone to talk to.

Q_PE.text: My previous workplace was a different story. I mentioned burnout once and got a pretty generic "make sure you're taking your breaks" response -- nothing concrete. It wasn't hostile, just kind of... dismissive. Honestly it made me appreciate how much culture actually matters.

Q_PC.text: It was pretty surface-level tbh. A few people were sympathetic when I seemed stressed, but no one really went deeper than "hope you feel better soon." I dont think anyone knew how to, and the culture there just didn't really encourage that kind of openness.

Q_CA.text: Honestly, not negatively -- at least not where I am now. Being open about depression has actually made me more approachable to colleagues who are going through something. I think it's helped me build trust with my team. earlier workplaces might've been a different story though.

Q_BH.text: It was at my previous job -- I'd mentioned to my manager that I was really struggling, not just tired but genuinely burning out. The response was basically a shrug and "everyone's busy right now." No follow-up, no check-in after. It just kind of got dropped, which honestly felt worse than saying nothing at all.

Q_SH.text: My current manager handled it really well. When I brought up my depression during that one-on-one, she didn't make it a big deal in a bad way -- she just took it seriously and moved on to problem-solving. we talked about what would actually help and made a real plan together. That kind of response makes all the difference.

Q_ID.text: More normalisation, honestly -- not just policies on paper but actual cultural shifts where people see their managers talking openly about mental health too. Training for managers would go a long way, because a lot of them just dont know how to respond. And making EAP resources genuinely easy to access, not buried in an HR portal no one checks.

Q_AE.text: I just want to say that surveys like this actually matter -- it helps to know someone's paying attention to this stuff. The tech industry has made real progress but there's still a gap between companies that have good policies and ones that have good culture. Those aren't always the same thing.

The conversation was concerning a coworker's trip to the therapist, and so we all began to pitch in with our own experiences with varying levels of counseling/therapy.

They have personal experience with depression and are comfortable sharing it in appropriate contexts, joining conversations naturally rather than initiating them. persona_portrait.writing_style: Sentences are moderate in length, conversational, and informal without being careless. Vocabulary is plain but precise, with a tendency toward inclusive framing ('we all', 'everyone') that reflects a collaborative orientation.

Q_EC.text: The conversation with my manager was more productive than I'd expected — she was genuinely receptive once I framed things in terms of output and workload rather than diagnosis. I disclosed that I was managing ADHD and depression, and that certain structural patterns, last-minute deadline shifts especially, were making it harder to function well. we agreed on clearer advance notice for deliverables and a standing biweekly check-in, which honestly has helped more than I anticipated

Q_CC.text: The dynamic with coworkers has been more reciprocal than I'd expected — a few colleagues came to me after word got around that I'd been open about my own experience, be it through the grapevine or a more direct conversation. Those exchanges tend to be the most meaningful ones, insofar as they rarely stay just about me; once someone knows you wont flinch at the topic, it opens a door. reactions have ranged from relief to surprising candor, and I'm genuinely glad that nothing has ever felt dismissive or uncomfortable.

Q_CW.text: It tends to start small — a comment about not sleeping, or an offhand remark about feeling like they're falling apart. One colleague in particular approached me after a rough sprint, and what began as venting about deadlines shifted pretty quickly into something more substantive; they were describing what sounded like severe anxiety, maybe burnout, and they hadn't said any of it out loud before. I mostly just listened and reflected back what I was hearing, which seemed to be what they needed. I did eventually share some of what I'd navigated myself, insofar as it felt relevant and might normalize the idea of seeking actual support — and they did, eventually, which I'm glad about.

Q_PE.text: The experience with my previous employer was considerably less straightforward — I disclosed primarily because my performance had started to visibly suffer, and the conversation felt more like damage control than genuine dialogue. my manager wasn't unkind, exactly, but the response was procedural in a way that foreclosed anything deeper: HR was looped in, I was pointed toward the EAP, and that was more or less the extent of it. the implicit message, insofar as I could read it, was that this was a private matter to be resolved off the clock — which I understand, even if it wasn't the kind of support that actually moves things forward.

Q_PC.text: The context at that job made those conversations harder to navigate — there was a culture of professionalism that read, at least to me, as a kind of agreed-upon silence around anything personal. a couple of colleagues were warm in a quiet way, checking in without pressing, which I appreciated more than I could say at the time. but I don't think I was as open as I've since learned to be; the institutional response had already signaled what the norms were, and I took the cue.

Q_CA.text: The effects have been genuinely mixed — in my current role, being open has, if anything, strengthened certain working relationships and made me more effective as an informal resource for colleagues. at previous jobs, there was a reputational caution I sensed after disclosing, nothing I could point to directly, but a subtle shift in how certain conversations included me. I've made a kind of peace with that, insofar as staying silent has its own costs.

Q_BH.text: The circumstances at my previous employer were, in retrospect, shaped as much by timing as by intent — I disclosed during a performance review, which meant the conversation was already framed around deficiency rather than support. the HR process that followed felt like it was designed to manage liability rather than address what I was actually going through; nobody followed up after the EAP referral, and when I tried to revisit the conversation a few weeks later, my manager made clear, gently but unmistakably, that she considered the matter resolved. what made it badly handled wasn't malice — it was the absence of any genuine curiosity about whether the intervention had actually helped.

Q_SH.text: The contrast with my current employer is pretty stark, honestly — what made it work, I think, was that my manager treated the conversation as ongoing rather than closed. she didn't just note what I'd shared and move on; she followed up at the next check-in, asked whether the adjustments we'd agreed on were actually helping, and adjusted again when one of them wasn't. there was no sense that disclosure had created a file somewhere with my name on it, which I realize sounds like a low bar but isn't, in my experience. what I carry from that conversation is less about any single accommodation and more about the feeling that I was being seen as someone navigating something, rather than as a liability being managed.

Q_ID.text: The most meaningful shift would be structural rather than programmatic — less emphasis on EAP referrals as a closing gesture, and more on building the kind of ongoing, low-stakes dialogue that makes disclosure feel safe before a crisis. managers need actual training, not just policy awareness; insofar as most of the conversations I've seen go well, it's because an individual happened to be thoughtful, not because the institution prepared them for it. I think the industry undersells how much normalisation at the team level matters — which isn't expensive, just intentional.

Q_AE.text: I suppose the thing I'd want to add is something about the cumulative weight of being an informal resource — which I don't say to complain, because it's work I find genuinely meaningful. but there's a version of this where the people who are most open about mental health end up absorbing a disproportionate amount of their team's emotional labor, and that can become its own kind of drain if there's no reciprocal structure supporting them. I've been lucky in that my current manager has noticed and named it, which helped. I think surveys like this one are useful insofar as they surface the shape of the problem — I hope the data is put to good use.

Q_EC.text: I told my manager I was struggling with anxiety -- it was really hard to get the words out. they let me to adjust my hours a bit, which helped I guess. it was a hard conversation but I think they actually cared

Q_CC.text: I haven't really talked to coworkers about it, not directly. I mentioned once that I was going through something and it kind of just... went nowhere. they moved on fast. that part is still hard to think about honestly

Q_CW.text: someone did open up to me once, briefly. they said they were really stressed and not doing okay. I didn't really know what to say, I just listened. I hope that was enough but honestly I'm still not sure it was

Q_PE.text: I didn't really have this kind of conversation with any previous employer. it wasn't something I felt safe bringing up back then, tbh. the place I'm at now is different but before... I wouldn't have even tried

Q_PC.text: I never talked to coworkers at previous jobs about it either. the culture was just... you keep things to yourself. I saw what happened to people who seemed too open about struggles and it didn't look good for them

Q_CA.text: I don't think it's directly affected my job, at least nothing I can point to yet. but socially... that already cost something. I'm kind of always wondering now how people see me, and that's pretty exhausting to carry around

Q_BH.text: the coworker thing I mentioned -- I said I was going through something difficult and they just kind of nodded and changed subject. no follow up, nothing. I know people dont always know what to say but it felt like I didn't exist for a moment

Q_EC.text: I told my manager directly that I was burning out -- the back pain had gotten bad enough that I was working from bed some days and I said that outright. his reaction was basically "we're all stressed, just push through" and then nothing changed. No reduced workload, no acknowledgment, just more of the same dysfunction, and honestly I ended up quitting because staying was making me physically sick.

Q_CC.text: A couple of coworkers noticed before I said anything, which honestly meant a lot -- one of them pulled me aside and asked if I was okay and I just kind of unloaded on her about the management situation and the back pain and how I couldn't sleep. She was really sympathetic and said she'd seen it happen to others there too, which was validating but also depressing because it meant the place had a pattern. Another coworker was supportive in the moment but then kind of backed away after, like he didn't know what to do with it, and I get that. nobody really knew how to fix anything because the problems were structural.

Q_CW.text: One of my coworkers -- actually the same one who'd been sympathetic when I vented -- came to me a few weeks later and told me she was struggling too, same kind of thing, the management chaos and feeling like nothing she did mattered. She was pretty matter-of-fact about it, said she'd been having anxiety attacks and was thinking about leaving, and I remember thinking it was almost a relief that someone else was naming it that clearly. I told her she should talk to someone outside work, like a therapist, because that's what I was doing and it helped, even if it didn't fix the actual job. She ended up leaving a couple months after I did and I think that says everything about what the place was like.

Q_PE.text: At a previous job I'd gone through a pretty rough patch with depression and eventually told my manager I was struggling and needed to adjust my hours temporarily. she was sympathetic in the meeting -- said all the right things about the company caring about people -- but then when I actually tried to flex my schedule I got pushback from HR about coverage and it never really happened. The conversation felt good and then nothing materially changed, which was its own kind of demoralizing. I was already in therapy at the time so at least I had somewhere to process it, but the gap between what they said they valued and what they actually did was hard to ignore.

Q_PC.text: At that previous job the conversations were a little more mixed. I mentioned to one coworker that I was dealing with depression and she was genuinely kind about it -- said she'd gone through something similar and we talked pretty openly for a while about how draining the job was. But a few others kind of went quiet when I brought anything up, not hostile exactly, just visibly uncomfortable, like they didn't want to be pulled into it. I dont think it was malicious, more like nobody had any vocabulary for it and the culture definitely didn't encourage that kind of openness. so you had these isolated pockets of real support surrounded by a lot of just... awkward silence.

Q_CA.text: Honestly it's hard to separate "being identified" from just having struggled, because I was never officially labeled anything -- I disclosed informally, not through any formal accommodation process, so there's no HR file somewhere that says "mental health issue." but I do think it changed how some people saw me. At the job where I burned out, once I'd told my manager I was struggling I noticed I got pulled off a high-visibility project pretty soon after, and I don't know if that was coincidence but it felt connected. And there's this background awareness you carry that if you're too honest, you might get managed out or passed over for things, so even when I've been open I've also had to calculate how open is too open. It hasn't derailed my career exactly, but it's added this extra layer of self-monitoring that I resent having to do.

Q_BH.text: The one that still bothers me most is the burnout conversation -- I came to my manager when the back pain was genuinely debilitating, I was working from bed, I told him that directly and named it as a burnout problem connected to the workload and the constant management chaos. And his response was basically to shrug and say everyone was under pressure right now. No follow-up, no checking in later, no offer to look at what I was carrying. just a door closing. I think what made it badly handled wasn't even the dismissal itself -- it was the complete absence of any curiosity about what was actually happening. he didn't ask what I needed, didn't loop in HR, didn't do anything. I ended up leaving a few months later and I'm pretty sure nobody connected my departure to that conversation, which tells you how little it registered for them.

Q_SH.text: The coworker who pulled me aside -- the one I mentioned who noticed before I even said anything -- that was probably the most well-handled response I got, and it came from a peer, not management, which I think says a lot. She didn't make it weird or clinical, she just asked if I was okay and then actually listened when I said I wasn't. no advice, no "have you tried meditation," just someone sitting with the reality of what I was describing. And the fact that she named what she'd seen in others there, confirmed it wasn't just me being fragile -- that mattered more than I expected. I also think about my therapist at the time as the thing that genuinely worked, but that's outside the workplace entirely. honestly the bar for "well handled" in every job I've had has been pretty low, and a coworker just being present and not flinching clears it by a mile.

Q_ID.text: Stop treating it as a wellness perk problem and start treating it as a management accountability problem. Every job I've been at had an EAP number on a poster and a Slack channel for mindfulness tips, and none of that touches the actual dysfunction. what would help is training managers to actually respond when someone raises something -- not with a script but with real follow-up -- and creating conditions where disclosing doesn't quietly tank your standing. the gap between stated values and actual behavior is where people get hurt, and closing that gap means holding managers responsible when they ignore it.

Q_AE.text: I just want to say that the framing of these questions -- employer conversations, coworker conversations, policy suggestions -- can make it sound like mental health at work is primarily a communication problem, and I think that undersells how structural it is. In my case the burnout wasn't because nobody talked to me nicely enough, it was because the organization was genuinely dysfunctional and no amount of supportive conversation was going to change that. I quit, I got better, and I've been careful since then about where I take jobs. But not everyone has the option to just leave, and I think surveys like this sometimes inadvertently center the people who did okay -- who have a narrative arc, who got help, who recovered -- and undercount the people who are still in those environments right now with no good options. I dont know if that's something you can address in the survey design but it's something I think about.

The stress was all related to incompetent management and political games that prevented me from moving to a better team within the organization. When I discussed issues with managers and requested moving to another team, they refused. After numerous conversations with HR I finally got a new manager but this did not resolve other incompetencies with management and the business strategy. I was told I could ask a dr for a note to use my sick time to recover. I was not given the option to take medical leave or short term disability for the back pain that was so severe I couldn’t stand up straight one day, and had to go home early several times. Eventually the back pain got bad enough I decided to quit the job and be unemployed rather than continue to suffer.

Q_CA.text: Honestly, I think it's made things worse in some ways. After raising it with my manager, I noticed I was being included even less in certain conversations — like I'd somehow confirmed I wasn't fully reliable. It's hard to prove that's why, but the timing felt pretty telling.

Q_BH.text: It was pretty situational — I'd just been left out of a planning meeting I should have been in, and I finally said something. My manager listened, nodded, said they'd "keep an eye on things." And that was it. No follow-up, no change, nothing. If anything the exclusion got quieter and more deliberate after that, like raising it had made things more awkward rather than better.

Q_SH.text: The coworker I mentioned — that's honestly the only time anything felt genuinely well handled. It wasn't a formal conversation or a structured check-in, just a moment where I said something real and they didn't flinch or redirect. They just sat with it, and that made a bigger difference than I expected it to.

Q_ID.text: More transparency in how decisions get made, honestly. When people feel like they're operating in the dark — not included in conversations that affect their work — that's its own kind of stressor that formal EAP programs don't really touch. I think employers could do a lot more to make sure people actually feel heard, not just processed through the right HR channels and then forgotten about.

Q_AE.text: I think the survey covers a lot, but one thing that doesn't quite fit into any single question is how cumulative this kind of thing is. It's not one bad conversation or one missed meeting — it's the pattern of it, over time, that wears you down. And the fact that the only real support I've found has been informal, peer-to-peer stuff says something about where the gaps actually are.

Q_PE.text: A previous job was a very different experience. I disclosed because I needed time off for a hospitalization and couldn't really hide it, and my manager at the time got kind of weird and distant after that -- never outright hostile but I could feel the shift. HR technically "accommodated" me by letting me use sick leave but there wasn't any real support, no check-ins, nothing. I ended up leaving that job within a year, tbh I think the environment made it harder to recover not easier.

Q_PC.text: Most of them didn't really know the details, just that I'd been out for a while. A couple were friendly enough but nobody really reached out the way my current coworkers did -- it was more like everyone just pretended nothing had happened. one person actually made a comment about me "taking a vacation" which stung more than I think they realized. The culture there just wasn't one where people talked about that stuff openly.

Q_CA.text: At my current job it honestly hasn't hurt me, if anything I think being open made my relationship with my manager stronger. But at the previous place I do think it affected how I was perceived -- I wasn't passed over for anything officially but I noticed I stopped being included in certain conversations and projects kind of dried up. hard to prove but it felt real.

Q_BH.text: It was at a previous job -- I had to disclose because I was being hospitalized and needed emergency leave, so there wasn't really a way to keep it vague. I told my manager directly, explained it was a mental health crisis, and I could see his whole demeanor change in real time. he didn't say anything unkind outright but he got very formal and clipped where before we'd had a pretty decent working relationship. HR processed the leave fine technically but when I came back there was no conversation, no "how are you doing", just here's your desk and here's your workload back. And then slowly over the next few months I just started getting left out of things -- fewer meeting invites, projects reassigned without explanation. Nobody ever said it was connected but the timing was pretty hard to ignore. I think what made it worst was the silence, like everyone had decided to just act like it hadn't happened, which honestly felt worse than if someone had said something uncomfortable.

Q_SH.text: That was my current job. I came back from medical leave and told my manager what had actually happened -- the suicide attempt, the hospitalization -- and I remember bracing for that same clipped formality I'd gotten before. instead he just kind of paused and said "I'm really glad you're still here" and I honestly wasn't prepared for that. We talked for probably an hour, he didn't rush it, and by the end we'd worked out a plan -- reduced hours for a few weeks, no client-facing stuff until I felt ready, a check-in every Friday just to see how I was doing. HR was looped in and they handled everything practically without making me feel like a liability. what really made it feel different was that people kept treating me like a person and not like a problem to be managed. the Friday check-ins kept going for months, not because anything was wrong but just because he'd made it a habit, and I think that consistency is what made me feel safe enough to actually recover while still working.

Q_ID.text: Honestly I think the biggest thing is just normalizing the conversation before a crisis happens -- like don't wait until someone is in a hospital to figure out how to respond. Training managers to actually be human about it rather than just defaulting to HR protocol would make a huge difference, because in my experience the formal stuff matters way less than whether the person across from you treats you like a person. And the culture thing is slow but it starts with leadership not flinching when mental health comes up.

Q_AE.text: I just want to say that filling this out has been kind of unexpectedly emotional -- in a good way mostly, because it made me realize how far I've come. I have PTSD and depression on top of everything else and for a long time I really didn't think I'd be able to hold down a job in this industry, so the fact that I found a place where I could be honest and still be treated as a professional feels significant. I also think surveys like this matter, like actually collecting this data and taking it seriously is part of how the culture shifts. So thank you for doing it.

Q_EC.text: I broke down on my second day, which honestly wasn't the introduction to the job I'd planned. I told my manager what was going on and they were genuinely understanding about it -- they arranged for me to work remotely while I got back on my feet, which made a real difference.

Q_CC.text: There was one colleague who knew what I was going through, and they were kind about it. At some point they opened up about their own experiences too, which felt like a kind of mutual understanding -- honestly that mattered just as much as the formal accommodation.

Q_CW.text: They came to me fairly quietly, not making a big deal of it. They shared that they'd been struggling for a while and hadn't told many people. I just listened, mostly -- I didn't have much advice to offer, but I think that was fine. It felt like they mostly needed someone to hear them without judgment.

Q_CA.text: It hasn't, as far as I can tell. My employer handled things well and I don't think it changed how I was perceived professionally -- or if it did, I never felt it. I count myself fairly lucky in that respect.

Q_SH.text: It was early enough that I hadn't really settled in yet, so I think my manager saw it as a situation that needed practical handling rather than anything to be concerned about long-term. They suggested remote work almost immediately -- no lengthy discussion, just a straightforward offer. that made it easier to focus on getting stable without feeling like my job was at risk.

Q_ID.text: More open conversations at the leadership level would help -- when managers actually model that mental health matters, it changes the whole tone. Practically, flexible working arrangements made a real difference for me, and I think making those available without requiring someone to hit a crisis point first would go a long way.

Q_AE.text: I think what stands out for me, looking back, is how much the timing mattered. Getting that support early -- before things got worse -- meant I could recover without it becoming a longer-term issue. I got lucky with my employer, and I'm aware not everyone does. I hope that changes.

Q_CC.text: I didn't really bring it up directly with coworkers. A couple of people noticed I seemed off and asked if I was okay -- I gave fairly vague answers, said it was a busy period. After how the conversation with my manager went, I wasn't inclined to say more to anyone else at the company.

Q_CW.text: A colleague pulled me aside once and mentioned they'd been having a hard time — burnout, mostly, and some anxiety around a project deadline. I listened and said I understood. I didn't share my own situation. I wasn't sure it would help them to know the company's track record on this kind of thing.

Q_PE.text: I haven't had this kind of conversation with a previous employer. The experience at my current job was enough to make me fairly guarded about disclosure in general, so it's not something I've pursued elsewhere.

Q_PC.text: It didn't really come up. I've generally kept that kind of thing to myself, and previous jobs were no different. The pattern's been to keep things professional and not bring personal struggles into the workplace.

Q_CA.text: I'm not sure how widely that conversation traveled, but I've been passed over for a couple of opportunities since then. Hard to say definitively that's the cause. I'm more careful now about what I raise at work — which probably affects how I show up day to day.

Q_BH.text: I raised it during a one-on-one. I'd been dealing with a family member's illness on top of a heavy workload, and I said I was finding it hard to manage. My manager's response was essentially to suggest the job might not be the right fit. No resources offered, no check-in afterward. That was it.

Q_ID.text: Clearer pathways to support would help — EAP programs that are actually communicated, not just listed in an onboarding packet. Managers need real training on how to respond when someone discloses, because "maybe this job isn't for you" shouldn't be a standard reaction. It shuts people down and probably keeps a lot of issues from ever surfacing.

Q_AE.text: The survey covers the main points. I'll just say that the gap between what companies list as resources and what actually happens when someone discloses is significant. A policy on paper doesn't mean much if managers aren't equipped — or willing — to respond constructively.

Q_SH.text: With regard to the well-handled moment, it was my previous manager who, after I raised anxiety concerns, took the time to actually follow up the next week -- they checked in without making it feel like a performance review, and we landed on a practical adjustment that stuck.

Q_ID.text: Normalising mental health conversations at the team level would go a long way -- honestly, the biggest shift I've seen comes from managers who check in consistently, not just when something goes wrong.

Q_AE.text: The aspect that feels most underrepresented in this survey is how much peer-to-peer support matters -- honestly, formal programs are great, but the culture shift I've seen comes from colleagues who just make it normal to ask "how are you actually doing?"

Q_EC.text: I brought it up with my manager during a one-on-one when things were getting pretty bad. They were sympathetic -- genuinely, I think -- but didn't really know what to do with it. They mentioned the EAP, which I was already using. So it felt like they cared but weren't really equipped to go further than that.

Q_CC.text: A few coworkers have been genuinely great about it, honestly more than I expected from a workplace. One time I had to step away after kind of hyperventilating at my desk and a colleague just came and sat with me -- didn't make it weird, didn't push. Others I've talked to more directly have been open about their own stuff too, which made it feel a lot less isolating.

Q_CW.text: One of my closer colleagues opened up to me about burnout and some ongoing anxiety, kind of out of nowhere during a lunch break. I think they'd been holding it for a while. I tried to just listen without jumping to solutions -- which honestly isn't always my instinct -- and they seemed to appreciate that. We checked in more after that, which felt good.

Q_PE.text: At a previous job I did bring it up, though less directly than I have more recently. My manager at the time was polite about it but pretty clearly uncomfortable -- the conversation kind of fizzled out and nothing concrete came from it. No mention of resources, no follow-up. it was one of those things that made me realize how much the culture around this stuff varies between workplaces.

Q_PC.text: At that job the dynamic with coworkers was more guarded overall. I mentioned to one person that I'd been dealing with anxiety and they were kind about it in the moment, but it kind of ended there -- no real follow-up, no reciprocal sharing. It wasn't cold exactly, just... not the same openness I've found elsewhere.

Q_CA.text: Honestly, I don't think it's hurt me in any concrete way I can point to -- no passed-over promotions I can definitively link to it. But there's a low-level awareness that some managers aren't entirely comfortable with it, and I do think about that sometimes when deciding how much to share in a new role.

Q_BH.text: It was at the previous job I mentioned -- I'd flagged that I was struggling with anxiety and the conversation just kind of died. My manager nodded, said something vague like "we all have stress," and that was it. No resources mentioned, no check-in afterward. it felt like I'd said something mildly embarrassing that everyone wanted to move past quickly.

Q_SH.text: The situation I described with my coworker coming to sit with me after I had to step away from my desk -- that's the one that stands out most. They didn't make a big deal of it, didn't ask a bunch of questions, just stayed nearby for a bit until I felt steadier. Later they checked in again, casually, which meant a lot. It's that kind of low-key, no-pressure support that I think actually works.

Q_ID.text: Training managers to actually handle these conversations would go a long way -- not just pointing people to an EAP and calling it done. And honestly, fostering a culture where peers feel okay checking in on each other matters just as much, maybe more, than any formal policy.

Q_AE.text: I just want to say that the peer-level stuff really doesn't get enough attention in these conversations. Formal policies matter, but what's actually gotten me through harder periods at work has been individual people showing up -- sometimes without even knowing that's what they were doing. that's worth studying too, I think.
