Q_CW.text: I'm not sure this one really applies to me in the same way, because I was so focused on managing my own situation at the time that I wasn't really in a position to be the person someone else came to, and I don't think any of my coworkers felt comfortable enough to bring something that personal to me either, or at least none of them did during that period. there was one person who seemed like they were going through something difficult and made a few comments that in hindsight were probably more than just venting, but they never actually said anything directly to me about it and I didn't push because I wasn't sure it was my place and also I wasn't really in a great space to take that on myself at the time

Q_PC.text: I think the situation with previous coworkers was pretty similar to what I've described -- I kept things vague and didn't really open up to anyone directly, because the fear of it spreading or changing how people thought of me professionally was always there in the background and I didn't feel like I could fully trust that a coworker relationship would hold the same confidentiality that I'd been able to rely on with my supervisor. I remember there being a general sense among some people that I was going through something, maybe from the changes in how I was working or just how I seemed, but nobody pushed and I didn't offer anything more than "just dealing with some things" which I think was understood as a signal to leave it alone. that distance felt necessary at the time even if it also felt a bit lonely

Q_CA.text: it's hard to say definitively because my supervisor kept it confidential so in a formal sense I don't think I was ever widely "identified" in a way that followed me around, but there was still that period where I was clearly operating differently and I think some people drew their own conclusions even without being told anything directly. honestly I'm not sure it hurt me in the long run, and the adjustments that were made at the time probably helped me stay functional enough to keep doing the job at all, though I still carry some anxiety about what might have happened if it had gone differently or reached the wrong person

Q_BH.text: it wasn't one specific conversation that went badly so much as the general environment that made me feel like disclosure was such a risk in the first place, because I had seen or heard of colleagues in similar situations who weren't given the same kind of discretion and whose situations seemed to quietly affect how they were perceived or assigned to work, and that created a kind of baseline anxiety in me that meant I went into my own conversation expecting the worst even though it didn't turn out that way, so in a sense the badly handled responses were ones I witnessed happening to other people more than anything that was directed at me directly

Q_SH.text: the supportive response was really the conversation with my supervisor that I've already mentioned, and what made it feel well handled was less about any single thing they said and more about the way they responded to the whole situation -- they didn't make it seem like a problem to be managed or a liability to be noted, they just listened and then quietly made some practical adjustments without drawing attention to it in the team, and the fact that it stayed confidential was the thing that mattered most to me because that was the condition on which I'd felt able to say anything at all, and looking back I think their handling of it is the reason I was able to stay and recover rather than feeling like I had to leave to avoid the fallout

Q_ID.text: I think the biggest thing is making it genuinely safe to say something before you reach a crisis point, because the barrier for most people isn't access to an EAP or a list of resources, it's the fear that disclosure will quietly change how you're perceived or assigned to work, and until that fear is addressed at the level of actual culture and manager behaviour rather than just policy documents, the support structures that exist won't really reach the people who need them most, and training managers to handle these conversations with real discretion would make a difference

Q_AE.text: I suppose the main thing I'd add is that it took me a long time to realise that what I was experiencing was serious enough to warrant saying something at all, because there's a version of working in tech where you just absorb a lot of stress and tell yourself it's normal and everyone is managing the same way, and I think that delay probably made things harder than they needed to be and I'm not sure what would have changed that for me except maybe knowing earlier that there were people who would handle it well rather than just hoping for the best

Q_PE.label: Describe the conversation you had with your previous employer about your mental health, including their reactions and actions taken to address your mental health issue/questions.
Q_PE.text: Had a major stress/depression breakdown and spoke to my supervisor about the treatment needed and the time that I was going to need to do the treatment. At the moment was that could either work or I could get fired but if I haven't had that talk I wouldn't know. That treatment was key for me to keep moving forward on the tech industry and, as far as I know, my confidentially was kept but I think that was major because of my supervisor.

persona_portrait.narrative: This person experienced a serious mental health crisis (stress/depression) while working in tech and took the risk of disclosing it to their supervisor, unsure of the outcome. The experience was precarious — they felt the implicit threat of job loss — but ultimately the conversation proved necessary for their recovery and continued career. They reflect on it with relief and gratitude, particularly toward their supervisor for maintaining confidentiality.
persona_portrait.writing_style: Sentences are long and run-on, connected loosely with conjunctions and relative clauses rather than proper punctuation. The tone is informal and personal, with some awkward phrasing that suggests a non-native or colloquial speaker working through a complex memory.

Q_EC.text: I mentioned I was struggling. my manager acknowledged it but didn't really follow through with anything concrete.

Q_CC.text: Most kept it surface level. one colleague made a comment that stuck with me -- not mean, just dismissive.

Q_CW.text: They shared something personal briefly. I tried to be supportive but I could tell they weren't sure it was safe to say more.

Q_PE.text: My previous employer was more understanding. the manager there had dealt with it personally, so there was less awkwardness.

Q_PC.text: It was a bit more open than my current workplace. a few people were willing to talk about it without making it weird.

Q_CA.text: I don't think it's been formal, but I've noticed shifts in how some people treat me.

Q_BH.text: My manager said the right things in the moment but nothing changed. it felt more like damage control than actual support.

Q_SH.text: My previous manager actually checked in afterward. it wasn't a big deal made of it, just quiet follow-through.

Q_ID.text: Better training for managers on how to actually follow through, not just say the right things. And normalizing the conversation so it doesn't feel like a liability issue.

Q_AE.text: The stigma from peers is harder to deal with than any policy gap. that part doesn't get talked about enough.

Q_CW.label: Describe the conversation your coworker had with you about their mental health (please do not use names).

Q_PE.text: My previous employer was much more understanding and accepting of mental illness, as they were bipolar themselves.

They have experienced or witnessed unsupportive peer attitudes at their current job, contrasted with a more empathetic previous employer who had personal experience with mental illness. They appear to have some personal familiarity with mental health challenges, suggesting quiet resilience rather than open advocacy.
persona_portrait.writing_style: Sentences are concise and declarative, with a restrained, matter-of-fact tone. Vocabulary is plain and accessible, with no ornamentation; the respondent conveys meaning efficiently without elaboration.

Q_EC.text: Told my manager I was dealing with anxiety -- he was understanding about it. we sorted out some flexibility around my hours and remote days.

Q_CC.text: A few of us have talked about it pretty openly, its just kind of normalized on our team.

Q_CW.text: One of my coworkers mentioned they were struggling with burnout and we just talked it through, pretty matter of fact.

Q_PC.text: Same kind of thing honestly -- brought it up casually and they were pretty receptive. no big deal was made of it

Q_CA.text: It hasn't really, tbh. my current team treats it as a non-issue so it hasn't held me back in any way I can tell.

Q_SH.text: Talked to my manager early on and he just got it. we adjusted my schedule and that was basically it -- pretty low drama overall.

Q_ID.text: Normalize it the same way physical health is treated -- flexible arrangements, no stigma around taking time off when you need it. most of it just comes down to managers actually listening.

Q_AE.text: Just that flexible work arrangements have made a real difference for me -- I think more teams could benefit from that kind of setup without much cost to the company

Q_EC.label: Describe the conversation you had with your employer about your mental health, including their reactions and what actions were taken to address your mental health issue/questions.
Q_EC.text: Briefly discussed my anxiety diagnosis; manager was understanding and we discussed ways I can manage that with a flexible work environment program

Q_CW.label: Describe the conversation your coworker had with you about their mental health (please do not use names).
Q_CW.text: Discussed issues with a coworker friend who also has issues, we traded advice mostly

persona_portrait.narrative: This person is a tech worker who has been diagnosed with anxiety and has found a supportive environment at work, successfully negotiating flexible arrangements with an understanding manager. They maintain peer relationships where mental health is discussed mutually and practically, suggesting a normalized, non-stigmatized view of mental health. persona_portrait.writing_style: Sentences are moderately short and functional, written in a calm, matter-of-fact register with no emotional hedging. Vocabulary is plain and professional, with a preference for summary over detail.

Q_EC.text: My manager noticed I was off before I would have brought it up myself. They were pretty understanding -- suggested I take some time and pointed me toward the EAP. Honestly it helped more than I expected, given I hadn't really planned to say anything

Q_CC.text: It was pretty low-key honestly. A couple of people noticed I seemed stressed and checked in, but I kept it pretty surface-level with them -- said I had some stuff going on outside work. They were decent about it, didn't push.

Q_CW.text: One colleague came to me after I'd been going through my own rough patch -- maybe they figured I'd get it. They didn't go into a lot of detail, just said they were struggling and weren't sure if they should say anything to their manager. I mostly just listened.

Q_PE.text: It came up during a period when things outside work were pretty messy. My manager at the time was decent about it -- didn't make it weird, just asked what I needed. There wasn't a formal process or anything, more just an informal check-in here and there. Looking back it probably could've been handled more proactively but it wasn't bad.

Q_PC.text: It was similar to my current job -- I didn't really open up much, maybe mentioned I was dealing with some personal stuff. A few people were kind about it, one of them actually checked in a couple times after. nothing formal, just kind of quietly looking out for me, which I appreciated more than I said at the time.

Q_CA.text: Honestly, less than I feared it would. I was pretty worried about how it might land, but it didn't seem to follow me in any obvious way -- no weird dynamics with management, no being passed over for anything I could point to. I guess I got lucky, or maybe the people I worked with were just decent about it.

Q_SH.text: The one that stood out was my current manager catching on before I said anything. I was having a rough stretch -- a breakup that kind of spilled into everything -- and they just pulled me aside, no big deal made of it, and mentioned the EAP like it was a normal option. That mattered.

Q_ID.text: Normalize the EAP as a real option, not something buried in an onboarding packet nobody reads. And honestly, just train managers to notice and not panic -- the thing that helped me most wasn't a policy, it was a manager who handled it like a normal human conversation.

Q_AE.text: I guess the main thing is that the personal stuff -- the non-work stuff -- hit harder than I anticipated, and I wasn't prepared for how much it would bleed into my job. the support I got was largely luck, not system. would've been easy for it to go the other way.

Q_EC.label: Describe the conversation you had with your employer about your mental health, including their reactions and what actions were taken to address your mental health issue/questions.
Q_EC.text: After a particularly messy non-work situation, my direct supervisor encouraged me to see a therapist in the interest of avoiding depression/anxiety/stress related issues.

Q_EC.text: I told my manager I was starting antidepressants and might need some flexibility while I adjusted. He was pretty straightforward about it -- said he appreciated me telling him and to just let him know if I needed anything. Nothing formal came out of it, but knowing he knew made things easier.

Q_CC.text: I mentioned it to one coworker I'm pretty close with. She was supportive, didn't make it weird. It was more of a casual heads-up than a real conversation. honestly I didn't feel the need to tell anyone else after that

Q_CW.text: A coworker mentioned they were dealing with anxiety and struggling to focus. I just listened and said I got it, that it's more common than people think. It didn't go much deeper than that but I think they just needed to say it out loud to someone.

Q_PE.text: I actually had a decent experience with a previous employer too. I brought up that I was going through something and needed a bit of flexibility. My manager at the time was understanding -- didn't push for details, just said we'd figure it out. It wasn't a big formal thing, just a quick check-in that went better than I expected.

Q_PC.text: Didn't really bring it up much with coworkers at that job. One person I was close to knew I was going through something but we didn't get into it. She just checked in every now and then which was enough for me honestly.

Q_CA.text: Honestly, not in any negative way that I can tell. I was a bit worried it might change how people saw me professionally, but it didn't seem to. If anything, being upfront about it made things less stressful than carrying it quietly would have.

Q_SH.text: It was pretty low-key, which is maybe why it worked. I told my manager one-on-one, just the two of us, and he didn't overreact or make it into a big thing. He just said he appreciated me being upfront and told me to let him know if I needed flexibility. no HR involvement, no formal documentation -- just a straightforward conversation between two adults.

Q_ID.text: Normalize the conversation early -- don't wait for someone to be struggling before you bring it up. Managers should get some basic training on how to respond. Most people just need to know they won't be penalized for being honest.

Q_AE.text: Just that my experience was genuinely better than I expected, and I think that's partly because I went in with a specific ask rather than just venting. Knowing what I needed made it easier for my manager to actually help. It doesn't always go that way, but it's worth trying

Q_EC.label: Describe the conversation you had with your employer about your mental health, including their reactions and what actions were taken to address your mental health issue/questions.
Q_EC.text: I told my manager I was starting antidepressants. He seemed surprised and concerned, and asked if there was anything he could do. Was very understanding that I might need to work from home or take more sick days.

persona_portrait.narrative: This person is a tech worker who proactively disclosed a significant mental health treatment decision—starting antidepressants—directly to their manager, suggesting a baseline comfort with vulnerability in professional settings. They experienced a supportive managerial response, which likely reinforces their willingness to be open. Their outlook appears cautiously optimistic, grounded in a concrete positive interaction rather than idealism.
persona_portrait.writing_style: Short, declarative sentences with a matter-of-fact tone and minimal emotional embellishment. Vocabulary is plain and conversational, with no jargon or formal register.

Q_EC.text: I approached my manager directly and explained that I needed to take time off for mental health reasons. The reaction was genuinely supportive — they arranged a month of leave without hesitation and checked in periodically while I was out. When I came back, I made the decision to address the whole company about what I'd been going through, which honestly felt like the right call given how open everyone had been throughout the process.

Q_CC.text: After I addressed the company, a lot of coworkers came up to me individually — some just to say they appreciated me sharing, others to open up about their own experiences. That part honestly surprised me. A few people I'd never spoken to about anything personal told me they'd gone through something similar and hadn't felt like they could say anything. the overall response was warm and I didn't get a single reaction that felt uncomfortable or judgmental.

Q_CW.text: One conversation that stood out was with a colleague I'd worked alongside for a couple of years but hadn't really connected with on anything personal. A few days after my company address, they pulled me aside and told me they'd been dealing with anxiety for a long time -- managed, but always present. they said seeing me talk about it openly made them feel like it was okay to name it out loud, at least to one person. It wasn't a long conversation, but it felt significant. I mostly just listened and tried to be the same kind of non-judgmental presence that my own manager had been for me.

Q_PE.text: My previous employer was a different story. I did have one conversation with my manager there, early on, but it didn't go anywhere productive — they acknowledged what I said and then essentially moved on, no follow-up, no adjustments. I left that job partly for other reasons, but looking back, the contrast with my current workplace is pretty stark.

Q_PC.text: At my previous job, I didn't really talk to coworkers about mental health at all -- the one conversation I had was with my manager, and when that didn't go anywhere, I didn't feel encouraged to try with anyone else. A couple of close colleagues probably sensed something was off at points, but it stayed unspoken. the culture there wasn't hostile exactly, just not one where that kind of conversation felt like a real option.

Q_CA.text: Honestly, the short answer is: not negatively, at least not in any way I can point to directly. I haven't been passed over for anything obvious, and my relationships with my manager and team haven't changed in a bad way. If anything, being open about it has made me more trusted, not less -- people know where I stand. That said, I'm aware the longer-term picture is harder to read, and I'd be naive to think there's zero professional cost to being that visible about it.

Q_BH.text: It was less a single incident and more a pattern of non-response. I went to my manager and explained I was struggling -- not in vague terms, I was pretty direct about what was going on. They listened, said something like "thanks for telling me, let me know if you need anything," and that was it. No check-in the next week, no adjustment to workload, no mention of any support resources. I don't think they meant to be dismissive, but the effect was the same -- I'd taken a real risk in saying something and nothing changed. That made it harder to bring up again.

Q_SH.text: My current manager handled it about as well as I could have asked. When I came to them and explained I needed time off for mental health reasons, they didn't ask me to justify it or probe for details -- they just said "okay, let's figure out the logistics" and that was that. A month of leave, no pushback. they checked in a couple of times while I was out, not in a way that felt like monitoring, just genuinely asking how I was doing. Coming back was also handled well: no awkward reset, no hovering. I felt like I came back on my own terms.

Q_ID.text: The biggest gap, honestly, is the difference between having a policy and actually using it. Most companies have EAP programs or leave provisions -- the problem is managers often don't know how to respond when someone actually brings something up. Training managers to do more than say "let me know if you need anything" would go a long way. Beyond that, normalizing the conversation at a company level, not leaving it entirely to individuals to take the risk of being visible, is probably the most structural change that would help.

Q_AE.text: One thing I'd add is that the decision to address the whole company wasn't something I planned well in advance — it was more of a considered impulse, if that makes sense. I'd been back for a week or two and it just felt dishonest to pretend the absence hadn't happened. I don't think that approach is right for everyone, and I got lucky that my workplace was the kind of place where it landed well. But I do think there's something to the idea that visibility at a senior or mid-level can shift what feels possible for people earlier in their careers. That wasn't really my motivation at the time, but it seems to have been part of the effect, based on the conversations I had afterward. I'm glad I did it.

Q_EC.label: Describe the conversation you had with your employer about your mental health, including their reactions and what actions were taken to address your mental health issue/questions.
Q_EC.text: I am currently taking a leave of absence from work in order to address some mental health issues I've had. I had an event related to mental health recently, and I knew I needed to address it in a significant way right now, so I told my boss what had happened and that I need to take this time to address it. I went in the next day to stand in front of the whole company to tell them that I would be out for the month to address my mental health.

Q_CC.label: Describe the conversation with coworkers you had about your mental health including their reactions.
Q_CC.text: I've told a number of coworkers about my situation (described above), and everyone has reacted positively, encouraging me to do what I need to in order to get better.

persona_portrait.narrative: This person is a tech worker who experienced a significant mental health event serious enough to prompt a month-long leave of absence. They demonstrated remarkable openness by voluntarily addressing the entire company about their situation rather than keeping it private. Despite the difficulty of their circumstances, they are surrounded by a supportive workplace and are taking proactive, self-directed steps toward recovery.
persona_portrait.writing_style: Sentences are moderate in length, clear, and structured chronologically. The tone is calm and matter-of-fact, with a slightly formal but personal register and no hedging or euphemism.

Q_EC.text: I've had this conversation a few times across different jobs, honestly. The most meaningful one was with a manager at my last company — I'd been struggling with a pretty bad depressive episode and my output had visibly dipped, so I figured it was better to get ahead of it than wait for a performance conversation I didn't want to have. I told him I was dealing with depression and anxiety that were affecting my focus, and that I wanted to talk about some adjustments that might help. He was genuinely great about it -- no awkward silence, no "have you tried exercise" kind of response. We agreed I could shift my core hours earlier in the day when my concentration is actually usable, and that I'd have a lighter ticket load during bad weeks rather than just having stuff pile up in my backlog. He kept it between us and checked in without being weird about it. I know that's not everyone's experience and I dont take it for granted, but it made a real difference in being able to stay functional at work instead of quietly falling apart.

Q_CC.text: It's been pretty mixed, honestly. A couple of close colleagues know -- not because I made a big announcement, but because when you work closely with someone for a while and then suddenly you're quieter or slower to respond to Slack, people notice. One coworker I was genuinely close with asked if I was okay in a way that felt like she actually wanted to know, not just being polite, so I told her roughly what was going on. She was really matter-of-fact about it, which was exactly what I needed -- no over-the-top concern, just "okay, thanks for telling me, let me know if there's anything on my end." A few others I've kept it vaguer with, just saying I had some health stuff going on, which is true enough. I haven't had anyone react badly, but I'm also pretty selective about who I tell. I think there's still enough ambient stigma in tech that I'm not gonna casually mention depression in a standup, you know? the people I have told, though, it's brought us closer, and that's been one of the genuinely good parts of an otherwise hard stretch.

Q_CW.text: One of my closer teammates came to me about a year ago, kind of out of nowhere — we were just wrapping up a code review on a call and after we finished the work stuff he went quiet for a second and then said he'd been having a really hard time, that he thought he might be dealing with anxiety and wasn't sleeping. I think he told me partly because he knew I'd had my own stuff going on. I tried to just listen and not make it weird, which is honestly harder than it sounds -- there's this reflex to immediately problem-solve or recommend a therapist app or whatever, and I had to consciously not do that. I mostly just told him it made sense that he was struggling given how brutal that quarter had been, and that I was glad he said something. He seemed relieved more than anything. I don't know exactly what he did after that conversation but he did eventually take some time off, and when he came back he seemed more like himself. I think about that conversation sometimes because it reminded me how much it matters to just have someone in your corner who isn't going to make it a whole thing.

Q_PE.text: That one went less well, tbh. It was earlier in my career, a different company, and I wasn't as practiced at having the conversation. I'd been struggling for a few months and finally said something to my manager at the time -- kept it pretty surface level, just that I was dealing with some mental health stuff and needed a bit more flexibility around deadlines. Her reaction wasn't hostile exactly, but it was... cautious? She said she appreciated me telling her and then kind of pivoted immediately into whether my current workload was "manageable," which felt like she was checking whether this was going to become a performance issue rather than actually engaging with what I'd said. Nothing concrete came out of it. No adjustments, no follow-up check-in. I think she just hoped it would resolve itself. And honestly it did, eventually, but not because of anything that happened at work. I came away from that one feeling like I'd taken a risk and gotten pretty much nothing back for it, which made me more guarded for a while after. It wasn't until the job I described before that I realized it didn't have to go that way -- that a manager actually responding well was possible, not just something that happened to other people.

Q_PC.text: At that job I was much more closed off about it — partly because of how the manager conversation had gone, and partly because the culture there was pretty heads-down, not a lot of personal stuff shared in general. I didn't really tell anyone directly. There was one colleague who I'd eaten lunch with fairly regularly who noticed I seemed off and asked, and I gave her the "just tired, busy quarter" answer, which wasn't a lie exactly but also wasn't the truth. She took it at face value and we moved on. I think part of me wanted to say more but the manager conversation had already left me feeling kind of exposed without much to show for it, so I wasn't eager to repeat that. Looking back I'm not sure it would've gone badly with her specifically -- she seemed like a decent person -- but I was in a mode of just getting through it quietly rather than letting more people in. That's probably the version of me I'm least proud of in hindsight, not because I owed anyone my diagnosis, but because the isolation made everything harder and I didn't need to make it that hard.

Q_CA.text: Honestly, it's hard to fully separate out the effect of being identified versus the effect of the mental health issues themselves — like, depression affects your output whether or not anyone knows why. But in terms of being known as someone who's dealt with this stuff... I think at my most recent job it actually worked in my favor in a quiet way. My manager knew, respected it, and I think it gave me a kind of credibility when I advocated for process changes around sustainable workloads — I wasn't just being precious, I had real skin in the game. At the earlier job, I'm less sure. I never got passed over for anything explicitly, but there was a stretch after that manager conversation where I felt like I was being watched more carefully, and I'll never know if that was real or just my own anxiety about it. I haven't experienced anything I could point to and call outright discrimination, which I recognize is a relatively good outcome. But I do carry this low-level awareness that I'm selectively out at work, not fully, and that managing who knows is itself a kind of overhead that people without this history don't have. It hasn't derailed my career. it has shaped how I move through it.

Q_BH.text: The one I described with my earlier manager is the one that fits here. I'd timed the conversation deliberately — I asked for a one-on-one, framed it as wanting to be proactive rather than reactive, and came in with a pretty clear sense of what I was asking for. I wasn't asking for anything dramatic, just some flexibility around hard deadlines during bad weeks and maybe a check-in structure that wasn't tied to performance reviews. She listened, said the right words in the moment, and then just... didn't do anything. No follow-up, no "let me think about what we can do," no acknowledgment of it the next time we met. It kind of disappeared into the ether. I think the thing that made it feel unsupportive wasn't hostility — it was the absence of any real engagement. Like the conversation happened in a sealed room and never touched the actual work environment at all. I had to figure out my own coping mechanisms without any structural help, which I did, but it took longer than it needed to and I burned through a lot of energy just staying afloat. The worst part was not knowing if she'd quietly noted it somewhere, flagged it somehow — that uncertainty sat with me for months.

Q_SH.text: The one I've already talked about — my most recent manager — is the clear example here. What made it work, I think, was partly him and partly how I went in. I'd had the bad experience by then, so I was more deliberate about it: I picked a one-on-one where we weren't rushed, I named what I was dealing with specifically rather than being vague, and I came in with concrete asks rather than just leaving it to him to figure out what to do with the information. And he met that with actual reciprocity — he asked a couple of clarifying questions, not in a suspicious way but more like he was genuinely trying to understand what would help, and then we worked out the flexible hours and the adjusted ticket load together in the same conversation. It didn't feel like I was petitioning for something and waiting to hear back. it felt collaborative. He also never made it a topic again unless I brought it up, which sounds like a small thing but is actually huge — there's nothing worse than someone treating you like a fragile variable every time they assign you work. The combination of actual structural change plus him just... treating me normally afterward, that's what made it feel genuinely supportive rather than just nicely handled on the surface.

Q_ID.text: More transparency at the hiring stage would help a lot — not just "we have an EAP" buried in a benefits PDF, but actual signals about how teams handle workload spikes and whether flexibility is real or theoretical. the thing I've noticed is that good support mostly comes down to individual managers rather than company policy, which means it's a lottery depending on who you get. Structural changes that would actually matter: normalizing accommodation conversations as a routine part of onboarding rather than something you have to work up the courage to initiate, training managers to respond to disclosure in a way that's useful rather than just legally cautious, and building in workload review processes that catch burnout before it becomes a crisis. I also think the industry needs to get more honest about the fact that crunch culture and mental health support are fundamentally in tension — you can't have both, and right now a lot of companies pretend otherwise.

Q_AE.text: I just want to say that surveys like this tend to skew toward the hard experiences, which makes sense — that's where the useful data is — but I'd be doing a disservice if I didn't note that the people in my life at work have also been a genuine source of support, not just a source of risk to manage. The colleague who checked in, the teammate who came to me, my last manager — those interactions shaped how I think about disclosure as much as the bad ones did. I don't think I'd be as functional or as willing to advocate for myself if I hadn't had evidence that it could go well. so I guess what I'd add is: it's not just about preventing bad responses, it's about actively creating conditions where good ones are more likely. That's the gap I see most clearly.

Q_EC.label: Describe the conversation you had with your employer about your mental health, including their reactions and what actions were taken to address your mental health issue/questions.
Q_EC.text: Last year I was dealing with an active episode of depression.  Nothing was getting done because I couldn't focus.  My anxiety was going crazy because I felt like I was letting everyone down, and that was making it harder and harder to come into the office.  Earlier in the year, a new 'no working from home' policy was brought in by the company owner, and so I felt like I had to stay and keep trying, despite not getting any progress made.  Eventually after discussing a plan of attack with my project manager, I met with HR and requested a few accommodations.  Specifically, a little more flexibility in hours and location of work.  If my anxiety was making working from the office impossible, I wanted to be able to go home, regroup for a couple hours, and make up that time later in the day / week.  HR and my manager were understanding and allowed this to occur.  There was a little followup from time to time just to ensure things weren't getting worse and that I wasn't taking advantage of the situation. Additionally, between the Project Manager and my manager, we ensured there weren't too many tickets assigned in my backlog as well, to reduce the sense of an unending series of tasks piling up.

Q_EC.text: I confided in my direct manager during a particularly difficult stretch, and his response was — honestly more empathetic than I'd expected; he adjusted my workload without making a production of it. When HR became involved, the tone shifted considerably. The conversation became procedural rather than personal, and I came away with the distinct sense that I had flagged myself as a potential liability rather than simply asked for support.

Q_CC.text: I've been selective about which colleagues I've confided in — a handful of people I'd worked alongside long enough to trust. The reactions were, by and large, kind, though I noticed a tendency to minimize or redirect toward productivity tips rather than actually sitting with what I'd said. And honestly, I don't fault them for that; most people aren't equipped to respond well, and I wasn't looking for therapy, just acknowledgment.

Q_CW.text: A colleague came to me a few years ago -- I think they chose me because they sensed I'd understand what it meant to say something like that out loud. They started with hypotheticals before getting more direct. I tried to do what I'd have wanted someone to do for me: just listen, and not immediately pivot to solutions or, worse, suggest they loop in HR.

Q_PE.text: At a previous company, I made the mistake of disclosing more directly than I should have — I was earlier in my career and hadn't yet calibrated how institutions use that information. My manager at the time was sympathetic in the moment, but the follow-through was essentially nonexistent, and I noticed afterward a subtle shift in how I was assigned to projects. nothing punitive on paper, but the pattern was hard to misread.

Q_PC.text: At a previous company, the colleagues I told were mostly people I'd worked with closely, and their immediate reactions were warm enough — the kind of concern that reads as genuine in the moment. But I noticed, over the weeks that followed, a certain recalibration in how some of them engaged with me. Not hostility, but a kind of careful management, like I'd introduced a variable they weren't sure how to account for. Tbh, I'm not sure they were even conscious of it, which in some ways made it harder to name.

Q_CA.text: The effects have been difficult to quantify precisely because they operate at the level of implication rather than action — no one has ever said anything directly. What I can say is that I've been passed over for opportunities I was qualified for, and I've occasionally sensed a shift in how my judgment is weighted in rooms where it previously wasn't questioned. My direct colleagues have largely treated me the same; the erosion, such as it is, seems to come from higher up or further out, from people for whom I'm more category than person.

Q_BH.text: The HR interaction I described stands out most clearly — not because anything overtly harmful was said, but because of what replaced genuine engagement. The conversation was managed rather than had; I was given a pamphlet and a referral to an EAP, which communicated, fairly efficiently, that the institution's priority was documentation and liability mitigation. I left feeling processed rather than heard, which is its own kind of harm.

Q_SH.text: My direct manager's response — the one I mentioned earlier — is honestly the clearest example I have. What made it effective was the absence of theater: he acknowledged what I'd said, asked one or two careful questions, and then made a concrete adjustment without requiring me to justify it further or route it through any formal process. It felt like being responded to as a colleague rather than managed as a risk.

Q_ID.text: The most meaningful change would be decoupling mental health disclosure from HR records and formal performance frameworks — so that an employee can ask for support without that request becoming permanent institutional data. Managers need actual training, not just awareness campaigns, and that training should be evaluated on outcomes rather than completion metrics. Structural change, not signaling, is what actually reduces the calculus of risk that shapes who discloses and who doesnt.

Q_AE.text: I'd note that the survey's framing — which asks about discrete conversations and identifiable events — may undercount the more diffuse forms of harm, the ambient recalibration that happens without a single precipitating incident. That kind of accumulation is harder to name and, consequently, harder to address. I think researchers and employers both tend to focus on the legible cases, and the illegible ones are where most of the damage actually lives.

HR flagged some EAP resources which I did actually use. it helped having that conversation framed around productivity rather than just "I'm struggling."

Q_CC.text: A few coworkers knew what was going on, and honestly the conversations were pretty low-key. I didn't make it a big announcement, but once it was out there it kind of opened the door — couple of them shared their own stuff too.

Q_CW.text: One coworker came to me after I'd been pretty open about my own situation — I think it gave them a kind of opening. They talked about burnout mostly, feeling like they couldn't keep up. I just listened and pointed them toward the EAP, same as it helped me.

Q_PE.text: It was a different experience — I raised it once with my manager there and the response was pretty surface-level, like "let us know if you need anything" and that was it. Nothing concrete came out of it, which honestly is part of why I approach it differently now.

Q_PC.text: Pretty much the same vibe as the response from management — people were polite but it didn't really go anywhere. I mentioned it to one or two colleagues and got the "yeah that's rough" kind of response. Supportive in the moment, but no real follow-through or ongoing conversation.

Q_CA.text: Honestly, it's been mixed. At my current job, being open about it has probably helped — I think people see me as someone who manages myself well. the previous employer situation was a bit of a black mark, I suspect, though nothing was ever said directly.

Q_BH.text: It was at the previous job — I'd flagged that I was struggling with stress and it was affecting my output. My manager acknowledged it, said the right things in the moment, but nothing changed. No follow-up, no adjustments. it just kind of got absorbed and forgotten.

Q_SH.text: My current manager was the difference. When I brought it up, we actually talked through what was driving the stress and came up with a plan — adjusted some deadlines, redistributed one project. HR followed up too, which I didn't expect. it felt like the conversation actually went somewhere, rather than just being acknowledged and dropped.

Q_ID.text: More normalisation of the conversation early, before it becomes a crisis — that's the main thing. Employers should build in actual check-ins rather than waiting for someone to raise it. And the EAP stuff is only useful if people know about it and dont feel like using it flags them somehow.

Q_AE.text: I think the framing around mental health at work still defaults too much to the clinical side — like it's only a problem once someone's in crisis. Connecting it earlier to performance and day-to-day function, the way I've tried to do personally, tends to land better with managers who might otherwise tune it out.

Q_EC.text: I've had a couple of these conversations over the years. The one that went well -- my manager at the time was pretty calm about it, referred me to HR, and the company ended up funding a course of CBT which honestly helped a lot. the one that didn't go well was after a psychotic episode, that felt a bit more like damage control than support.

Q_CC.text: Most of my coworkers have been pretty decent about it, honestly. A few close ones knew about the depression before I ever said anything official, and they just kind of... carried on normally, which was what I needed. the psychotic episode was trickier -- I think some people didn't really know what to say, so they said nothing, which was fine.

Q_CW.text: One colleague came to me after I'd been open about my own stuff -- I think that made it easier for them. they were dealing with anxiety, hadn't told anyone else, and mostly just wanted to vent. I tried to just listen, didn't make it weird.

Q_PE.text: Pretty similar to my current employer, tbh -- one conversation went fine, the other didn't. the fine one was early in my career, manager just said take whatever time you need and left it at that. the one that went badly was around the psychotic episode, felt like they were more concerned about liability than me.

Q_PC.text: Pretty mixed, same as with current coworkers. Some people were great -- one colleague in particular checked in on me regularly without making a big deal of it. the psychotic episode stuff was harder, a couple of people got noticeably awkward around me for a while. it settled down eventually but you notice it at the time.

Q_CA.text: Honestly, it's hard to separate out. I don't think it's held me back in any obvious way -- no promotions blocked, nothing like that. But after the psychotic episode there was definitely a period where I felt like people were watching me more carefully, and I second-guessed how much to share after that.

Q_BH.text: The psychotic episode one, at my previous job. I'd been hospitalised briefly, came back and my manager sat me down -- not to check in, but to go through what I could and couldn't discuss with the team. it was framed as "protecting" me but felt more like protecting the company. no follow-up after that conversation, just kind of pretended it hadn't happened.

Q_SH.text: The CBT thing was probably the best of it. I'd gone to my manager at the time -- not really expecting much, just flagging that I was struggling with depression. they actually listened, didn't minimise it, and within a week HR had come back with options including a funded course of therapy. I didn't have to fight for it or justify myself. it felt pretty matter-of-fact on their end, which oddly made it easier for me.

Q_ID.text: Less lip service, more actual resource. Most companies have an EAP that nobody uses because nobody trusts it -- funded therapy that doesn't go through your line manager would make a real difference. And honestly just training managers to respond like humans rather than HR departments. that part costs almost nothing.

Q_AE.text: Just that the survey felt pretty thorough, actually. The one thing I'd add is that the experience of serious mental illness -- psychosis specifically -- still feels like a different category to most people, including employers. Depression gets more acceptance now, which is good, but the moment something sounds more extreme people don't know what to do with it. that gap is probably worth more attention.

Q_CA.text: Honestly, it's had minimal formal impact -- no demotion, no explicit pushback. But it definitely recalibrated who I trust with information about myself at work. I'm more selective now about what I disclose and to whom. The filter I mentioned? It applies to management too, not just peers

Q_BH.text: The HR meeting is the clearest example. I came in with a specific, low-stakes request -- adjusted hours during a difficult period. The response was a pamphlet on "employee wellness resources" and a form documenting that the conversation had occurred. it was designed to close a loop, not open one.

Q_SH.text: The coworker conversations, honestly. One in particular — a colleague pulled me aside after I'd had a visibly rough week and just said "I've been there, what do you need?" Q_EC.text: I had two pretty different experiences depending on the manager. One was genuinely good — I told him I was going through a rough patch, mentioned the depression, and he adjusted my sprint load for a few weeks without making it a whole thing. the other one kind of nodded along but then started cc'ing my skip-level on everything, which felt like being put on watch. So, mixed results honestly.

Q_CC.text: I actually make a point of telling my close teammates when I'm not in a great headspace — not like a big announcement, just a heads up so they don't take it personally if I'm quieter than usual. most of them were really understanding, a couple even shared their own stuff back which I didn't expect. it made the team feel a lot more human honestly.

Q_CW.text: One of my teammates came to me after I'd shared my own stuff — I think it made them feel like it was safe to say something. they mentioned they'd been dealing with anxiety for a while, mostly around deadlines and performance reviews. I just listened, didn't try to fix anything. told them it made sense given the pressure we're all under. felt like a real moment of trust.

Q_PE.text: At my previous job the conversation went pretty badly, tbh. I was going through the divorce at the time and it was affecting my focus, so I tried to be upfront about it. my manager basically said "everyone has personal stuff, just keep it outside the office." No follow-up, no EAP mention, nothing. I learned pretty quickly that place wasn't somewhere you could actually be honest.

Q_PC.text: At that job I was a lot more guarded after the manager reaction, so I only really opened up to one person I trusted. she was great about it, checked in on me a few times without making it awkward. the broader team though -- I never got the sense that kind of conversation would land well, so I just didn't go there.

Q_CA.text: It's been mixed, honestly. At my current job I don't think it's hurt me in any obvious way — the manager who handled it well has actually been pretty supportive since. But at the previous place, after I opened up, I definitely noticed I got passed over for a project lead role I was expecting. cant prove it was connected but the timing was hard to ignore.

Q_BH.text: That previous manager response really stuck with me. I'd just explained that my divorce was making it hard to concentrate and I was asking for maybe a bit of flexibility on deadlines — nothing dramatic. And he just kind of looked at me and said everyone deals with hard stuff, keep it out of the office. No acknowledgment, no resources mentioned, just... get on with it. The project lead thing came a few months after that, and I never got a real explanation.

Q_SH.text: That conversation with my current manager was honestly a relief after the previous experience. I kept it pretty simple — told him I was dealing with depression and it was affecting my concentration. He didn't make it weird, just asked what would actually help and we figured out between us to lighten my sprint load for a couple weeks. no big HR process, no weird follow-up emails, just a practical fix and then we moved on. felt like being treated as a person rather than a liability.

Q_ID.text: Honestly the biggest thing is just normalizing the conversation before someone's in crisis. Training managers to actually respond — not just nod and move on — would make a huge difference. the current manager I have figured it out on his own but that shouldn't be luck. EAP programs exist at most companies but nobody talks about them until things are already bad, so making that stuff visible and low-stakes to access would help a lot.

Q_AE.text: I guess the thing I keep coming back to is that so much of this comes down to individual managers, and that feels fragile. I got lucky the second time around but I've seen colleagues who weren't. It shouldn't be a lottery. Also -- and maybe this is obvious -- the people most likely to need support are often the ones least likely to ask for it, so waiting for someone to raise their hand doesn't really work.

Q_EC.text: I did speak with my manager about needing some flexibility for therapy appointments — mostly because my family history made it feel important to be proactive about things before they became a crisis. their response was generally supportive, at least on the surface, and we arranged for me to shift some hours around. But I noticed a real change in how certain coworkers treated me afterward, which honestly made me question whether the disclosure had been worth it

Q_CC.text: It wasn't really a conversation I initiated — more something that became apparent through changed dynamics. A couple of coworkers made offhand comments when I'd leave early for appointments, nothing overtly hostile but clearly pointed. I never disclosed directly to them; they'd drawn their own conclusions. it was a reminder, honestly, that visibility in this area comes with social costs I hadn't fully anticipated.

Q_CW.text: A coworker approached me -- I suspect they'd picked up on the fact that I'd had my own conversations with management. They mentioned struggling with anxiety and not really knowing how to ask for accommodations. I mostly just listened and tried to be present; felt like the right thing, and honestly it was the kind of response I'd wanted myself.

Q_PE.text: With a previous employer, I was less forthcoming — I'd mentioned needing occasional time off for "personal health reasons" without elaborating, partly because the culture there felt less safe and partly because I hadn't yet worked out how to frame things clearly. They didn't push, which I was grateful for, though the vagueness meant I also didn't get much real support either.

Q_PC.text: At that previous job, I kept things pretty close to the chest — I hadn't disclosed anything formally, so there wasn't really a conversation to have. A few people probably noticed I seemed stressed at times, and I got the occasional "you doing okay?" but nothing deeper. I didn't feel the environment was safe enough to go further than that, and honestly, I don't think I'd have gotten much back if I had.

Q_CA.text: It's hard to point to anything concrete — no missed promotion I can trace directly, no formal consequence. But the shift in how certain colleagues engage with me has been real. there's a kind of low-level wariness I sense sometimes, like I've been quietly recategorized. I'm more careful now about what I share and with whom, which is its own cost I hadn't expected.

Q_BH.text: The unsupportive part wasn't really my manager's response — it was what followed from certain coworkers. Once it became clear I was leaving regularly for appointments, comments started surfacing. Nothing direct enough to escalate formally, but clearly pointed — "must be nice to have flexible hours," said in a tone that wasn't quite neutral. nobody addressed it, and raising it myself would've meant drawing even more attention to the thing I'd hoped to keep low-key.

Q_SH.text: My manager's initial response was the supportive part — she didn't press for details I wasn't prepared to share, and worked with me to adjust my schedule without making it feel like a formal negotiation. that kind of matter-of-fact accommodation was what I actually needed. it didnt fix everything downstream, but I could get to appointments without adding more stress to an already complicated situation.

Q_ID.text: The policy piece feels less urgent to me than the cultural one — most employers already have EAP programs and stated commitments. What's actually missing is accountability for what happens after someone discloses. if managers don't actively model that mental health conversations don't change how you're treated, the formal policies don't do much. That gap between stated support and lived experience is where I think the real work needs to happen.

Q_AE.text: One thing I haven't mentioned directly is that part of what motivates me to engage with this topic -- and to take surveys like this seriously -- is my family history. watching a parent navigate what was likely bipolar disorder without adequate workplace support shaped how I think about all of this. I didn't come to these questions abstractly. I hope the data collected here actually informs something concrete, not just a report that sits somewhere.

Q_EC.text: I spoke directly with my director about my depression -- framing it as something I was actively managing, not a crisis. The response was genuinely supportive; they adjusted my workload for a stretch and connected me with the EAP. Honestly, that's the kind of culture I try to model for my own reports.

Q_CC.text: A few of my direct reports know I've dealt with depression -- I've been deliberate about sharing that, because it lowers the barrier for them to come forward. one colleague told me it made them feel comfortable disclosing their own anxiety, which was honestly exactly the point.

Q_CW.text: One of my direct reports came to me during a one-on-one and disclosed they'd been struggling with burnout that had tipped into something more serious. They were clearly anxious about how I'd respond -- I think they half-expected me to redirect them to HR and move on. I made sure to listen properly, shared that I'd navigated something similar myself, and we worked out a short-term adjustment to their responsibilities together.

Q_PE.text: At a previous company, I disclosed to my manager that I was working through depression. The reaction was polite but fairly hands-off -- a referral to HR and not much follow-up. honestly, that experience is part of what made me more intentional about how I show up as a manager now.

Q_PC.text: At that earlier company, I was less open than I am now -- I mentioned to one close colleague that I was going through a difficult period, but didn't name it explicitly. They were kind about it, checked in once or twice afterward. I think the culture there didn't really invite that kind of disclosure, so it stayed pretty contained.

Q_CA.text: I haven't experienced significant negative career consequences -- being in a leadership role offers some insulation, and I've been deliberate about context and timing. if anything, being open has strengthened trust with my team and reinforced the kind of manager I want to be.

Q_BH.text: At that previous company, the manager's response was technically appropriate -- I was pointed to HR and told I'd be fine. But there was no follow-up, no check-in, no acknowledgment that this might affect my work. it felt like the conversation had been closed rather than opened.

Q_SH.text: The response from my current director was the clearest example I can point to. They listened without rushing to fix anything, asked what would actually help, and then followed through -- adjusted deadlines, flagged me for EAP access, and checked in a couple weeks later unprompted. it felt like being treated as a whole person rather than a performance risk.

Q_ID.text: Normalize it structurally, not just rhetorically -- mental health days need to carry the same weight as sick days, and managers need actual training, not a one-hour module they forget by Friday. I think the biggest lever is leadership modeling: when executives talk openly about their own experiences, it shifts what's permissible for everyone below them.

Q_AE.text: I'd just add that surveys like this one matter -- the data shapes policy, and policy shapes culture. I'm glad this research exists. If there's anything useful in my responses, I hope it's that disclosure from people in leadership roles isn't just personally meaningful, it's structurally important.

Q_EC.text: My manager was pretty understanding when I brought it up — I told them I was dealing with depression and anxiety and needed some time off. They didn't make it weird, just asked what I needed and helped me sort out the leave. When I came back, they checked in occasionally without making it feel like surveillance, which honestly made the transition back a lot easier.

Q_CC.text: My team was generally supportive, though I didn't go into a lot of detail with most of them. A couple of colleagues reached out when I was back and just said they were glad I was doing better — nothing intrusive, just kind of a quiet acknowledgment that meant a lot. Q_CW.text: A colleague came to me a while back and shared that they were struggling with burnout — not a dramatic conversation, just a quiet one-on-one where they said they were having a hard time keeping up. I tried to just listen and not immediately jump to problem-solving mode. I mentioned that I'd gone through something similar, which seemed to help them feel less alone in it.

Q_PE.text: At my previous job I didn't really bring it up directly — I had a sense the culture wasn't going to be receptive, so I kept things vague when I needed time away. My manager was fine, not hostile, but there wasn't much follow-up or support offered. It was honestly a pretty stark contrast to how things went more recently.

Q_PC.text: At my previous job, I didn't really talk about it openly with coworkers. I kept things pretty surface-level — if anything came up I'd just say I wasn't feeling well. There wasn't a strong culture of that kind of openness, so it didn't feel like a safe space to get into it. No one was unkind, it just wasn't something people talked about.

Q_CA.text: Honestly, not in any dramatic way — at least not in my current role. I think there was a moment early on where I wondered if it would change how people saw me, but it hasn't seemed to affect my responsibilities or opportunities. I got lucky with my team.

Q_BH.text: At my previous job, I eventually told my manager I was dealing with some personal health stuff and needed a day or two. The response was basically just "okay, let me know when you're back" — no follow-up, no check-in, nothing. It wasn't hostile, but it felt like the conversation was over the moment it was inconvenient. I think that kind of indifferent response can be its own form of unsupportive — it sends a pretty clear message that you're on your own.

Q_SH.text: My current manager was the contrast I didn't know I needed. When I brought it up, they took it seriously without making it feel like a crisis — asked practical questions about what I needed, helped me navigate the leave process, and made sure there wasn't pressure to rush back. When I did come back, they checked in here and there, just enough to signal they hadn't forgotten but not so much that it felt like monitoring. it made a real difference to know someone in a position of authority was actually in my corner.

Q_ID.text: More consistent manager training would go a long way — not just policies on paper but actual practice in having these conversations without making it awkward. And normalizing mental health leave the same way physical sick leave is treated would help a lot. The stigma often comes from the top down, so it has to start there.

Q_AE.text: I just want to say that I think surveys like this matter — it's useful data and I hope it leads somewhere. The thing that doesn't always get captured in yes/no questions is how much individual managers shape the experience. Policy is only as good as the person implementing it, and I got lucky. A lot of people don't.

Q_EC.text: I disclosed my depression (it developed after surgery) and was let go not long after. The stated reason had nothing to do with mental health, but the timing was pretty hard to ignore.

Q_CC.text: A couple of colleagues were actually pretty decent about it — no judgment, just checked in occasionally. Nothing formal, more like they knew and quietly didn't make it weird.

Q_CW.text: One coworker mentioned they were dealing with anxiety — kind of offhand, not a big sit-down conversation. I just listened, didn't push. They seemed more relieved to say it out loud than to actually get advice.

Q_PC.text: Pretty similar to my current workplace, honestly. A few people knew — I didn't make an announcement — and they handled it quietly, which was about all I wanted. No one made it a bigger deal than it needed to be.

Q_CA.text: It cost me a job, most likely. The termination came shortly after I disclosed, and while the official reason was something else, I've never really shaken the sense that those two things were connected. It's made me a lot more careful about who I tell since then.

Q_BH.text: The termination itself, really. I disclosed my depression to my manager — framed it professionally, explained it was being treated — and within a few weeks I was let go for reasons that didn't quite add up. No conversation about accommodations, no follow-up. just a sudden performance concern that hadn't come up before.

Q_SH.text: The coworkers I mentioned — that was genuinely fine. A couple of them knew what was going on and just... acted normal. Checked in occasionally without making it a whole thing. That kind of low-key acknowledgment was actually more helpful than anything formal would have been.

Q_ID.text: Better protections against retaliation would be a start — awareness campaigns don't mean much if disclosing still carries real career risk. People need to believe there are actual consequences for mishandling it, not just a policy on paper.

Q_AE.text: The PTSD piece didn't come up much in the questions — that's been its own separate thread, and honestly harder to talk about at work than the depression was. I've mostly kept that one to myself.

Q_AE.text: Post-traumatic Stress Disorder

persona_portrait.narrative: This person is a tech worker who has navigated serious mental health challenges—depression following surgery and PTSD—while employed in the industry. They experienced what appears to be retaliatory termination after disclosing their depression to an employer, a deeply disillusioning experience that contrasts with more supportive peer-level interactions. Despite the institutional betrayal, they maintain a measured, matter-of-fact tone rather than an embittered one.
main_themes: workplace retaliation after mental health disclosure
persona_portrait.writing_style: Sentences are moderate in length, plainspoken, and factually grounded with minimal emotional embellishment. The respondent uses parenthetical asides to layer detail and context, and favors understated phrasing to convey serious events.

Q_EC.text: I told my manager directly. They were actually pretty supportive -- more than I expected. we agreed on some flexibility around deadlines during rough patches, which honestly helped a lot.

Q_CC.text: I was actually the first person on my team to bring it up -- kind of came out of the closet about it. Once I did, others started opening up too. it felt like I'd broken the ice for everyone.

Q_CW.text: After I shared my own experience, a coworker pulled me aside privately. they said they'd been struggling for a while but hadn't felt safe saying anything. honestly it meant a lot that I could be that person for them.

Q_PE.text: At my previous job I didn't feel safe enough to bring it up at all. So I just quietly managed it on my own -- honestly that experience is part of why I decided to be more open later.

Q_PC.text: Kept it pretty close to the chest back then. I didn't trust the culture enough to say anything real. a couple of colleagues probably noticed something was off but no one ever asked, and I wasnt going to volunteer it.

Q_CA.text: Honestly it's been mostly positive. Some people look at me a little differently -- but in a good way, like I'm someone they can actually come to. I think being open made me more credible, not less.

Q_BH.text: At a previous job, HR found out indirectly and basically suggested I "look into EAP resources" and left it at that. No follow-up, no real conversation. it felt like a box-ticking exercise honestly.

Q_SH.text: My current manager handled it really well -- when I brought it up they actually listened, asked what would help rather than assuming. The flexibility we worked out around deadlines was their idea, which meant a lot.

Q_ID.text: Normalize it the same way physical health is normalized. Stop treating mental health days as suspicious and actually fund EAP programs that are worth using -- not just a hotline number buried in an FAQ. Honestly, the biggest thing is leadership modeling it. when managers talk about it openly, it changes everything.

Q_AE.text: Just want to say -- I think this kind of research actually matters. the more workplaces are asked these questions directly, the harder it is to ignore the answers. I came out of the closet about my mental health at work years ago and I'd do it again. it gets easier when more people do it.

Q_EC.text: Hard to separate "employer" from "dad" in my case, honestly. He's pretty supportive but we don't really do formal check-ins -- it just comes up when it comes up, usually over dinner.

Q_CC.text: Most of those conversations happened after a few drinks, tbh. Easier to get into it that way. The reactions were fine -- sympathetic, nothing weird -- but I doubt we'd have gone there sober.

Q_CW.text: Similar deal -- it came up after drinks at a work thing. They mentioned some anxiety stuff, I listened, it felt okay in the moment but we never really revisited it sober.

Q_PC.text: Similar vibe to my current job, honestly -- drinks were usually involved. previous coworkers were pretty decent about it, no one made it weird, but it wasn't really a sober-conversation kind of thing for me.

Q_CA.text: Honestly, hard to say for certain. I don't think it's hurt me -- but I also work for my dad, so the usual career risk calculus doesn't really apply in the same way.

Q_BH.text: At an old job, I mentioned I was struggling and my manager basically said to just take some time off. Very scripted, zero actual engagement -- like she'd googled "what to say" and stopped there.

Q_SH.text: My dad, actually. I mentioned I was having a rough stretch and he just... didn't make it a whole thing. Asked a couple of questions, dropped it. That was enough.

Q_ID.text: Less scripted EAP stuff, more actual culture shift. If the only place people feel safe talking is after drinks, something's off. Make it normal before someone's already in crisis.

Q_AE.text: Just that the family business angle makes a lot of these questions skew weird for me -- the power dynamics are different and the stakes feel both higher and lower at the same time. Not sure that comes through cleanly in the standard answer choices.

Q_EC.text: Honestly it was pretty low-key — I mentioned I was struggling with anxiety and my manager just kind of nodded and said "yeah, same, we've all been there." They let me shift my hours around a bit so I could avoid the worst of the commute crush.

Q_CC.text: My team is pretty open about this stuff — one coworker brought up her ADHD diagnosis in a standup once like it was just a normal update, and nobody blinked. I've mentioned my anxiety to a couple of people and the response was basically "oh yeah, me too" which honestly makes it so much easier to just... exist there.

Q_CW.text: It kind of goes both ways on my team, which is nice. One person told me pretty candidly they were dealing with burnout and were gonna take some time off — they weren't asking for anything, just letting me know in case things got quiet on their end. And another coworker mentioned they have social anxiety and we ended up having a whole side conversation about sensory overload at open-plan offices, which honestly felt more like bonding than anything heavy.

Q_PE.text: Previous job was a different story — I mentioned offhand that I had anxiety and my manager kind of just... moved on? Like it got acknowledged and then immediately dropped. Nothing changed, no follow-up. It wasn't hostile, just weirdly neutral in a way that made me not bring it up again.

Q_PC.text: Tbh it was pretty different from where I am now. I mentioned anxiety to one coworker and they were sympathetic but kind of awkward about it — like they didn't know what to say so they just said "oh wow, that's tough" and changed the subject. not a bad reaction exactly, just... surface level. Nobody there really talked about that stuff openly so I mostly kept it to myself after that.

Q_CA.text: It hasn't really, at least not that I can tell — I think being at a place where this stuff is normalized means it just doesn't register as a liability. if anything it's maybe made me seem more approachable to people who are also dealing with stuff.

Q_BH.text: Probably the previous job situation — it wasn't dramatic, which almost made it worse. I mentioned anxiety in what felt like a real moment and my manager just kind of... filed it away mentally and moved on. No check-in later, no "hey how are you doing," nothing. The implicit message was that it was a personal problem to manage on my own time, not something the workplace had any role in.

Q_SH.text: My current team honestly — the whole dynamic there is just different. When I mentioned my anxiety my manager actually followed up a few days later to ask how I was doing, which sounds small but felt huge after years of it just being ignored. And the flexibility with hours was real, not performative. I think what made it well-handled was that it was just... treated like a normal workplace thing, not a confession.

Q_ID.text: More normalizing it at the structural level honestly — like making it a regular part of how teams operate rather than something you only address when someone's already in crisis. Flexible hours and remote options help a lot for people with anxiety or sensory stuff. And managers just... following up. that one small thing makes such a difference

Q_AE.text: Just that I think surveys like this actually matter — it's easy to feel like mental health conversations at work are a niche concern, but the fact that my current team is better partly because people have talked openly about this stuff (in part through initiatives like this one, I'd guess) feels worth naming. Also ngl, the neurodivergent/anxious corner of tech is bigger than most companies realize, and when workplaces accidentally become good at supporting that — through flexibility, low-pressure communication norms, that kind of thing — everyone benefits. So thanks for doing this.

Q_CC.text: I've actually brought it up pretty openly with a few colleagues — sharing that I'm in therapy, partly to normalize it. Most were receptive, and a couple even mentioned they'd been considering it themselves, which felt like exactly the kind of shift I was hoping for.

Q_CW.text: A colleague pulled me aside after I'd shared my own experience — they were dealing with burnout and honestly didn't know where to start. I mostly just listened, and mentioned that therapy had been really helpful for me.

Q_PE.text: My previous employer was a different story — I brought up that I was managing some anxiety and wanted to discuss workload adjustments, and the response was pretty surface-level. They acknowledged it but nothing really changed, which is part of why I'm more deliberate now about creating a better environment for my team.

Q_PC.text: At my previous job, I mentioned to a couple of coworkers that I was seeing someone for anxiety — mostly just to be honest about why I was occasionally stepping out. The reactions were kind, but kind of quiet, like they weren't sure what to say. it made me realize how much the culture around you shapes whether people feel safe opening up at all.

Q_CA.text: Honestly, it's been mostly positive — being open has made me more approachable to colleagues who are struggling. There was some early hesitation about how it might look, but if anything it's strengthened my credibility as someone who takes wellbeing seriously.

Q_BH.text: It was at my previous job — I raised my anxiety and asked about adjusting my workload, and my manager just said "we all have stress" and moved on. No follow-up, no real acknowledgment that what I'd shared even mattered.

Q_SH.text: My current manager was great about it — when I mentioned I was in therapy and needed schedule flexibility, they just said "whatever works for you" and made it happen. No awkward follow-up questions, no change in how they treated me professionally.

Q_ID.text: Normalizing mental health conversations starts at the top — if leadership talks openly about therapy or burnout, it reduces the barrier for everyone else. Concrete benefits and manager training would go a long way too.

Q_AE.text: I just want to say that surveys like this matter — they signal that someone is paying attention. The more we measure and discuss mental health in tech, the harder it becomes to ignore, and that's how culture actually shifts.

Q_EC.text: I told my manager I needed to be hospitalized for depression. they were genuinely supportive -- arranged short-term leave without any pushback and checked in with me when I came back.

Q_CC.text: My coworkers were mostly kept out of it — I didn't share the details. A couple of close ones knew I was out for health reasons and just said to take care, which was honestly enough.

Q_CW.text: One coworker mentioned they were struggling with anxiety and weren't sure if they should tell HR. I shared a bit of my own experience and told them the process had been straightforward for me. They seemed relieved to hear it.

Q_PC.text: My previous workplace was different. I mentioned I'd dealt with depression to a couple of people I trusted, and the reactions were pretty mixed — mostly sympathetic, but a few didn't really know what to say and kind of went quiet.

Q_CA.text: It hasn't had a lasting negative impact, honestly. My employer handled it well and I came back without any real change in how I was treated. I don't think it held me back.

Q_SH.text: I was upfront with my manager about needing hospitalization, and they didn't make it complicated. HR got involved quickly, the leave was sorted with minimal back-and-forth, and when I returned there was a check-in to make sure I was settling in okay.

Q_ID.text: Training managers to respond appropriately is probably the most impactful thing -- my own experience shows that a single well-handled conversation can make a real difference. Beyond that, normalizing leave for mental health the same way physical illness is treated would go a long way.

Q_AE.text: The hospitalization was the hardest part, but honestly the aftermath was more manageable than I expected. I hope more people feel comfortable disclosing -- the stigma feels bigger than the reality, at least in my case.

Q_EC.text: I was hospitalized for depression and had to take time off of work. My employer was empathetic and asked if there was anything he or the company could do to help my recovery.

persona_portrait.narrative: This person is a tech worker who has faced serious mental health challenges, including a hospitalization for depression that required time away from work.
