persona_portrait.writing_style: Sentences are concise and declarative, with a calm, matter-of-fact tone. The writing is clear and moderately formal, with no hedging or emotional embellishment.

Q_EC.text: I brought it up with my manager mostly out of desperation. The reaction was sympathetic but kind of vague -- they suggested taking some time off and left it at that. It helped a little knowing they were aware, but honestly nothing about the environment actually changed

Q_CC.text: There was one colleague I trusted enough to be really honest with, and that conversation was genuinely different. She didn't just offer sympathy -- she told me flat out that the environment was the problem, not me. Hearing that from someone on the inside, it helped me stop second-guessing myself so much

Q_CW.text: Someone came to me a few months into what I'd call the worst stretch of that job. They were pretty clearly burnt out, and I think they picked me because they'd noticed I wasn't exactly thriving either. It felt less like a confession and more like two people finally admitting the same thing out loud.

Q_PE.text: At a previous job I did try to raise it once, more obliquely than I have since. My manager at the time basically reframed it as a productivity issue and suggested I look into time management. No follow-up, no resources offered. I left that job not long after, which probably tells you everything.

Q_PC.text: At that job the culture wasn't really one where people opened up, so I kept it pretty close to the chest. There was one person who noticed I seemed off and asked, and I gave a vague non-answer. They didn't push, which I think was mutual — neither of us wanted to go there.

Q_CA.text: Honestly it's hard to separate cause and effect. At the previous job, once I'd raised it I got the sense I was quietly categorized as someone who couldn't handle pressure. Whether that actually changed how I was treated or I just became more attuned to it, I'm not entirely sure.

Q_BH.text: The time management suggestion was the moment I knew it wasn't going to go anywhere useful. I'd tried to describe feeling like I was losing perspective on what was normal, and he pivoted almost immediately to talking about workload prioritisation. It felt like the actual thing I'd said just hadn't landed at all.

Q_SH.text: That conversation with my colleague was the one that actually helped. I hadn't planned to be as honest as I was, but she asked directly and I just... told her. She listened without trying to fix it, and then said something like "I don't think you're the problem here." No caveats, no suggestions to just take care of myself. It was pretty simple but it meant a lot at the time.

Q_ID.text: I think the biggest gap is between having policies on paper and actually building an environment where raising something doesn't carry a quiet cost. Managers need real training, not just a link to an EAP portal. And honestly, peer support -- informal, trusted -- probably does more than most formal programs ever will.

Q_AE.text: I just want to say that the colleague I mentioned -- the one who told me the environment was the problem -- probably kept me from leaving the industry entirely. I don't think she knew that at the time. Informal support like that is undersold, and I hope whoever reads these takes it seriously.

Q_EC.text: I told my manager I was struggling with depression and that my medication was affecting my concentration. Their response was basically to suggest I take more breaks and "try not to overthink things" -- which, honestly, felt pretty dismissive given what I'd just shared. Nothing formal was put in place, no referral to EAP or anything like that. I don't think they knew what to do with the information, so they just... didn't do much with it.

Q_CC.text: That was honestly a much better experience. A couple of close friends on my team already knew I was dealing with depression, and when I brought up that my meds were making things harder, they were genuinely supportive -- checking in, covering for me on rough days without making it a big deal. It felt like being seen in a way my manager just couldn't manage.

Q_CW.text: One of the same friends actually came to me not long after, which felt like the trust going both ways. They were dealing with anxiety and had been masking it pretty hard at work -- they said they felt like they could tell me because they knew I'd get it. I tried to just listen and not immediately problem-solve, which I think is what they needed. It was one of those conversations that reminded me why having people who actually know you on a team matters so much.

Q_PE.text: At a previous job I actually didn't disclose much at all -- I'd learned early on that the culture wasn't going to be receptive to it, so I kept things pretty surface level. The one time I did mention I was dealing with some health stuff affecting my focus, my manager nodded and moved on like I hadn't said anything. No follow-up, nothing. Honestly that experience is probably part of why I was at least willing to try being more open later, even if the result wasn't much better.

Q_PC.text: Previous coworkers were mostly just... colleagues, not people I'd have opened up to. The culture kind of set the tone for everyone -- it wasn't a place where that kind of conversation happened. There was one person I was friendlier with who I think suspected something was off, but it never went further than "you okay?" and I'd say yeah, fine. which honestly felt like the right call at the time.

Q_CA.text: It's hard to say definitively -- I don't think I've been passed over for anything I can point to directly. But there's a low-level awareness that it's out there now, at least with my manager, and I'd be lying if I said that never crosses my mind. I'm pretty careful about how much I bring it up in broader contexts, like in meetings or with people I don't know well. the peer support side has been genuinely positive for my ability to actually do my job, but the professional layer feels more like something I'm managing around than something that's been accommodated.

Q_BH.text: The one that stands out most is the conversation with my current manager -- the one where I mentioned the depression and the medication affecting my concentration. I'd picked what felt like a reasonable moment, kept it professional, gave them something concrete to work with. And the response was just... "take more breaks, try not to overthink it." I mean, I get that they probably didn't have training for this and didn't know what to say, but it still stings a bit to share something that took nerve and have it basically brushed aside. No follow-up the next day, no "hey how are you doing," nothing routed to HR or an EAP. It just dissolved into the workday like it hadn't happened. That's the part that stuck with me -- not even hostility, just a kind of blankness, like the information had nowhere to go.

Q_SH.text: The contrast with my coworkers is what made the manager thing harder to sit with, honestly. When I told my team friends what was going on -- the depression, the meds, the concentration stuff -- they didn't flinch or pivot to advice mode. One of them just said "okay, what do you need from us right now" and meant it. They covered for me on a day I was really struggling without announcing it or making it weird, just quietly redistributed some things so I could get through the afternoon. No performance of support, just actual support. it's the kind of thing that makes you realize how low the bar often is elsewhere -- they cleared it so easily because they were actually paying attention to me as a person, not just managing a situation.

Q_ID.text: Actual training for managers would go a long way -- not a one-hour module, but enough that someone knows what to do when an employee discloses something real. And honestly, normalizing peer support structures rather than routing everything through HR would help too. The informal networks are already doing a lot of the work; it'd be nice if the industry acknowledged that instead of pretending formal channels cover it.

Q_AE.text: I just want to say that the gap between formal support structures and what actually helps people day-to-day feels like the central problem -- and I'm not sure the industry has really reckoned with it yet. The conversations that helped me most weren't facilitated by anyone, weren't logged anywhere, didn't go through a portal. they just happened because I was lucky enough to be on a team with people who gave a damn. that shouldn't be luck.

Q_PE.text: At a previous job I went through a period of burnout and eventually told my manager I was struggling. His response was kind but fairly hands-off -- he acknowledged it, suggested I take a few days off, and left it at that. it helped in the short term, but there wasn't really any follow-through. still, the fact that he didn't make me feel small for saying something meant a lot at the time.

Q_PC.text: At a previous job I confided in a couple of coworkers when I was going through that stretch of burnout -- not in a big dramatic way, just over lunch one day. They were kind about it, asked a few thoughtful questions, though I could tell one of them wasn't quite sure what to say. honestly that's fine, I think just the willingness to listen is what matters most. Q_CA.text: Honestly, I don't think it's hurt me -- if anything, being open about it has deepened some of my working relationships in ways I didn't expect. there have been moments of uncertainty, wondering how it might be perceived, but my experience has mostly been that the people who matter responded with respect. I feel like it's made me a more trusted colleague, not a less credible one.

Q_BH.text: The closest thing I can point to is that previous job situation -- my manager acknowledged what I shared and suggested time off, but there was no check-in afterward, no conversation about whether anything had actually changed. it wasn't unkind, but it felt like the door opened and then quietly closed again. I think that kind of well-meaning but incomplete response can leave you feeling more alone than before.

Q_SH.text: The conversation with my current manager stands out. She didn't treat it as a problem to be managed -- she just listened, asked a few gentle questions, and then took concrete action by adjusting my workload. What made it feel genuinely supportive was the follow-through; she checked in the next week, unprompted. That consistency is honestly what turned it from a nice moment into real trust.

Q_ID.text: I think the biggest shift would be moving from reactive support — EAP programs that nobody knows how to access — to building cultures where mental health conversations are just normalized. Managers should be trained not to fix, but to listen. And honestly, follow-through matters as much as the initial response. A check-in the week after someone shares something vulnerable costs almost nothing and means everything.

Q_AE.text: I just want to say that surveys like this one feel meaningful -- the fact that someone is asking these questions at all signals that the conversation is shifting. Mental health in tech has been treated as a personal failing for too long, and I think the more people share honestly, the harder it becomes to keep pretending otherwise. I'm glad this work is happening.

We followed up with a more structured conversation about what accommodations might be helpful, and he helped connect me with some institutional resources I hadn't known were available.

Q_CW.text: A colleague approached me during a low-key moment -- after a team lunch, I think. They shared that they'd been managing some anxiety for a while and had recently started seeing someone. It wasn't a long conversation, but it felt significant. I tried to be present and not offer too much unsolicited advice. Honestly, I think they just needed to say it out loud to someone they trusted, and I was glad to be that person.

Q_PC.text: With previous coworkers, it was handled more carefully -- I didn't disclose anything specific about my diagnosis. There were a few moments where I mentioned being under some stress, and the responses were generally kind but pretty surface-level. I wasn't looking for deeper engagement from that group, and I think that came across. A couple of colleagues checked in periodically, which was appreciated, but the conversations stayed fairly light and I kept the details to myself.

Q_CA.text: Honestly, the impact has been pretty limited -- which I think is a direct result of how carefully the disclosure was handled. Because it wasn't shared beyond my manager, I haven't experienced anything that felt like professional consequences. If anything, having that one conversation opened up access to support I didn't know existed, which has probably helped me stay more consistent at work. I'm aware that outcome depends a lot on context, and I know not everyone is as fortunate with their management situation.

Q_SH.text: The context mattered a lot -- it was during an off-site event, in a quieter moment away from the usual office dynamic. That made it easier to speak more honestly than I might have otherwise. My manager listened without interrupting, didn't minimise what I was sharing, and was careful not to make it feel like a formal HR interaction. He followed up a few days later with some specific resources, which showed it hadn't just been acknowledged and forgotten. That follow-through was probably what made it feel genuinely well handled.

Q_ID.text: More than anything, I think it comes down to managers being genuinely prepared to have these conversations -- not just pointing people toward an EAP and moving on. The difference in my own experience was having a manager who listened well and followed through, and that's something that can be trained and cultivated. I'd also say that protecting people's privacy around disclosure matters enormously; knowing that sharing with one person won't ripple out to the whole organisation is what makes disclosure feel safe in the first place.

Q_AE.text: One thing the survey didn't quite capture is how much the timing and setting of a disclosure can shape the outcome -- it's not just about whether a workplace is "supportive" in the abstract, but whether there's ever a natural moment to have the conversation at all. I got lucky in that regard. I'd also say that the experience made me more attentive to creating those moments for others, which honestly feels like the most meaningful thing to have come out of it.

My disorder was not disclosed to anyone else at the company.

Q_EC.text: It was actually a really positive experience. I brought up that I'd been dealing with anxiety and my manager was genuinely supportive -- they encouraged me to look into the EAP and even helped me adjust my workload while I got things sorted. I didnt feel judged at all, which honestly made it so much easier to follow through with finding a therapist.

Q_CC.text: My coworkers have been really great about it too, honestly. I mentioned to a couple of close colleagues that I was going through some anxiety stuff and they were pretty understanding -- one of them actually opened up about their own experiences, which I wasn't expecting but made me feel way less alone. it kind of normalized the whole thing for me.

Q_CW.text: It was pretty organic actually -- we were just grabbing coffee and they mentioned they'd been struggling with burnout and had started seeing a therapist. I think they brought it up partly because I'd shared something first, which felt like a real moment of trust. I just listened and told them I thought it was great they were getting support. it was a genuinely good conversation.

Q_PE.text: My previous employer was actually pretty decent about it too. I brought up some stress-related stuff during a one-on-one and my manager listened without making it weird -- they pointed me toward HR and said to let them know if I needed any flexibility. it didn't go quite as deep as conversations I've had more recently, but I didn't feel dismissed either, which was the main thing.

Q_PC.text: Things were a bit more surface level with previous coworkers -- it wasn't really a culture where people talked openly about that stuff, so I kept it pretty vague. I mentioned I was dealing with some stress at one point and they were sympathetic enough, but it didn't go much deeper than "hope you feel better soon." not a bad reaction, just not as connected as what I have now.

Q_CA.text: Honestly, I don't think it's hurt me. If anything, being open about it has made me more approachable to colleagues and I think my manager respects that I take my wellbeing seriously. I've never felt passed over or treated differently because of it -- maybe I've been lucky with my workplace, but it's never felt like something I needed to hide to get ahead.

Q_SH.text: It was during a regular one-on-one with my manager -- I just brought it up directly, said I'd been dealing with anxiety and it was starting to affect my focus. They didn't flinch or get awkward about it, which I really appreciated. they asked what would help, we talked through some workload adjustments, and they followed up a week later just to check in. felt like a real conversation, not a box-ticking exercise.

Q_ID.text: Normalize it from the top down, honestly. If leadership talks openly about mental health and EAPs aren't just buried in an onboarding doc nobody reads, it changes the whole culture. I also think manager training is underrated -- my experience was good partly because my manager knew how to respond without making it weird, and not everyone gets that.

Q_AE.text: Just wanted to say this is a really valuable survey -- these conversations need to happen more and I'm glad someone's collecting this data. I feel pretty fortunate to work somewhere that takes mental health seriously, but I know that's not the norm and I think about that a lot. if this helps push things in the right direction, even a little, it's worth taking the time to fill out

Q_EC.text: I've had a few of these conversations, honestly. The most direct one was asking my manager to give me more positive feedback — I was upfront that it was part of how I manage my depression, and they were genuinely receptive, which made more difference than I expected. We also ended up co-creating a Slack channel for mental health discussions at work, so the culture around it has shifted pretty noticeably over time

Q_CC.text: The Slack channel has made a lot of those conversations happen more organically, which I think lowers the stakes. I've had coworkers open up to me after seeing me post there first — kind of a "oh, you too?" moment. Reactions have been mostly warm, occasionally a bit awkward, but never hostile. Honestly the channel has done more for normalising it than any one-on-one conversation I've had.

Q_CW.text: They came to me after seeing something I'd posted in the channel — just a low-key message about having a rough week, SAD kicking in hard. They messaged me privately to say they'd been dealing with something similar and hadn't really told anyone at work before. Honestly it felt like a real moment of trust. I mostly just listened and pointed them toward the EAP, which I don't think they knew existed. the conversation was pretty brief but I could tell it meant something to them to just have it acknowledged

Q_PE.text: That was a different era, tbh. I was earlier in my career and much less confident about naming what was going on with me. I mentioned burnout more than depression specifically, and my manager was sympathetic in a vague way — "take some time if you need it" — but nothing structural came of it. No follow-up, no resources offered. It wasn't hostile, just kind of... empty.

Q_PC.text: Didn't really open up much to coworkers at that job — I hadn't yet figured out how to talk about it myself, so I definitely wasn't bringing it to the people I sat next to. There was one person I was closer to who probably picked up that something was off, and I remember a pretty gentle "you doing okay?" conversation that I gave a pretty non-answer to. No one was unkind about it, I just wasn't ready to be honest yet, even with myself.

Q_CA.text: It's hard to disentangle cleanly. At my current job, being open about it has honestly been a net positive — I think people see me as someone safe to talk to, and I've taken on a bit of an informal advocacy role that I actually find meaningful. Earlier in my career I wonder if there were quieter costs I couldn't see at the time, opportunities or credibility I didn't get, but nothing I can point to directly. So: mixed, probably, with the balance tipping positive now.

Q_BH.text: The previous employer one, really. It wasn't dramatic — no one said anything cruel or explicitly dismissive — which almost made it harder to process at the time. I mentioned I was struggling, my manager said the right-sounding words, and then absolutely nothing changed. No check-in the following week, no "hey, did you look into that EAP?" — I'm not even sure they knew what resources existed. It just got absorbed and forgotten, and I was left feeling like I'd taken a risk for nothing. the absence of follow-through was the thing, more than anything that was actually said.

Q_SH.text: My current manager, no question. When I asked for more positive feedback and explained it was tied to how I manage my depression, they didn't flinch or get weird about it — they just said "okay, that's useful to know, I can do that." And then they actually did it. That sounds small but it genuinely wasn't. The follow-through was what made it land. And then when the Slack channel idea came up, they were actively enthusiastic rather than just tolerating it — helped get it off the ground, checked in on how it was going. it didn't feel like accommodation, it felt like they actually gave a damn.

Q_ID.text: Normalize it structurally, not just rhetorically — an EAP buried in an onboarding doc nobody reads isn't support, it's liability coverage. Managers need actual training, not a one-hour module they forget by lunch. And honestly, create low-stakes venues for people to talk before things become a crisis. that doesn't have to be expensive or complicated, it just has to be real.

Q_AE.text: I guess the main thing I'd add is that a lot of what I've described — the Slack channel, the manager conversations — happened because I pushed for it, and I'm aware that takes a certain amount of energy and privilege that not everyone has when they're already struggling. the structural stuff matters precisely because it shouldn't require one proactive person to bootstrap it every time. Also, for what it's worth: I had a pretty serious depressive episode before I got into tech, and I think that history actually made me more deliberate about building the kind of workplace culture I wish I'd had access to earlier. So there's something to be said for the long game, even if it's a slow one.

Q_EC.text: I actually brought it up myself -- told my manager I was dealing with anxiety and had started therapy. Their reaction was genuinely good. they adjusted my meeting load for a few weeks and made it clear I could take time without it affecting my performance review. Honestly it was the conversation that made me realize how much environment matters -- and it shaped how I show up for my own team now.

Q_CC.text: A few coworkers have come to me after I've mentioned my anxiety in team settings -- like, openly said "me too" in a way they clearly hadn't felt safe doing before. One person told me they'd been struggling for two years and never said anything. that conversation hit me hard. The reactions have been mostly relief, honestly -- people seem to appreciate that someone in a leadership role isn't pretending everything is fine all the time.

Q_CW.text: One conversation that stays with me -- a direct report came to my office and closed the door, which already told me something. They'd been having panic attacks before standup every morning for months. hadn't told anyone. They said they came to me because of something I'd mentioned offhandedly in a team retro about my own anxiety. That was the moment I understood that modeling vulnerability isn't just feel-good leadership -- it actually opens doors that would otherwise stay shut.

Q_PE.text: The previous place was a different story. I brought up burnout once -- framed it carefully, kept it vague -- and my manager basically said "yeah, this time of year is hard for everyone" and moved on. No follow-up, no adjustment, nothing. I dont think they knew what to do with it. And honestly, that experience is a big part of why I do things differently now -- I remember exactly how it felt to say something real and watch it just... evaporate.

Q_PC.text: At the old job, I kept it pretty close to the chest -- I didn't have the same sense that it was safe to be open. I mentioned stress once to a coworker I was friendly with and they were kind about it, said something like "yeah same, it's brutal here." But it stayed surface level. nobody really went deeper than that, and I didn't push it either. the culture just wasn't one where you'd go further -- you'd have a quick commiseration and then both go back to pretending you were fine.

Q_CA.text: Honestly, it's been net positive -- at least where I am now. Being open about my anxiety has made me a more trusted manager, I think. People come to me. they feel like they can be real, and that changes everything about how a team functions. The earlier job is where it felt riskier -- I kept things vague for a reason -- but even there, I don't think it actively cost me anything. I was careful enough. The bigger career impact has been the positive one: it's become a genuine part of how I lead, and that's opened doors, not closed them.

Q_BH.text: It was during a stretch where I was genuinely running on empty -- too many competing priorities, a team restructure, and some stuff going on at home. I'd thought carefully about how to raise it, kept it professional, didn't make it dramatic. Just said I was feeling burned out and wanted to talk about workload. My manager nodded, said something sympathetic about the quarter being tough for everyone, and then pivoted straight into a project update. that was it. No check-in afterward, no adjustment, no "let's revisit this." I don't think it was malicious -- I think they just had no idea what to do with the information. But the effect was the same either way: I learned to stop bringing it up there.

Q_SH.text: The current job -- that conversation was different from the start. I'd asked for thirty minutes with my manager, came in prepared to justify myself, and she just... didn't make me do that. She listened, asked a couple of real questions about what was actually making things hard, and within the same week had moved two recurring meetings off my calendar. She also said explicitly that this wouldn't factor into my review -- which sounds like a small thing but its not, that's the thing people are actually scared of. She checked in two weeks later, not in a big way, just a quick "how's the load feeling?" and meant it. the whole thing took maybe forty minutes total and it genuinely changed how I thought about what good management looks like. I've basically tried to replicate that conversation a dozen times since, from the other side of the table.

Q_ID.text: The biggest lever for me is leadership behavior -- not policy, behavior. You can have an EAP and a mental health day policy and still have a culture where nobody uses them, because the people at the top never model it. Managers need real training -- not "here's how to refer someone to HR" training, but how to actually have the conversation and not just nod and pivot. And honestly, the performance review piece needs to be addressed out loud, repeatedly, because that fear is what keeps most people quiet. its not a small thing.

Q_AE.text: I just want to say -- I think surveys like this matter, and I hope the data actually gets used. There's a lot of research that sits in a drawer. The experiences people are sharing here are real, and the patterns are probably pretty consistent: leadership behavior is the variable, policy is mostly theater without it. if I could flag one thing I didn't get to say clearly elsewhere, it's that middle managers are the under-resourced piece of this. Senior leaders get the mental health keynotes. Individual contributors get the EAP link. The people actually fielding the hard conversations at 4pm on a Tuesday -- the team leads, the senior ICs who've become informal counselors, the managers with no training and a full sprint board -- they're doing the heaviest lifting with the least support. That's where I'd focus if I were designing an intervention.

Q_ID.text: Training managers to respond well is probably the single highest-leverage thing -- a lot of the harm I've seen (and experienced) comes not from bad policy but from individual responses that inadvertently shut conversations down. Beyond that, normalizing mental health the same way physical health is normalized would help: most people don't hesitate to say they have a doctor's appointment, and that same ease should extend to therapy. EAPs are underutilized largely because people dont know they exist or trust them.

Q_AE.text: One thing the survey doesn't quite capture is how much the cumulative effect of small, low-key interactions matters -- not just the big conversations. The colleague check-ins, a manager who doesn't make it weird, an EAP that actually works: none of those are dramatic, but together they create an environment where getting support feels like a reasonable option rather than a risk.

Q_EC.text: My manager was genuinely kind about it, which I appreciated -- but it stopped at "let us know if you need anything." nothing actually changed. No formal accommodations, no follow-up. Good intentions, pretty hollow in practice.

Q_CC.text: A couple of colleagues were surprised but genuinely decent about it. One told me she'd had similar experiences, which I honestly didn't expect. Felt more real than the management conversation -- like they weren't just reading from a script

Q_CW.text: One colleague -- the same one I mentioned -- told me she'd been dealing with anxiety for years but never felt safe saying anything. My disclosure kind of opened the door. She wasn't looking for advice, just wanted someone to know. I mostly listened.

Q_PC.text: Honestly similar to my current team -- a bit of surprise, then real warmth. One person said they'd had no idea and seemed to genuinely care. Nobody made it weird.

Q_CA.text: Honestly, hard to say for certain. I don't think it's cost me anything concrete -- no promotions I can point to and say "that was it." But I'm aware it's in the room now, and I cant fully unknow that.

Q_BH.text: The management response is the clearest example. Kind words up front, then nothing. No check-in a week later, no actual process change, just a sort of mutual agreement to move on. I raised it again a few months in and got essentially the same response. good intentions dont really land when theres no follow-through.

Q_SH.text: The colleagues, genuinely. No fanfare, no awkward HR-speak -- just people treating it like normal information. One said "that makes sense, actually" and moved on. That mattered more than I expected. The bar wasn't high, but they cleared it.

Q_ID.text: Stop treating disclosure as the finish line. Acknowledgement is easy -- follow-through is the part that actually costs something. Real support means process, not just a kind word and a closed door. Train managers, not just on empathy, but on what to actually do next.

Q_AE.text: The gap between stated values and actual practice is real and pretty common from what I can tell -- not unique to my workplace. I disclosed, it was handled warmly and then not at all. I don't regret being open, but I'd think harder about it in a different environment. That's probably the most useful thing I can add.

Q_EC.text: I told my manager about my depression and postpartum history pretty early on. She was professional about it -- adjusted my schedule during a rough patch and connected me with the EAP. No drama, just practical.

Q_CC.text: A few coworkers know -- I brought it up casually, not as a big disclosure moment. Reactions were fine, mostly just "thanks for sharing" energy. No one made it weird, which honestly was all I needed.

Q_CW.text: One of my coworkers pulled me aside after a team meeting -- said they'd been dealing with anxiety for a while and were considering asking for accommodations. I think they came to me because they knew I'd been open about my own stuff. I just listened, shared what the EAP process looked like, and told them it was worth asking.

Q_PE.text: A previous manager was less receptive -- I mentioned I was dealing with depression and the response was basically "let us know if you need time off." Nothing proactive, no EAP referral, no follow-up. it was fine but pretty hollow compared to what I have now.

Q_PC.text: At a previous job, a couple of coworkers knew -- I mentioned my depression during a rough stretch and they were sympathetic but didn't really know what to do with it. mostly just "hope you feel better" stuff. Supportive enough, but surface level.

Q_CA.text: Honestly, not dramatically. There was a period at the previous job where I wondered if being open had quietly cost me a project assignment, but I can't prove that. Where I am now, it hasn't hurt me as far as I can tell.

Q_BH.text: It was the previous job. I'd flagged that I was struggling with depression and my manager acknowledged it once, briefly, then never brought it up again. No check-ins, no EAP mention -- just radio silence. I had to manage it entirely on my own.

Q_SH.text: That was my current employer. I disclosed my depression and postpartum history early on, my manager adjusted my schedule without making it a thing and connected me with the EAP. She followed up a few weeks later to check in. it felt like they actually had a system for it, not just goodwill.

Q_ID.text: More proactive EAP promotion -- most people dont know what's available until they're already in crisis. Managers should get actual training, not just a one-hour module. And normalize the check-in conversation, so employees aren't always the ones who have to raise it first.

Q_AE.text: The substance use piece doesn't really fit neatly into most survey questions -- for me it was tied directly to stress and an abusive relationship, not separate from mental health. I think surveys like this undercount that overlap. it's all connected.

Q_PE.text: My previous employer was actually pretty decent about it too. I mentioned I was going through a rough patch and they pointed me toward HR without making it weird.

Q_SH.text: My manager at my current job was genuinely great about it. they listened, didn't make it a big thing, and got me EAP info the same day -- honestly couldn't have asked for more.

Q_ID.text: More open conversations from leadership would help a lot. if managers normalize talking about mental health it makes it easier for everyone. EAPs are great but people need to actually know they exist

Q_EC.text: I spent some time gauging my manager before saying anything — trying to get a read on how they'd likely respond before committing to disclosure. When I did bring up the depression and anxiety, they were pretty measured about it, didn't push for details I wasn't ready to share. we landed on some informal schedule flexibility for harder days, which has honestly helped. I'm still not entirely sure what formal accommodations would make the most difference, but having that awareness there has taken some pressure off.

Q_CC.text: With coworkers its been more reciprocal, honestly. I have a couple of colleagues who disclosed their own experiences to me first, which made opening up feel much lower-stakes — once I knew they were carrying similar things, saying something myself felt like the natural response. The reactions have been pretty good. More solidarity than sympathy, which is what I'd actually prefer.

Q_CW.text: One colleague brought it up pretty casually -- mentioned they'd been dealing with anxiety for a while and had started seeing someone. I think they weren't necessarily looking for a specific response, just putting it out there. it ended up opening a door for me too, which I don't think either of us really anticipated going in.

Q_PE.text: I didn't, really. The environment wasn't one where I felt comfortable testing the waters — there was nothing in how my manager operated that suggested it would land well, so I kept it to myself. in hindsight I think that was the right call, though it did make some stretches harder to get through than they needed to be.

Q_PC.text: With previous coworkers I kept things pretty close to the chest — there wasnt really the kind of mutual openness that would've made disclosure feel safe. I shared a little with one person I was closer to, and they were fine about it, kind about it even. But I never felt like the culture there made that kind of thing easy, so mostly I didn't go there.

Q_CA.text: It's hard to fully separate cause and effect, honestly. I don't think it's cost me anything concrete — no missed promotions I can point to, no visible shift in how I'm treated. But there's always some background uncertainty about whether being open carries a slow, invisible toll that I just can't measure. I try not to let that anxiety drive me toward secrecy, but I'd be overstating my confidence if I said I was sure it hadn't affected anything.

Q_BH.text: The previous employer situation is what comes to mind, even though I never fully disclosed — there was a point where I was clearly struggling and my manager at the time made a comment about needing people to "stay switched on" during a difficult stretch. It wasn't directed at me specifically, but it made it pretty clear where the bar was. I don't think they even realized how it landed. That was enough to confirm I'd made the right call staying quiet, but it also made those months harder than they needed to be, knowing support wasn't something I could realistically reach for.

Q_SH.text: The conversation with my current manager is the clearest example. I'd been watching for a while — picking up on how they talked about workload and stress with the rest of the team — before I said anything. When I finally did bring it up, they didn't overcorrect in either direction, didn't make it a big moment or brush past it awkwardly. they just took it in and asked what would actually help. The schedule flexibility we landed on wasn't a formal accommodation, more of a quiet understanding, but it came from them genuinely asking rather than offering something generic. I think what made it work was that they didn't treat it as a problem to solve on the spot — more like information they were willing to hold carefully. that kind of response is harder to come by than it should be.

Q_ID.text: The culture matters more than formal programs, I think. Employers can put policies in place, but if managers aren't modeling openness — or if disclosure still carries implicit risk — those resources won't reach the people who need them most. the peer-level stuff, where colleagues actually feel safe being honest with each other, is honestly where it seems to make the most difference.

Q_AE.text: One thing I don't think the survey quite captured is how much of this happens in the informal gaps — the conversations that aren't with HR or a manager, but with a colleague over coffee where something just comes out. That's where a lot of the actual support I've experienced has lived. the formal infrastructure matters, but it often just isn't where people find each other.

Q_AE.text: Mental health in tech isn't just a benefits problem -- it's a culture problem. you can have all the policies in the world but if managers dont know how to respond when someone's actually struggling, none of it matters.

Q_EC.text: My manager was great, honestly -- I told him I was struggling with depression after losing someone close, and he just said take whatever time you need. pto was already on the table. he also pointed me to our EAP which I actually used, and it helped a lot.

Q_CC.text: Pretty open with a few close colleagues, they were supportive. one of my reports actually came to me after I shared a bit about my own stuff, which felt like it mattered -- like it gave them permission to bring things up too.

Q_CW.text: One of my reports came by after a team meeting, said they'd been dealing with anxiety and weren't sure they could keep up with the workload. honestly it was a pretty vulnerable thing to share. we figured out a plan together -- adjusted some deadlines, I pointed them to the EAP. they're doing a lot better now.

Q_PE.text: Different vibe at my last company tbh -- I didn't really bring it up directly, just asked for some flexibility during a hard stretch. my manager said sure but it kind of stopped there. no EAP mention, no follow-up. it was fine, just not what I have now.

Q_PC.text: Pretty similar story -- I had one or two people I trusted there, shared a little, they were kind but it didn't go deep. no one really knew what to do with it beyond just saying "hang in there." supportive enough I guess but not the same culture I have now where people actually follow up

Q_CA.text: Honestly, I think it's helped more than hurt -- at least where I am now. Being open about my own stuff has made me a better manager and I think my team trusts me more for it. I haven't felt any professional blowback, which I know isn't everyone's experience.

Q_BH.text: At my previous company, when I asked for some flexibility during a hard personal stretch -- that was it really. my manager said yes to the schedule change but never checked back in, no mention of any resources, no follow-up conversation. it wasn't hostile, just kind of hollow. like the box got ticked and we moved on.

Q_SH.text: My current manager honestly nailed it -- when I told him what I was going through, he didn't make it weird or clinical. just said "whatever you need" and meant it. followed up the next week without me having to ask, which made a real difference. and pointing me to the EAP wasn't just a checkbox thing, he actually asked later if I'd found it useful.

Q_ID.text: More visibility and less performative wellness stuff. the real shift happens when managers are actually trained to have these conversations, not just handed a flyer about an EAP they never mention again. I've seen what it looks like when it's done right -- it's not complicated, it's just consistency and follow-through. celebrity blogs and public figures talking about their own struggles help too, normalizes it before it ever gets to the workplace.

Q_AE.text: Just that I think peer support programs are underrated -- trained colleagues who can have that first conversation before it ever reaches hr or a formal channel. I've seen it work. and honestly the more managers talk openly about their own mental health, the faster the culture shifts. it compounds.

Managers should actually be trained to have these conversations, not just handed a one-pager. Q_EC.text: When I first brought it up with my manager, I was honestly a little nervous -- even knowing our company's culture, there's always that moment of vulnerability before you speak. She was incredibly receptive, asked thoughtful follow-up questions (not in an intrusive way, more like she genuinely wanted to understand what I needed), and within a week we'd adjusted my schedule to include protected focus time during my highest-anxiety hours. She also pointed me toward our EAP, which I hadn't fully explored yet, and that ended up being really valuable.

Q_CC.text: A few coworkers have actually opened up to me in return after I shared -- which I didn't expect but honestly made it feel so worth it. We have a mental health Slack channel at work, and a lot of the deeper conversations have happened there, which makes it feel a bit lower-stakes than face-to-face. The reactions have been overwhelmingly warm; one colleague told me my being open about anxiety made it easier for her to ask for accommodations she'd been putting off for months.

Q_CW.text: One that's stayed with me was with a colleague on my team who came to me after seeing something I'd posted in our mental health Slack channel. She told me she'd been managing anxiety for years but had never mentioned it at work because she assumed it would affect how people saw her professionally -- which, honestly, I totally understood. We ended up talking for about an hour (over coffee, not a formal thing), and what struck me most was how relieved she seemed just to say it out loud to someone at work. She did eventually ask our manager for some scheduling flexibility, and it was granted without any friction.

Q_PC.text: The environment at my previous job was pretty different -- mental health wasn't really part of the culture the way it is now, so I was a lot more guarded about sharing. I did mention to one close colleague that I was going through a rough patch with anxiety, and she was kind about it personally, though I could tell she wasn't quite sure what to say. the broader team dynamics made it feel risky to be more open, which is honestly part of why the contrast with my current workplace feels so significant.

Q_CA.text: Honestly, at my current company it hasn't -- if anything, being open about it has made me more effective because I stopped burning energy on concealment and started actually advocating for what I need to do good work. I won't pretend there weren't moments early in my career where I worried it might count against me, but those fears didn't materialize here. the culture really does make the difference.

Q_BH.text: At my previous job, I made the mistake of mentioning my anxiety to a manager during a check-in -- I'd framed it as context for why I was requesting a deadline extension. His response was essentially to tell me to "keep it separate from work," and he moved on pretty quickly (no follow-up, no acknowledgment that anything had been said). It wasn't hostile, but the dismissiveness stung, and it confirmed what I'd sensed about the culture there: mental health was something you managed privately, not something the workplace had any role in supporting.

Q_SH.text: My current manager's response is honestly the gold standard for what this can look like -- when I brought up my anxiety and what I needed, she treated it as a practical problem to solve together rather than an awkward disclosure to get past. the scheduling adjustment happened fast, the EAP referral came with a personal note about which services she'd heard good things about, and she checked in (without making it a big deal) over the following few weeks to see if things were actually working. what made it feel genuinely supportive rather than just procedurally correct was that she remembered specifics in later conversations -- it wasn't a one-time checkbox, it was the start of an ongoing dialogue.

Q_ID.text: More than anything, I think normalization has to start at the top -- when leadership talks openly about mental health (not just in a wellness-month email blast, but in real conversations), it changes what feels permissible for everyone below them. Practically speaking, that means training managers to respond well when someone discloses, making EAPs actually accessible rather than a buried link in an HR portal, and building in structural accommodations like flexible scheduling that don't require an employee to justify themselves at length. honestly the thing that's made the biggest difference in my own experience is just having a manager who knew what to do -- that doesn't happen by accident, it happens because companies invest in it.

Q_AE.text: I've been really glad to fill this out -- surveys like this feel meaningful when you're someone who's benefited so much from a workplace that got this right, and I think the data they generate actually matters. One thing I didn't get to say explicitly anywhere is how much peer-to-peer culture shapes this, not just top-down policy. Our mental health Slack channel wasn't mandated by HR; a few employees just started it, and it grew because people found real value in it. that kind of organic community is hard to manufacture but worth fostering, and I'd love to see more companies create the conditions for it to emerge. thanks for doing this research.

Q_EC.text: I did raise some things with my manager a while back — not in great detail, but enough to ask for some flexibility around deadlines during a rough stretch. the reaction was decent, more neutral than supportive I'd say, but nothing was actively made worse. I've had far more damaging experiences in other contexts, so I kind of set my expectations accordingly going in.

Q_CC.text: Honestly, most of my conversations have been more on the listening end than the disclosing end — a coworker has been going through a difficult stretch with anxiety and depression, and I've tried to be someone they can talk to without it feeling like a HR situation. I've shared a little of my own history to make the space feel less one-sided, but carefully, and only what felt useful rather than cathartic for me. I'm pretty guarded about how much I put out there at work, so it stays measured.

Q_CW.text: It started gradually — they'd mention being tired or overwhelmed in passing, and over a few weeks those asides became more direct. Eventually they told me they were struggling with anxiety and depression and were finding it hard to keep up. There was a lot of worry about how it might affect their standing on the team, which I understood deeply, even if I didn't say exactly why. We've talked a few times since then, and I think just having somewhere to put it that isn't a formal channel has helped them somewhat.

Q_PE.text: The one experience I'd describe as genuinely significant happened during my PhD — not a tech job, but it shaped everything that came after. I disclosed some mental health difficulties to my supervisor and it went badly in ways that were hard to recover from: the dynamic shifted, expectations changed, and I came away with a lasting lesson about the gap between what institutions say about support and what actually happens. I don't want to be overly dramatic about it, but it's honestly why I'm so measured about disclosure now — that experience set the baseline.

Q_PC.text: In the same PhD context, I was pretty closed off after things went sideways with my supervisor — I didn't really want to risk compounding the situation by having it spread further. A couple of people I was close to picked up that something was wrong, and I gave vague answers, something like "things are complicated right now." they were kind about it, which honestly made the contrast with the institutional response feel sharper rather than better. I didn't elaborate much then, and I still don't, really.

Q_CA.text: It's hard to separate the direct career effects from the more diffuse ones — I haven't been formally penalised as far as I know, but the PhD experience left me with a strong prior that disclosure changes how people see you, and I've managed my choices accordingly ever since. honestly that caution is itself a kind of career effect, shaping what I say and to whom without anyone explicitly making it so.

Q_BH.text: The context was a PhD environment where your supervisor has outsized control over your trajectory. I'd been managing significant anxiety and what I'd now recognize as depression, and reached a point where I felt I needed to say something. The response wasn't overtly hostile, but the dynamic shifted almost immediately — comments about "commitment" surfaced that hadn't before, and the warmth that had been there just... wasn't. Whatever formal support structures existed were never mentioned. It became pretty clear that having said anything had been a mistake in that particular relationship.

Q_SH.text: The closest I can point to is my current manager's response — it wasn't warm, exactly, but nothing shifted afterward, and the flexibility I'd asked for was quietly accommodated without it becoming A Thing. I'm aware that "nothing bad happened" is a pretty low bar, but given my history it honestly registered as a meaningful positive. The peer conversations I've been part of, on both ends, have felt more genuinely supportive — but I think those operate by different rules than institutional responses, and I try not to conflate them.

Q_ID.text: The most meaningful change would be closing the gap between what organisations say about mental health support and what actually happens when someone uses it. Policies matter less than the specific response of the specific manager in the moment, and right now there's no obvious way to hold those responses accountable. Training helps at the margins, but what would really shift things is making it demonstrably safe to disclose — not just technically protected, but actually without consequence in practice. Honestly, some of the most effective support I've seen has come from peer-level conversations rather than anything institutional, and I think there's something worth building on there rather than routing everything through HR.

Q_AE.text: I suppose the thing I'd add is that this survey format, with its focus on individual conversations and events, maybe undersells how much the accumulation of smaller signals matters — the offhand comments, the way a topic gets changed, the absence of follow-up. Those aren't discrete incidents to describe, but they're part of how people calibrate their sense of safety at work over time. I don't have a tidy recommendation attached to that, just the observation that the texture of a culture is harder to capture than its policies, and probably more predictive of whether someone actually discloses.

Q_EC.text: Told my manager pretty early on. Said I have Tourette's, here's what that looks like. They said okay, thanks for telling me. No action taken -- I wasn't asking for anything, so.

Q_CC.text: Same deal, basically. I tell people before they notice something. "Just so you know, I have Tourette's." Most say oh okay, cool, thanks for telling me. A few ask questions. that's fine, I'd rather that than the staring.

Q_CW.text: One person mentioned they were dealing with anxiety. Just said they were having a rough time. I said, yeah, that's hard. That was kind of it.

Q_PE.text: Same approach. Mentioned it upfront, told them what Tourette's looks like in practice. They were fine with it. Nothing came of it -- didn't need anything to.

Q_PC.text: Pretty much the same as now. I tell people early. "I have Tourette's, here's what you might notice." Usually they just say thanks for letting me know. Sometimes a few questions. no big drama.

Q_CA.text: Not much, honestly. I control when people find out, so it hasn't really been used against me. I don't ask for accommodations, so theres nothing to flag.

Q_BH.text: One manager, years back. Told them about the Tourette's and they kind of went quiet, then started treating me differently. More careful around me. Like I'd suddenly become fragile. I hadn't asked for that.

Q_SH.text: Most of them, actually. Tell people, they say okay, we move on. That's all I want.

Q_ID.text: More education probably. People dont know what to do when someone discloses, so they either overcorrect or go quiet. just... act normal.

Q_AE.text: Just that the focus tends to be on support and accommodations -- which is fine, but some people just want to be treated normally. That's the thing nobody asks about.
